News.title: 'Let football fans have a pint — it’s time to scrap this outdated drinking in stands ban'
News.content:
The ban on drinking alcohol in the stands is horribly outdated.

And it is great that the United Kingdom has a real football fan as a Prime Minister who is ready to change the law which is so unfair on supporters. Everton fan Andy Burnham is right to speak up and push for supporters to be able to enjoy a pint within sight of the pitch.

You can have a drink at cricket and it is time football fans were allowed to do the same. Times change and it is wrong for football fans to be treated as second class citizens.

In my experience, if you treat people as grown ups - then they will behave like adults. Of course we should be sensitive. Just as we have been in the reintroduction of safe standing. Do it sensibly and, as Burnham suggests, even on a trial basis. Fans will prove him right.

‌



View 2 Images Football's drinking restrictions date back to the hooliganism of the 1980s (Image: PA)

Harry Kane defends Declan Rice after Arsenal star explained England drop out READ MORE :

Harvey Elliott enduring second loan nightmare as Liverpool star branded 'overweight' READ MORE :

No one can forget the booze and drug fuelled scenes outside Wembley ahead of the Euros final in 2021. It has to be policed but being able to drink in your seat would actually ease the binge drinking culture which exists at football games before and at half time.

We have moved on from the bad old days of hooliganism in the 1980s which led to this ban in the first place. Football has a new generation of fans and stadiums are generally safer, there is a different vibe within grounds and it is time to move on.

The other compelling argument which emerged in Tracey Crouch’s independent review into football back in 2021 was that League Two and National League clubs lose up to an estimated £100,000-per-year in sales because of the ban.

‌



This is an important change for all levels of the game - and it is great that we have a PM who understands and respects football fans.

News.title: Tories slammed for benefits pre-loaded cards scheme - 'built on stigma, not solutions'
News.content:
Tories slammed for benefits pre-loaded cards scheme - 'built on stigma, not solutions'

A similar model of pre-paid cards was proposed by ex-Tory Work and Pensions Secretary Iain Duncan Smith during the austerity years - but it was eventually dropped

View 2 Images Tory chief Kemi Badenoch has been slammed for 'unworkable' proposals (Image: Getty Images)

Kemi Badenoch's Tories have been slammed for "unworkable" plans to give some people on benefits pre-loaded cards - rather than cash.

‌



The party faces accusations the scheme is "built on stigma" with proposals to ban long-term unemployed people using the cards from spending on alcohol, cigarettes, and gambling.

‌



A similar model of pre-paid cards was proposed by ex-Tory Work and Pensions Secretary Iain Duncan Smith during the austerity years - but it was eventually dropped.

‌



A Labour Party spokesman said: "The Conservatives had 14 years to fix our welfare system but they completely failed to make meaningful reforms.

"Now they are proposing an unworkable new card scheme, which does nothing to tackle the numbers of people their system left signed off and written off."

Under Tory plans those on the Universal Credit standard allowance - which stands at £424.90 a month for single people over the age of 25 - face their payments being slashed after six months.

‌



The party said those who have not contributed to the welfare system through their taxes will see their benefits cut at this point by almost a third to a 70% rate of the allowance.

View 2 Images Ex-Tory Work and Pensions Secretary Iain Duncan Smith proposed a similar scheme during the austerity years - but it was eventually dropped (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Those individuals would then have their payments loaded on a "back to work" pre-payment card, which would ban spending on cigarettes, alcohol, betting and cash withdrawals.

‌



The Conservatives said those already working and claiming Universal Credit to top-up their low-income will be exempt along with those with health conditions.

Tory chief Kemi Badenoch said: "Some will say this is unfair on people claiming benefits. What is unfair is a system where someone who can work chooses not to and earns more from benefits than someone in a job."

But Amnesty International UK's Jen Clark said: "These proposals are built on stigma, not solutions. You cannot solve poverty by making people poorer."

‌



She added: "Our social security system is already consciously cruel, often treating people without basic dignity. We know that the existing sanctions system is driving people into debt, removing food from children's tables and placing people at risk of homelessness.

"Politicians talking about restricting what people can buy on social security may grab headlines, but it does nothing to address the reality that millions of people are already struggling just to get by."

Helen Barnard of anti-poverty charity Trussell said the proposals were "deeply misguided" .

‌



She said: "Universal Credit already falls well short of what people need to afford the essentials like food and heating, forcing people across the UK to the doors of food banks. We see people's health being damaged and their ability to find and maintain work undermined by the severe hardship so many are facing."

"The Conservatives introduced Universal Credit to make work pay, and there are already stringent conditions applied within our social security system and a strong focus on ensuring people look for work whenever they are able to.

"But if you're struggling to afford food and rent, childcare or the bus fare to an interview - then finding and keeping a job becomes harder not easier. Cutting support would only make things worse."

‌



It comes as separate research from the Child Poverty Action Group (CPAG) found almost half of parents are finding it hard to manage their budgets in the past year due to the cost of living crisis.

They found 49% of struggling families are also struggling to spend quality time together - rising to 56% of households in receipt of Universal Credit.

Among parents struggling to manage, CPAG also said 28% said they could not afford swimming lessons for children, and one in four struggled to afford visiting a sports club.

Article continues below

Director of policy at Child Poverty Action Group Sara Ogilvie said: "The cost of living is busting family budgets, undermining family life and increasing the risk of social isolation for kids.

"This cost-of-living government can and must restore investment in child benefit in the forthcoming Budget so that all parents are able to give their children a fair shot at success."

News.title: Missing American, 46, found dead abroad in padlocked room with limbs bound
News.content:
Missing American, 46, found dead abroad in padlocked room with limbs bound

Tamir Nadav, 46, had been missing for more than two weeks when cops found him locked in a room with his hands and feet bound at his home in Maringá, Brazil

View 2 Images Tamir Nadav had not been heard from in weeks (Image: Jam Press)

A missing man has been found dead inside a padlocked room with his hands and feet bound after neighbours reported a foul smell.

‌



American Tamir Nadav, 46, had not been seen for more than two weeks before cops made the horrific discovery at his home in Maringá, Brazil.

‌



On entering his home on Friday officers found food still sitting on the table, the television switched on and belongings scattered across the floor.

‌



Tamir’s home office had been “completely ransacked” while his computer was still switched on upstairs. Officers then found a room which had been secured with a padlock and a yellow liquid on the floor outside.

View 2 Images Tamir Nadav worked in games development (Image: Jam Press)

After breaking down the door, officers found Tamir’s body inside with his hands and feet bound with adhesive tape. His identity was confirmed through dental records yesterday.

‌



Tamir, originally from New York, moved to Brazil for work in 2021. He worked in online game development and had previously worked for companies in San Francisco, Montreal, Rio de Janeiro and Maringá.

Investigators are now trying to establish when he died and determine his cause of death.

Police chief Adriano Garcia said a man and woman who had been living with Tamir are suspected of involvement in his death. Their names have not been released and police have requested the man’s pre-trial detention.

‌



Investigators allege the couple made several purchases in Maringá using Tamir’s money on September 1. These allegedly included two watches worth a combined BRL 10,000 (£1,473).

Two days later, a friend visited Tamir’s home and was met by the couple, whom she did not know. They allegedly told her Tamir had travelled to São Paulo. Suspicious, she alerted authorities and filed a missing person report.

She returned to the property with another friend on Friday but nobody answered the door. Neighbours reportedly told the women the lights had been on for several days despite nobody appearing to be inside. They also noticed a strong smell coming from the property.

Article continues below

Police believe the couple fled the house on September 3 after Tamir’s friend visited. The untouched food was among the clues investigators said suggested those inside had left suddenly. Garcia said: “Presumably because they were caught off guard, they left the house and never returned.”

Tamir’s friend Luiza di Pietro told local media: “He was the most Brazilian gringo, you know? He absolutely loved our country. He was someone who had really learned Portuguese – he spoke it very well and understood it perfectly. Wherever he went, he embraced Brazilian culture.”

Police believe the motive for Tamir’s death was financial. The investigation continues.

News.title: Andy Burnham says Budget needs to 'get balance right' on tax hikes
News.content:
Andy Burnham says Budget needs to 'get balance right' on tax hikes

The Prime Minister said he was conscious that taxes had gone up in 2024 and 2025 as previous Chancellor Rachel Reeves battled to fix the mess the Tories left of the public finances

View 2 Images Andy Burnham said the situation in the Middle East was putting pressure on the UK finances (Image: Getty Images)

Andy Burnham has said he wants to get the "balance right" in the upcoming Budget for Brits squeezed by tax hikes.

‌



The Prime Minister said he was conscious that taxes had gone up in 2024 and 2025 as previous Chancellor Rachel Reeves battled to fix the mess the Tories left of the public finances.

‌



But the PM and his new Chancellor John Healey face a darkening economic picture ahead of a high stakes Budget next month. Government borrowing rose more than expected to £18.3bn in August, as inflation hit its highest level in five months, driven by higher fuel prices.

‌



Asked if the UK had the balance right between taxing wealth and income, Mr Burnham said: "We have two budgets in 2024 and 2025 and we have to be conscious of the extent to which we have raised revenue. And we have to make sure we get the balance right." Pressed further, Mr Burnham said these were "matters for the Budget".

Chancellor John Healey urged to end housing benefit freeze hitting low-income families at Budget READ MORE :

View 2 Images Chancellor John Healey is facing a battle to balance the books (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

The squeeze on the public finances means the Chancellor faces a raft of difficult choices to balance the books - tax rises, spending cuts or more government borrowing. Mr Burnham has committed to Labour's manifesto pledge to protect working people from hikes to income tax, VAT and national insurance.

‌



This has triggered speculation he could target property, capital gains tax or business, such as the energy sector or banks.

Meanwhile, the PM rejected reports that the dire state of the economy had caught his team by surprise. He said: "It's not the case that we were surprised when we came in - not least because I was in access talks and understood very clearly the position.

"The truth of the matter is that because of the situation in the Middle East, the position changed, and has changed over the time I've been in. That's just the reality of the situation that we're in.

‌



"And of course the message is that we want to see an end to the conflict as quickly as possible and we stand ready to play our part."

It came as the PM stood by his warning that Britain should be less “in hock” to the bond markets, saying high levels of borrowing has left it “over-exposed” to global shocks.

Mr Burnham made the comments last year while he was still Greater Manchester Mayor, triggering criticism from Keir Starmer's government and jitters from investors.

Article continues below

In an interview with The New Statesman, he said: “I mean, the point about the bond markets, it holds – in that what I was saying was the country has left itself over-exposed.”

He accused Mr Starmer's team of taking his comments out of context. He said: "They couldn’t understand why I was saying some of the things that I was saying… [They] didn’t know what to do with it, but they did what they always do, which is they pulled one line out of it and then framed that one line within their world, rather than the one that I was talking about.”

News.title: Andy Burnham hints 'unfair' ban on football fans drinking in stands could be lifted
News.content:
Andy Burnham hints 'unfair' ban on football fans drinking in stands could be lifted

Prime Minister Andy Burnham, a staunch Everton fan, said it was unfair that football supporters can’t enjoy a match-day pint in the stands like rugby or cricket fans

PM suggests football drinking ban could be abolished

The decades-long ban on football fans drinking alcohol in the stands could be lifted, Andy Burnham has signalled.

‌



The Everton-mad Prime Minister said it was unfair that supporters can’t enjoy a match-day pint in the stands like rugby or cricket fans. He said outdated legislation meant football fans were "singled out" and there was a case to review the rules.

‌



But a move to rip up the ban is likely to meet with heavy pushback from the police, who have argued boozing on terraces fuels disorder.

‌



Drinking alcohol in sight of the pitch has been banned in England and Wales since 1985 under a law introduced by Margaret Thatcher to crack down on football hooliganism at a time when matchday violence was high. The current rules apply within 15 minutes of kick-off and the final whistle.

Andy Burnham doesn't rule out rejoining EU in next Labour election manifesto READ MORE :

Wes Streeting slaps down backlash over UK unit to combat Russian online lies READ MORE :

View 2 Images Andy Burnham with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney watching Everton (Image: Alan Martin/Action Plus/Shutterstock)

Fans are still allowed to have a pint inside the concourse under the current rules. But critics say this can mean people binge drink before matches or rush to down their drinks during half time.

‌



Mr Burnham was grilled on his previous criticism of the ban before he became Prime Minister. Asked if he would scrap it, he said: "I don't think it's fair for football fans to be singled out in that way and I made that point.

“I think that legislation dates to an era where football was very different. And I do believe there is a case to remove that discrimination. There are different ways it could be done, perhaps on a trial basis.

“But I'm not going to back away from what's been a long held view of mine. I don't see how it can be fair that some supporters of one sport can be treated differently."

‌



Toffees fan Mr Burnham previously said it was wrong that he could have a drink watching rugby league at the club’s Hill Dickinson Stadium but not during the football.

In a social media clip while holding a pint, he said: “How come these lads can do that in my seat here when we can’t do that at an Everton home game? There’s something wrong there, we need to take a look at that.”

View 2 Images Football fans have been banned from drinking in the stands since the 1980s (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Tom Greatrex, chair of the Football Supporters’ Association, said: “The FSA has always argued that it’s unfair to criminalise football fans for having a pint while watching the match - especially since you can sit in the same seat drinking alcohol whilst watching an Oasis gig or rugby league.

“Many clubs are in favour as well. WSL and WSL2 ran a successful pilot, meaning fans can now drink in the stands at many grounds, while the EFL has long supported a trial. We welcome the prime minister’s comments and totally agree that the legislation is outdated and deserves to be reviewed.”

A fan-led review of football governance in 2021 suggested piloting alcohol sales on terraces in League Two and National League games to help lower league clubs boost their coffers. Pilots have been carried out in the women's game but not for men's matches.

‌



Ex-Sports Minister Tracey Crouch, who led the review, told the Mirror: "Running a pilot on permitting alcohol in the stands was a key recommendation of the fan led review and this will be welcome news for clubs lower down the pyramid, where every penny of income helps with financial stability."

York Outer MP Luke Charters told the Mirror: "I absolutely welcome the comments the PM’s made on this, he’s totally spot on.”

But police chiefs have warned relaxing the law could fuel disorder. Mark Roberts, the head of UK Football Policing, said at the time there was a "clear correlation in and around football between alcohol and poor behaviour.”

‌



And earlier this year he warned that the relaxation of licensing laws in England for the World Cup contributed to the disturbing rise in violence.

A UK Football Policing Unit (UKFPU) spokesperson said, “The UKFPU would welcome a meeting with the Prime Minister to discuss his views and explain the challenges these proposed changes would bring to policing and the safety of staff and fans at football games.

“Other sports simply don’t see the violence and criminal behaviour from their supporters that football does, albeit a minority, with alcohol often playing a significant part in violent and disorderly behaviour. It would be irresponsible to fuel this by allowing greater alcohol consumption during games.

Article continues below

“Following a number of football-related tragedies, changes in legislation were implemented after the Taylor Report for good reason and we are currently in the longest ever period without a significant football related disaster. It would be incredibly rash to make fundamental changes without a full examination of the evidence and meaningful consultation with police practitioners who have the expertise in this area.”

News.title: RAF Valley crash: Video shows Hawk jet coming down and exploding on Anglesey
News.content:
The Hawk T2 plummeted to the ground in North Wales moments after taking off, with witnesses reporting a 'big bang' and flames coming from the jet

An RAF jet crashed in North Wales on Wednesday as witnesses spotted flames erupting from the aircraft.

The T2 Hawk aircraft had just taken off from RAF Valley on Anglesey when the jet ran into trouble, with two crew members ejecting using parachutes shortly before it hit the ground. Eyewitness heard an "enormous bang" and saw a "huge wall of fire" as the jet crashed.

North Wales Police said two pilots were being treated "for what are thought to be minor injuries and at this stage".

One witness said: "We watched take-off, we're on shoreside and have watched hundreds take off. I said to my wife it's in trouble as I could see flames as it took off."

A Royal Air Force spokesperson told the Mirror: "An incident involving an RAF T2 Hawk aircraft, flying out of RAF Valley, occurred near Anglesey. An investigation is underway and we will not comment further at this time."

News.title: Putin suffers 'humiliating' loss as Zelensky warns of further 'pain' for Russia
News.content:
Putin suffers 'humiliating' loss as Zelensky warns of further 'pain' for Russia

Volodymyr Zelensky says that if Vladimir Putin's forces continue to target Ukraine's energy system, then it will be a 'painful' winter for Russia

View 2 Images Zelensky threatened a "painful" winter for Russia (Image: SARAH YENESEL/EPA/Shutterstock)

Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine will make it a "painful" winter for Vladimir Putin as he echoed Donald Trump's claim that Russia had "lost control" of its oil industry.

‌



The Ukrainian leader used a speech at the United Nations in New York to call on countries to choke Russia’s revenues and impede its war efforts, claiming that Putin is the only person who wants the conflict.

‌



He said that Russia will try to make this winter "very harsh" for Ukraine, but added that it will also be tough for them, with major disruption having been caused to energy supplies from drone attacks.

‌



Ukraine has taken the attack to Russia in recent months by targeting fuel facilities deep inside the country. Zelensky said that nobody inside the Putin regime would have expected that the winter now could be used as a weapon against them.

View 2 Images Putin has faced attacks from Ukraine on fuel facilities (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

Ryanair warns passengers to brace for 'dramatic' fare increases across the industry next summer READ MORE :

Russian military helicopter enters NATO airspace as fighter jets scrambled READ MORE :

"We will make that happen this winter," Ukraine's president told the UN General Assembly. "If Russia continues to target our energy system and our heating, Ukrainians understand that this winter could be very harsh for us. But in response, we will have no choice but to make it painful for Russia too."

‌



Zelensky went on: "That's exactly why we say that de-escalation steps are important - and are needed before winter. Now, we need diplomacy and we need strength, and step by step, we are closing the gaps in both."

He said it was "humiliating" for Russia to have lost its control over the oil industry. It was after Trump said on Truth Social this week: "Russia has unfortunately lost control of its Diesel Oil Industry due to its War with Ukraine."

The US President added: "A large number of their diesel refineries have been blown up and are, at least temporarily, out of commission."

‌



Zelensky told the UN today: "It is hard to imagine a more humiliating loss for a country that has a permanent seat on the UN Security Council, and takes so much pride in its oil exports."

While on Trump's wishes to see the end of the war, Zelensky added: "I do not know a single world leader who would say otherwise. I do not know anyone who is openly for this war except one man."

It comes as US Secretary of State Marco Rubio says both Russia and Ukraine have expressed interest in a limited ceasefire that would halt attacks on grain shipments and each country’s energy sectors.

Article continues below

Speaking to reporters Wednesday after meeting with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, Rubio said reaching even a partial deal would be difficult but worthwhile even if it doesn’t completely end the conflict.

“It won’t be easy but it’s something that both sides have expressed an interest in,” he said, noting that Zelensky has publicly endorsed such a plan.

“If we can play a constructive role in making that happen, we would be very open to, again, recognising it doesn’t end the war, but it does deal with something, and maybe it can serve as the baseline or a platform for a broader agreement.”

News.title: Jet2 flight from Edinburgh U-turns over 'disruptive passenger' as police meet plane
News.content:
Jet2 flight from Edinburgh U-turns over 'disruptive passenger' as police meet plane

A Jet2 flight was forced to land back at Edinburgh Airport where police removed a man who was charged with various alleged offences including assault and endangering an aircraft

View Image The plane was forced to turn back shortly after taking off from Edinburgh (Image: Alan Simpson Photography)

A flight from the UK to Cyprus was forced to turn back following reports of a "disruptive passenger".

Jet2 flight LS721 from Edinburgh to Larnaca headed back to Scotland around 30 minutes after departing as a result of the incident.

Emergency services met the flight after it landed safely back in Edinburgh, the Daily Record reports, and a man was taken off the aircraft by a number of police officers.

Police Scotland confirmed a 32-year-old man has been arrested and charged in connection with various alleged offences including assault and endangering an aircraft.

Jet2 apologised to customers for the disruption to their flight and said it takes a "zero-tolerance approach" to disruptive passenger behaviour.

One eyewitness said: "We were only in the air about half an hour when the guy kicked off... We finally made a very bumpy landing back in Edinburgh."

Fire crews and airport staff were seen outside the plane after it landed before several police officers made their way down the stairs carrying a person off the flight and into a van.

Data from flight tracking app FlightRadar24 shows the Boeing 737 took off from Edinburgh before turning south on its way to Cyprus. The aircraft had barely crossed the border into England before it turned around near Newcastle.

A spokesperson for Jet2.com said: "As a family-friendly airline, we take a zero-tolerance approach to disruptive passenger behaviour, and we strongly condemn any behaviour of this nature.

"We will not hesitate to take appropriate action against disruptive passengers, including through the courts where necessary, and we will seek to recover the costs incurred as a result of their behaviour.

“"We would like to apologise to all customers and our colleagues onboard who had to experience this."

A Police Scotland spokesperson said: "Around 4.30pm on Wednesday, September 23, police received a report of a disruptive passenger on a flight that had departed from Edinburgh Airport.

"The flight returned to the airport and a 32-year-old man was arrested and charged in connection with various offences including assault and endangering an aircraft.

"He is due to appear at Edinburgh Sheriff Court on Thursday, September 24. Anyone with any footage which could assist our enquiries is asked to contact officers via 101, quoting incident number 2320 of Wednesday, September 23."

News.title: Blood tests find high level of cancer-causing forever chemical in residents near factory
News.content:
Blood tests have found "really high levels" of a cancer-causing forever chemical in dozens of people living near a major chemical factory in the UK.

The residents, from Thornton-Cleveleys, Lancashire, have been told they could be at elevated risk of serious health conditions from the substance, known as PFOA.

The village has been under investigation for years by the Environment Agency over contamination of soils and locally grown food from the substance, which is a type of forever chemical - so-called because they do not easily break down.

That investigation said high levels likely came from the nearby AGC Chemicals factory, which used it to manufacture coating for frying pans until 2012.

Sam and her husband, both from the village, have been told they were at increased risk of health impacts from PFOA. However, she told the BBC was more shocked by her son's result.

"When we opened the results...it was like, my God, that is ridiculously off the scale.

"I feel guilty because I've introduced [my children] to that way of life. I know it isn't my fault, but the guilt is horrific. Knowing that I've offloaded what levels I probably had over the years into those children when I breastfed them - that's heartbreaking," she said.

News.title: UK military jamming other nations' satellites to defend itself, BBC told
News.content:
The British military has been jamming or blocking satellites from other countries in order to defend itself from hostile threats, the BBC has been told.

The RAF has been using a ground-based system for the past year, which a defence source said had already been used "to deter our adversaries".

It is understood the system could be used to prevent a hostile nation's satellites from tracking the movement of the UK's nuclear armed submarines or other sensitive military operations, such as those involving special forces.

It comes as the head of the RAF said the UK faced "unprecedented threats" from adversaries in space, coinciding with the creation of a new RAF unit set up to defend Britain's satellites.

The Ministry of Defence (MoD) said the new Space Effects Squadron will be focused on "disrupting, degrading and denying hostile threats in space".

The squadron will protect British satellites used to warn of incoming missile attacks, provide communications and help guide ships, the MoD said.

In a speech on Wednesday, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said daily lives depend on satellites that power everyday technologies like mobile phones and banking apps, adding the loss of GPS would cost the UK economy Â£1.4bn a day.

"Our dependency on space is precisely why it is increasingly under threat from our adversaries." he said.

"We depend on them for everything from weather forecasts, energy supplies, and financial transactions to sat-navs, mobile phone connections, and Amazon deliveries," said Streeting, adding that the loss of "everyday conveniences would undermine our daily freedoms, and trust in our institutions."

Speaking at the UK Space Conference, Streeting said that threat from Britain's adversaries was growing in "scale, speed and sophistication", adding that the "challenges in space increasingly mirror the geopolitics on Earth".

A number of nations are believed to have similar ground-based systems against satellites. Last year the then head of the UK's Space Command said Russia was trying to jam UK satellites with ground based systems "every week".

The defence source described the UK's terrestrial electronic warfare capability as "world leading, and more".

Last week US confirmed for the first time that it had also deployed an unspecified "weapon" in space to defend its own satellites.

Both China and Russia condemned the move - warning of an arms race in space.

However, Washington has already accused both Russian and China of developing their own space weapons - ranging from electronic jammers, lasers to blind other satellites and even projectiles that can be fired from satellites in orbit.

News.title: Watch: Moment pilots eject as RAF jet crashes in Anglesey
News.content:
Two RAF pilots ejected and parachuted out of an RAF jet before it crashed during a training exercise.

North Wales Police said the pilots were being treated for minor injuries following the incident in Anglesey.

Helicopters from the Coastguard and the Wales Air Ambulance were sent to the scene close to RAF Valley on the island, the force said.

A spokesperson for the RAF said it is currently investigating the crash.

Read more about the incident here.

News.title: Home secretary says undetected migrant landings 'unacceptable'
News.content:
The Home Secretary has said migrant landings on UK beaches are "not acceptable", as she ordered an urgent review after two boats reached Kent without being intercepted.

Shabana Mahmood told Border Security Command to carry out the review after vessels came ashore at Samphire Hoe, between Dover and Folkestone, on Tuesday, and near Folkestone on Monday.

Twenty-one people were detained on Tuesday after the arrival at Samphire Hoe.

Five people were also detained on Monday after the uncontrolled landing near Folkestone, the first undetected landing for a year. The Home Office has not said whether more people are being sought.

News.title: Burnham brands ban on football fans drinking alcohol in stands as 'discrimination'
News.content:
Andy Burnham has branded a ban on fans being allowed to drink alcohol in the stands during men's football matches as "discrimination".

The prime minister told reporters that "I don't think it's fair for football fans to be singled out", as he suggested a change could be trialled.

Laws have been in place since 1985 which have prevented drinking in view of the pitch at stadiums for clubs in the top five tiers of men's football in England. Other sports do not face such a restriction.

The Football Supporters' Association (FSA) said the "outdated" legislation should be reviewed, but police chiefs have warned against relaxing the law and would like to meet the PM to "explain the challenges".

The legislation was introduced in 1985 by Margaret Thatcher's government for English and Welsh football grounds. At the time, then-Home Secretary Leon Brittan said that alcohol was a "major contributory factor in violent and disorderly behaviour" in football grounds.

Burnham is a keen football fan and a season-ticket holder at Premier League team Everton.

Shortly before he became prime minister, he criticised the restriction on football fans as he attended a rugby league game at Everton's Hill Dickinson Stadium where it was possible for supporters to have a drink in the stands.

Speaking to reporters on his trip to the United Nations in New York, Burnham was asked if it was still his view now he is in Downing Street.

Burnham replied: "I think that legislation dates to an era where football was very different.

"And I do believe there is a case to remove that discrimination. There are different ways it could be done. It could happen on a trial basis.

"But I'm not going to back away from what's been a long held view of mine. I don't see how it can be fair that some supporters of one sport can be treated differently."

A trial or pilot scheme to look at whether a change would be possible is not being ruled out by government sources.

But any wider move would require extensive consultation involving football clubs, fans and the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport - none of which is currently planned.

News.title: Family tribute to 'devoted' mum and 'precious' children who died in fire
News.content:
The family of a mother and three children who died in a house fire have said they are experiencing an "unimaginable" loss.

Elisha Brabin, 36, and her children, Leo, 16, Ellis, 8, and Prudence, 7, died after a blaze "spread rapidly" inside a house on Stone Square in Bootle, Merseyside, in the early hours of Tuesday.

Paying tribute, their relatives said they had been left "heartbroken" and the loss would be "felt forever".

The statement added that "Elisha was a devoted and loving mother" and "our beautiful babies, Leo, Ellis and Prudence, were loved beyond measure".

The family said they were "devastated by the loss of Elisha, Leo, Ellis and Prudence".

"Elisha was our beloved daughter, wife, mother, sister, auntie, niece and cousin," they said.

"She was a devoted and loving mother who lived for her children. They were her whole world, and she meant everything to us."

News.title: Police examine video of anti-migrant activist slashing dinghy with knife
News.content:
Police are looking into a video appearing to show anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas slashing at an inflatable boat with a knife in the English Channel.

The boat had been carrying about 50 migrants who had launched from a beach in Normandy. They were picked up by two RNLI lifeboats once they had reached the UK search and rescue area. They were then transferred to a UK Border Force vessel and taken to Dover for processing.

Daniel Thomas, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, had been filming the transfer from a yellow speedboat while giving commentary to a live stream audience of more than 15,000 people.

The video then shows him sailing up to the boat, taking out a small knife and starting to slash at the side of the migrant boat.

There were no migrants on board, but there was a French official from the coastguard vessel Abeille LibertÃ©.

As the Frenchman boarded the empty migrant boat mid-Channel Thomas shouted "Right, you are on English territory. This is England. This is not France any more."

Then he made a series of stabbing and slashing movements against the rubber side of the large inflatable boat.

"Get off - get off," he shouted. "You've got time to get off the boat."

It was not clear from the live stream if he did any damage to the boat.

"We just wanted to make sure that boat was not taken back to France and used again," Thomas told his followers.

Posting on X, campaign group Stand Up To Racism described the footage as "disgusting".

News.title: Singer Michael Kiwanuka reveals he is recovering from a stroke
News.content:
"I'm very happy to be announcing to you my new album Fudge," his message said.

"I'm especially happy because the last few months I've been battling some health problems which would heavily hinder and get in the way of me making music for the foreseeable future. A few months ago I suffered a stroke brought on by a bleed in my brain brought on by high blood pressure.

"It's a long journey recovering from a stroke, which is why I missed some gigs recently out in the US, but I look forward to seeing you all soon.

"I'm not sure when I'll be able to be back out on the road or what that will look like, the brain injury I suffered was quite severe so there's a lot of rehab to be done, it's a long, tough journey ahead but I'm fighting to get better.

"It has been a difficult few months I must say but it feels like I'm on my way there now."

News.title: RAF pauses fighter jet training after two pilots eject from plane before crash
News.content:
High-speed Hawk fighter jet training has been "temporarily" paused as a "precautionary measure", the RAF has said, after two of its pilots ejected and parachuted out of their plane moments before it crashed, narrowly missing homes.

The Hawk T2 aircraft had been flying out of the RAF Valley base on Anglesey when it plummeted to the ground at nearby Pencarnisiog.

North Wales Police said the pilots, who had been flying a training aircraft, were being treated for minor injuries.

The RAF said it had decided to pause Hawk operations whilst investigations are ongoing.

Eye witnesses described how the plane came down near village homes, with debris ending up near a caravan site.

A video of the crash shared on social media appears to show the two pilots ejecting from the aircraft before it nosedives, crashes and bursts into flames

The footage shows a plume of smoke and fire erupting as the aircraft hits the ground, appearing to narrowly miss residential properties.

The Hawk T1, and newer T2 versions are transonic, two-seat training aircrafts used to train fast jet pilots.

The BBC understands the Red Arrows, based at RAF Waddington in Lincolnshire, are included in the pause as the aerobatics display team use the T1.

However, they were not due to fly again until Le Touquet Airshow in France this weekend in any event. It is not known when the restriction will be lifted.

News.title: UK to review Chagos Islands deal over lack of US support, Streeting tells BBC
News.content:
The UK is reviewing its deal to hand over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, the defence secretary has said.

Wes Streeting confirmed the deal was being looked at again after US President Donald Trump called it "terrible" at the UN General Assembly on Tuesday.

The original agreement would see the UK cede sovereignty of the territory to Mauritius and pay an average of Â£101m ($136m) per year to lease back a joint UK-US military base there, prized for its strategic location in the Indian Ocean.

In April the deal, agreed under Sir Keir Starmer, was paused indefinitely because Trump pulled his support.

Streeting said "we have to" review the deal "because the United States doesn't support it".

"What President Trump said yesterday wasn't new but I think it does provide absolute clarity that his position on this Chagos deal as currently drafted is not changing," he told BBC Breakfast.

"So we have to do more work with our American allies, with President Trump and his administration, to get the deal to a place where he can support it."

Streeting said the focus now would be to secure a long-term certainty for the base on Diego Garcia, the Chagos archipelago's largest island.

He said it had been the view of every UK prime minister since Boris Johnson that an ongoing legal process - as Mauritius argues it was illegally forced to give away the islands in 1965 to gain independence - risks the security of the base.

News.title: Barrecore and Boom Cycle owner suddenly shuts studios
News.content:
The fitness company behind high-end exercise classes Barrecore, Boom Cycle, and Kobox has suddenly shut all its studios.

Common Bond emailed customers announcing its locations, all of which are currently in London, were closed "until further notice".

The firm describes itself as a wellness collective and charges Â£2,400 for 12 months of unlimited classes. It also runs Reformcore and Triyoga brands and said in August last year it had ten sites.

Its website is no longer publicly accessible. The BBC has contacted Common Bond for comment.

The email sent to customers on Wednesday seen by the BBC said: "We're sorry to let you know that all Common Bond studios are closed until further notice.

"We sincerely apologise for the inconvenience and disruption this may cause . We understand this is frustrating, and we appreciate your patience while we work through this."

Instructors have told the BBC they were told last week they would not be paid on time and that they only found out about the studios closures from the Wednesday email.

One instructor said she and her colleagues were told their pay would be delayed on the day it was due on 14 August.

She said: "In good faith, I continued to teach my classes without any news on when or if payment would be made. I have heard absolutely nothing since."

News.title: UK warned over ballooning debt costs and slower growth ahead of Budget
News.content:
The UK has been warned over ballooning debt costs and slower economic growth ahead of Chancellor John Healey's first Budget next month.

The UK was among countries facing downgraded growth forecasts in a report by the influential Organisation of Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) on Wednesday.

That came as the head of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) told the BBC that Britain and the US needed to reduce debt due to spiralling borrowing costs.

The ongoing conflict in the Middle East and the Russia-Ukraine war has pushed up the cost of crude oil leading to higher fuel and energy costs, which in turn has driven up inflation around the world.

The UK economy will grow by slightly less than expected next year, according to the OECD which now expects growth of 1% next year rather than 1.1%.

However, it said the UK had proved more resilient than expected this year, upgrading its forecast for growth 0.9% to 1.1%.

Meanwhile, IMF head Kristalina Georgieva told the BBC on Tuesday that global economic shocks had been "pushing debt levels up like a staircase not to heaven" but that governments had taken "no action to contain that service cost".

"[It's] time to take that action," she said, adding that "courage" was needed by politicians to take the necessary steps.

Inflation has also pushed up the cost of interest on government debt, which alongside an unexpected surge in government borrowing in August has added to the pressure on Healey.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Wednesday that the UK's high level of borrowing had left it "over-exposed" to global shocks.

However, he said he stood by his point - made a year ago - that Britain should be less "in hock" to investors in the bond markets. At the time, the comments spooked investors due to fears he was calling for spending restraints to be eased.

Burnham has made easing the cost-of-living for households one of his key aims, while the government is under pressure to spend more on defence.

He and Healey face a difficult balancing act, trying to offer more support to households while sticking to Labour's manifesto commitments on tax and the government's self-imposed fiscal rules.

The impact of higher fuel prices next year depends on how long supply disruptions last, and stockpiles of oil and supplies from outside the Gulf states have helped cushion the effects on economies so far, the OECD said.

Budget airline Ryanair will put up prices next summer as a result of persistently higher oil prices. Chief executive Michael O'Leary said ticket prices will be "materially higher", adding that carriers are in an "almost unprecedented" situation.

Ryanair's fuel bill could jump by $1.5bn (Â£1.1bn) next year to $7.5bn, he said.

Risks to the global economy include weaker-than-expected returns on AI investment and climate-change related supply shocks, the OECD said.

Next year, global growth is expected to also be 0.1% lower, with countries affected including Australia, Canada, and the Euro-area.

Weather-related shocks, including from a strong El Nino, could hit farmers and help push up food prices, it added.

In addition, tariffs and export restrictions on trade continue to add to uncertainty, it said. New US tariffs from July as part of the Trump administration's ongoing volatile trade policy have raised its effective tariff rate by 1%.

News.title: Man died of cardiac arrest on flight, inquest told
News.content:
A British man who died on board a Singapore Airlines flight suffered a cardiac arrest after the plane was hit by severe turbulence, an inquest has been told.

Geoff Kitchen, from Thornbury in South Gloucestershire, died on 21 May 2024 after the Boeing 777 plane travelling from London Heathrow to Singapore encountered a sudden drop in altitude near the south western region of Myanmar.

The plane was later diverted to Bangkok, Thailand, where the 73-year-old was pronounced dead.

Dr Peter Harrowing, assistant coroner for Avon, said: "I am satisfied that it was the physiological effect of the aircraft turbulence which precipitated the cardiac arrest and ultimately Geoff's demise."

Harrowing reached the narrative conclusion into Kitchen's death at a hearing at Avon Coroners' Court earlier.

He told the inquest Kitchen, who had a history of coronary artery disease, had also been "thrown from his seat and landed on an adjacent passenger" during the incident.

News.title: Police worker jailed after death of boy in her care
News.content:
A woman who worked at Nottinghamshire Police has been jailed after the death of a nine-year-old boy in her care.

Catherine Walker, 47, was the legal guardian of the boy, who was found unresponsive in his bedroom in Warsop, Nottinghamshire, on 16 December 2024. Despite the efforts of paramedics and people at the scene, the boy died in hospital.

The force said an investigation found "clear mistreatment of the boy over a prolonged period of time".

Walker, of Appleton Street in Warsop, was jailed for six years at Nottingham Crown Court on Monday after pleading guilty to two counts of assault/ill-treat/neglect/abandon a child/young person to cause unnecessary suffering/injury.

The force, which has not revealed what Walker's role was, said her former husband was the boy's primary carer and had been mainly responsible for his treatment.

He died shortly after the boy's death, police added.

News.title: On-the-run killer who absconded after father's funeral arrested
News.content:
A man who was convicted of murder and has been unlawfully at large for over a week has been arrested in the Republic of Ireland.

Gary Anderson, 29, was jailed for life in 2023, alongside his brother, for the murder of Karol Kelly in Londonderry.

He was on temporary release from prison to attend his father's funeral when he absconded.

He was arrested on Wednesday by An Garda SÃ­ochÃ¡na (Irish police) at a property in the town of Buncrana in County Donegal.

Karol Kelly's sister had said the family felt "let down" by the justice system after learning that he was on the run.

The Justice Minister, Naomi Long, welcomed Anderson's arrest.

She said she hopes the arrest "goes some way towards alleviating the anxiety and uncertainty" that Karol Kelly's family have experienced.

Long is due to meet the family later this week.

She added that she recognises that "questions remain about the circumstances surrounding" Anderson's release and abscondment.

"Work is progressing to establish an independent review, and further details will be announced shortly."

The circumstances surrounding Anderson's release sparked a political row in Northern Ireland, with Long denying on Monday that she had misled the assembly over the matter.

MP for Foyle, Colum Eastwood, welcomed Anderson's arrest and said "confidence has been damaged in the institutions involved".

News.title: Admiral insurance firm to cut 500 jobs in the UK
News.content:
Insurer Admiral will cut 500 jobs in the UK as part of plans to save Â£100m, it has announced.

The proposals are related to Admiral's UK insurance business only, and will affect about 5% of its workforce.

"We recognise this will be a difficult time for affected colleagues," said Alistair Hargreaves, Admiral Insurance UK's chief executive .

While the Cardiff-based company uses artificial intelligence (AI) in its operations, adoption of AI is not believed to be responsible for these changes.

Admiral said the job cuts would make the firm "faster and more efficient".

Earlier this year, Admiral said it needed to save Â£100m, and has added the proposed redundancies are part of that cost-cutting effort.

"These changes are aimed at making us faster and more efficient so we can continue to deliver great customer outcomes," said Hargreaves.

Staff members who are affected will be offered "enhanced" redundancy payments and redeployment opportunities where possible.

Hargreaves said Admiral was also "making a significant investment in meaningful support to help colleagues consider future options".

The Welsh government said it was "disappointing to learn that Admiral will be making these redundancies".

"A meeting will be arranged with the company to understand the reasons for this action and to offer additional support to those affected," it added.

Andy Burnham’s best hope of winning the next election and stopping Nigel Farage from reaching No 10 is by committing to reversing Brexit and getting Britain to rejoin the European Union, new polling has revealed.

The research by YouGov for a Best for Britain report across the 632 constituencies in Great Britain (excluding Northern Ireland) revealed that Labour would win 321 seats – just five short of an absolute majority – if they pledge to rejoin the EU.

It would give the prime minister a “working majority” because of the fact Sinn Fein MPs do not take up their seats, while the appointment of a Commons Speaker and deputies reduces the number needed for a majority.

It would mean pro-EU parties – including the Lib Dems, Greens, SNP and Plaid Cymru, along with Labour – would have a clear majority in parliament and nullify the threat from Mr Farage and Reform.

open image in gallery Prime minister Andy Burnham meets with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen ( PA )

It follows similar MRP polling – which looks at how constituencies would vote – published by The Independent last week, which revealed only four constituencies in England, Wales and Scotland do not support rejoining but still come out as “don’t know”.

It also comes after Mr Burnham refused to rule out putting rejoining the EU in Labour’s manifesto at the next election when asked by The Independent on his recent trip to the United Nations in New York.

The latest polling suggests Labour could get as few as 136 seats if it does not change its red lines on Brexit and sticks with the status quo, while Reform UK would be on 300.

The number of seats for Labour increases to 256 with a commitment to join the customs union, 257 with a promise to join the single market and 321 if Mr Burnham pledges to rejoin the EU entirely.

Reform’s seats fall to 235 with Labour supporting the customs union reentry, 230 if Labour goes for the single market and just 191 if Mr Burnham backs fully rejoining the EU.

A promise of EU membership could also see Labour unseat key Conservative MPs including Tory leader Kemi Badenoch (North West Essex) and shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith (Arundel and South Downs), as well as Reform UK’s Robert Jenrick (Newark), the polling suggests.

Naomi Smith, chief executive of Best for Britain, which campaigns for UK-EU reintegration, said: “These numbers are a wake-up call for both the prime minister and Labour backbenchers in previously Leave-voting constituencies.

open image in gallery Promising to Rejoin offers Labour its best chance of stopping Nigel Farage ( PA )

“EU membership is the only policy lever that takes Labour close to a majority at the next election and keeps the architects of Brexit out of power.

“Labour’s electoral strategists must get their heads around the irony that seats they are most concerned about losing to Reform UK are less winnable if they pursue a low-ambition EU reset.

“Public opinion has shifted, a majority of voters in each seat support EU membership, and – crucially – are prepared to vote tactically to achieve it.”

The findings come as the government shapes its policy on Europe ahead of the heavily delayed UK-EU summit, the Labour Party’s conference in Liverpool, and Mr Burnham’s upcoming speech in which he is expected to set out his ten-year vision for the country.

They also emerge as the first ministers of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland said the future of their nations belongs “in the European Union.”

Tom Brufatto, policy and research director at Best for Britain and lead author of the report, said: “These findings are the latest in a data series which clearly show that halfway houses will simply not do for voters, who want to return to Europe and all of the benefits it offers, or for Labour who are looking for manifesto entries.

“We have a prime minister who not only sees the damage caused by Brexit but the opportunity for his party to do things differently- that starts with a manifesto pledge to renew the UK’s membership of the EU.”

McDonald's Monopoly promotion is back this year, but with a twist, bringing the game into the age of apps.

After a 10-year hiatus, McDonald's brought the Monopoly game back in 2025 — and it’s back again this year, but will be played exclusively through the fast-food giant’s app.

For diners who enjoyed the experience of peeling the game pieces off various McDonald's items, fear not; you'll still have to peel your piece off your fry box in order to play.

However, in order to receive a food item with a game piece, diners will have to download the McDonald's app, opt into its Rewards program, pre-register for the game, and then order eligible food items off its "Monopoly at McD's" app menu.

In the past, anyone could play so long as they ordered a food item with a game piece attached to its packaging.

McDonald’s Monopoly promotion is back, but this year diners will have to use the chain’s app in order to participate

Once all the prerequisite registration is done, McDonald's visitors will then have to peel their game piece off their food and scan it into the chain's app.

The food items that will carry the game pieces include large fries, large hot and cold drinks and more, including some breakfast items, according to McDonald's.

The new Monopoly game will begin on October 6.

McDonald's said in a statement that the new, app-focused experience is "simplified" and offers a "one-of-a-kind prize list."

This year's game pieces will be carried at participating locations and only while supplies last. McDonald's said that approximately 640,591,900 game pieces will be distributed to restaurants.

Prizes range from free food items to a Carnival cruise, a 2027 Jeep Cherokee, up to $50,000 toward a home down payment or college debt, and cash prizes up to $1 million, according to Delish.

McDonald's stopped running its Monopoly game for a decade following the fallout of the "McMillions" scandal.

The original scandal, which involved former police officer Jerome Jacobson stealing game pieces to net himself $24 million in prizes, occurred during the 1990's, but only came to light in August 2001, when the FBI began arresting individuals involved in the scheme.

McDonald's faced backlash from customers, as the scam ensured that few honest players ever won anything significant from the promotion during the 1990's. The company ended the promotion in 2015, replacing it with its NFL-themed "Game Time Gold" promotion until it revived Monopoly last year.

Jobless benefits claimants could be banned from spending their welfare payments on alcohol, cigarettes and gambling under a Conservative plan to slash the UK’s welfare bill.

An estimated 350,000 benefits claimants would face receiving their payments on a pre-loaded card, which it would be impossible to use for cash withdrawals, betting, or buying cigarettes or alcohol.

Under the Tory scheme, anyone who claims Universal credit (UC) when they are looking for work would get six months of full benefits – but after that, anyone who has not consistently contributed to the welfare system over years would have their payments slashed.

The full rate would be available only to people who have contributed to the welfare system through their taxes for a sustained period.

Under the plans, every two years a UC claimant has worked would buy them an extra year on the full rate of the benefit.

But jobseekers who do not have a record of working and contributing would have their UC standard rate cut by a third to a new “subsistence allowance”.

And that payment would be loaded onto a “back-to-work” pre-payment card that came with the restrictions on spending.

The card could be used for food and other everyday essentials, and to pay for bills.

People who are off sick or disabled, or who are claiming UC while in work, would be exempt.

The Conservatives estimate the shake-up could save taxpayers £538m a year.

Party leader Kemi Badenoch claimed the current system was unfair to workers.

“Some will say this is unfair on people claiming benefits. What is unfair is a system where someone who can work chooses not to and earns more from benefits than someone in a job,” she said.

“Helping people into work is not punishment. The best welfare is a well-paid job. So we will be tough on those who exploit the system because the current system is unfair to workers, taxpayers and those who truly need support.”

open image in gallery Long-term jobless people face curbs under the Tory plans ( PA Wire )

She said the UK should not “be borrowing from our children and grandchildren to support people who simply refuse to work”.

Helen Whately, the shadow work and pensions secretary, said: “We cannot go on like this – with millions of people living on benefits instead of in work. Britain can’t afford it.”

Further plans for welfare reform are likely to be revealed at the Conservative conference this month.

Prime minister Andy Burnham has indicated that reforms to the benefits system will be revisited under his government.

A Labour Party spokesperson said: “The Conservatives had 14 years to fix our welfare system but they completely failed to make meaningful reforms.

“Now they are proposing an unworkable new card scheme, which does nothing to tackle the numbers of people their system left signed off and written off.

“While the bill for the taxpayer rose by £33 billion in their last year in government, this Labour government is introducing effective and sustainable welfare reform alongside a £3.5 billion employment support package to help people stay in or return to work, and the national rollout of the jobs guarantee for young people who have been on Universal Credit.”

Organisations representing the hospitality and betting industries and human rights in the UK declined to comment.

This is no funny business.

The Laughing Cow, the animated red mascot who has smiled from packages of spreadable cheese wedges for more than 100 years, has suddenly stopped laughing.

Select packages of The Laughing Cow Creamy Original cheese wedges rolling out nationwide now feature the normally cheerful cow with a serious expression and a cryptic message: “We need to talk.”

But what happened? That’s the mystery behind the brand’s new “The Not Laughing Cow” campaign, which is inviting fans to speculate about what could have wiped the grin off her face, the brand announced Tuesday.

“The Laughing Cow has spent more than 100 years reminding us not to take life too seriously. So when she suddenly gets serious, you pay attention,” Jamee Pearlstein, chief marketing officer of Bel Brands USA, U.S. Cheese, said in a news release.

open image in gallery Select Laughing Cow cheese packages nationwide now feature the usually smiling mascot with a serious expression and a mysterious message: 'We need to talk' ( The Laughing Cow )

“Whatever finally got to her must be worth talking about. We’ll let her explain when she’s ready,” Pearlstein added.

The special packages are available in select markets in every state across the U.S. and can be found in more than 4,700 stores, according to the company. Each package also features a QR code directing shoppers to TheNotLaughingCow.com, where they can investigate the mystery and share their theories.

The campaign’s videos only add to the intrigue. One shows the usually upbeat mascot sitting alone in a diner, while another has her somberly swinging by herself as messages flash across the screen: “The Laughing Cow stopped laughing,” and “We need to talk.”

open image in gallery Campaign videos show the usually cheerful mascot looking downcast and alone, including one clip in a diner and another on a swing with ominous messages ( The Laughing Cow )

The serious-faced mascot has also popped up in parks, diners and across the brand’s social media accounts, according to Bel Brands USA.

Thankfully, her frown will soon turn upside down.

The change is temporary, and the mystery behind her sad face will begin to unravel in the coming days, Bel Brands told Fox News Digital.

Until then: "We’ve been excited to see that curiosity and conversation continue to build as more of The Not Laughing Cow packages appear on shelves," the company told the outlet.

The Independent has contacted The Laughing Cow for comment.

Elon Musk is being eyed as a potential investor in Paramount as the company's merger with Warner Bros. Discovery nears completion, according to a new report.

As they seek to shore up the media company’s finances, Paramount executives have talked about asking the billionaire CEO of SpaceX and Tesla to join a “syndicate of equity investors into Paramount,” Semafor reported Wednesday, citing sources familiar with the matter.

Such a maneuver could make Musk — an ally of and major donor to President Donald Trump — a partial owner of CBS News, currently owned by Paramount, and CNN, owned by Warner Bros. Discovery.

Though a cash infusion from the billionaire businessman may not necessarily give him formal influence over operations, it could nevertheless raise alarm among Democrats. Many Democrats became critical of him after he purchased X, donated millions to Republicans and slashed the federal workforce as the de facto head of DOGE.

Musk has a long-established relationship with Larry Ellison, the billionaire father of Paramount CEO David Ellison. In 2022, the elder Ellison poured $1 billion into Musk’s bid to take X private, and in 2018, he invested in Musk’s electric car company, Semafor reported.

Paramount executives have talked about asking Elon Musk to become an investor in the company as its merger with Warner Bros Discovery moves closer to completion, according to a new report ( Getty Images )

The Independent has contacted Paramount and Musk for comment.

This week, Paramount announced a proposed settlement with a dozen states, which had sued to block its merger with Warner Bros. Discovery.

The merger, valued at roughly $111 billion, would establish one of the largest media conglomerates in the world.

There have been accusations that CBS News has become more supportive of the Trump administration since Bari Weiss, the founder of the anti-woke media outlet The Free Press, was appointed editor-in-chief last October after Paramount, the network’s parent company, was acquired by billionaire David Ellison.

Since then, critics have accused her of steering coverage to favor the Trump administration and Israel. She has reportedly responded that she is not “a mouthpiece for anybody” and that her goal is to restore trust in journalism.

Actor Hayden Panettiere spent time in a rehabilitation facility weeks prior to dying from an accidental drug overdose, according to a coroner’s report.

While specific details of her care remain unknown, people struggling with drug addiction face a heightened risk of a fatal overdose right after a period of sobriety. Medical experts note that physical tolerance drops during abstinence, meaning a dose previously tolerated could overwhelm the body.

Panettiere, 36, was discovered unresponsive inside a Greenville, South Carolina apartment on Aug. 16. The Greenville County Coroner’s Office said that multiple substances were detected in her system, including fentanyl, its chemical byproduct, the anti-anxiety drug alprazolam, a muscle relaxer, and a medication used to treat major depression alongside other serious mental health disorders. A case file notes that a senior deputy learned she had spent two or three weeks at a facility in Malibu, California.

Provisional government statistics published in May show roughly 70,000 Americans died of drug overdoses last year, marking a 14% decrease compared with the prior year.

How opioid addiction can be treated

For people struggling with addictions, there are various types of care, including therapy and counseling, medication and support groups.

open image in gallery While specific details of her care remain unknown, individuals struggling with drug addiction face a heightened risk of a fatal overdose right after a period of sobriety. ( Getty )

With addictions to fentanyl, heroin, oxycodone and other opioids, treatment may include medications and behavioral therapy. The National Institute on Drug Abuse says medications are the standard of care for opioid use disorder. Treatment options include methadone, buprenorphine and naltrexone, which research shows can reduce the risk of resumed drug use and a fatal overdose. Behavioral therapy for opioid use disorder is most effective when combined with medication, the institute says.

Using drugs after stopping them can be deadly

Using opioids again after withdrawal can be especially dangerous.

According to the National Library of Medicine’s MedlinePlus, most opioid overdose deaths occur in people who have just undergone detoxification. Because withdrawal reduces the person’s tolerance, those who have just gone through withdrawal can overdose on a much smaller dose than they previously took.

This risk has long been known. A 2003 study in the British Medical Journal said “treatment reduces mortality but can sometimes increase mortality transiently," including among people with prior opioid addiction after their release from prison.

Experts at Pennsylvania State University's Social Science Research Institute said the risk of overdose death is higher immediately after opioid use disorder treatment, including after detox and stopping medication for the disorder.

They cited research showing that the month after completing treatment is associated with a much higher risk — five times higher for ending treatment without medications and two times higher after ending medication treatment. That’s compared to periods more than a month after ending treatment.

What friends and family can do to reduce risk of overdose death

The first thing to know is that someone who recently stopped using drugs is at higher risk for an overdose if they relapse. Be ready to respond if that happens.

Death following opioid overdose can be prevented if the person gets prompt basic life support and the medication naloxone, an antidote that rapidly reverses the effects of an opioid overdose if administered in time.

The New York State Department of Health recommends taking these steps if someone witnesses an overdose:

1. Call 911 and say, “I think someone may have overdosed.”

2. If the person isn’t breathing, begin mouth-to-mouth breathing by pinching the nose and blowing into the mouth

3. Administer naloxone if available.

4. Place the person on their side once they have resumed breathing

5. Stay with the person until the ambulance arrives

A federal judge overseeing a lawsuit to restore White House access to three major news organizations says Donald Trump’s administration appears to have failed longstanding legal precedent that requires due process before stripping passes from reporters.

Last week, the White House stripped press passes for CNN, MS NOW and Politico journalists after the president announced he was “banning” the publications “effective immediately” for what he called their “FAKE” reporting. Letters explaining how they can get those passes back weren’t sent out until yesterday.

U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, was appointed by the president during his first administration, had previously ordered the White House to restore then-CNN reporter Jim Acosta’s press pass in 2018.

When deciding that case, Kelly relied on previous court decisions that determined journalists are entitled to a “pre-deprivation notice and opportunity to be heard” before those passes are revoked, the judge said during Wednesday’s court hearing in Washington, D.C.

“I think it is fair to say that the process the court laid out [in those cases] wasn’t followed here,” Kelly said before arguments began Wednesday. The judge said he will have a ruling “as soon as I can” but ended the 45-minute hearing without an immediate decision.

open image in gallery CNN, MSNOW and Politico are suing the Trump administration to restore press access to the White House after the president announced he was ‘banning’ the outlets ( Reuters )

Trump and the Department of Justice have accused the outlets of endangering national security by reporting sensitive and classified information that the president has also called “fake news” that is “negative, wrong and, in many cases, DANGEROUS for our Country.”

“Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America,” he wrote on Truth Social September 18. “Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow.”

A federal lawsuit filed by lawyers representing the outlets accuses the Trump administration of “brazenly” violating their First Amendment rights and due process requirements under the Fifth Amendment by discriminating against them based solely on their editorial viewpoint.

Other news organizations agreed to an effective blackout of pool coverage in solidarity with the banned networks. ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC and Fox News — major networks that cover the president as part of the well-connected TV pool that patches transmissions to outlets worldwide — suspended their coverage, and other outlets announced they were temporarily withholding the publication of pool photographs.

Theodore Boutrous Jr., a lawyer for the outlets, said there hasn’t been a “semblance of due process here.”

But if the judge was to merely force the Trump administration to provide reporters with some recourse, “the shenanigans will continue,” he told Kelly.

“You can see where we’re headed here,” with “a series of faux due process efforts” to satisfy the courts while continuing to violate the outlets’ First Amendment rights, Boutrous Jr. said.

“I think we all know … none of us are that naive,” he said. “That’s not due process.”

open image in gallery Trump has denied launching an ‘assault on the Free Press’ while claiming ‘FAKE NEWS’ that publishes reporting he doesn’t like amounts to a ‘cancer’ and ‘a threat to our National Security’ ( Getty )

On Monday, Trump denied launching an “assault on the Free Press” and said he is instead “instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America.”

“It is corrupt, purposeful, pervasive, fully coordinated, and totally out of control,” he wrote on Truth Social. “It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!”

Sensing a potential loss in the federal court battle, he vowed an appeal “because Fake News people and publications that only write negatively, and who violate our National Security by writing false and defamatory stories with unknown ‘sources,’ shouldn’t be allowed access to the most important Office anywhere in the World.”

He lashed out at “Third Rate Clowns” who “purposefully distort, twist, and degrade with everything they write or publish.”

“Virtually every story about me, or anything having to do with me, is negative, wrong and, in many cases, DANGEROUS for our Country!” he wrote. “No matter how GREAT my Achievements, they trivialize and demean.”

He also said he regretted appointing Judge Kelly.

In late-night filings on Tuesday, the Justice Department accused the outlets of threatening national security and breaching standards of conduct, including “trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues, and publishing sensitive or classified information.” No law explicitly makes it a crime for a journalist to obtain or publish classified information.

“Access to the White House is a privilege — not a right,” the filing states.

open image in gallery Trump’s actions have escalated his ongoing war with the press and threats to First Amendment protections as he publicly rages against critical and antagonistic reporting ( AFP/Getty )

The filings included copies of letters from the White House Press Office to the three outlets sent on September 22. The letters point to their reporting on the U.S. military’s munitions shortages due to the ongoing Iran war as well as the administration’s proposed security additions to the White House ballroom — details that the Justice Department itself has discussed at length in court filings stemming from the ongoing lawsuit against the project.

The White House also pointed to a report about low attendance at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas that “cites unnamed sources” to paint the event “as a disaster.” (That report from Politico cited a Republican lobbyist close to the White House who said “the vibes are very bad.”)

Only one of the four articles published by CNN and one of the three offending MS NOW articles were written by reporters with White House passes, according to officials at the network.

The White House also pointed to reports of an alleged FBI leak investigation focusing on a journalist and an apparent U.S. military strike on an Iranian girls’ school that killed 156 civilians, including 120 children.

“Publication of sensitive security information, and misinformation about national security information, diverts White House resources and those of the national security team in particular, which must evaluate whether the leaked information is classified, the source of any leak, and the security implications of any such disclosure,” the White House Press Office wrote in letters to the news outlets.

“The spread of misinformation, especially relating to national security, is a threat that undermines the President’s ability to safeguard the national security,” the letters state.

The outlets were given until 5 p.m. September 25 to “contest this initial decision or the factual basis” for their removal.

“It’s so over the top,” Boutrous said Wednesday. “It’s clear retaliation.”

After media outlets sued, “all of a sudden this is a national security case,” he said.

“A light bulb went off: ‘start talking about national security,’” he said. “The idea that reporters can be punished for reporting on national security issues … that the government would rather not be reported on is contrary to First Amendment principles.”

He called the administration’s shifting rationale a post-hoc, pretextual attempt to ban coverage the president doesn’t like.

On Wednesday, a coalition of more than 50 news organizations and press freedom groups filed a brief in support of the outlets, writing that the White House ban over the content of their reporting amounts to unconstitutional viewpoint discrimination.

“It is designed to have a chilling effect,” they wrote, “with the hope that it discourages other outlets from publishing stories that they fear might provoke similar sanctions.”
