Sports.title: Battle of boxing's most unlikeable stars: Conor Benn takes on troubled Ryan Garcia after burning Eddie Hearn with $10MILLION payday in his sights - but here's why Briton's fate rests solely in the hands of his narcissistic American rival
Sports.content:
Battle of boxing's most unlikeable stars: Conor Benn takes on troubled Ryan Garcia after burning Eddie Hearn with $10MILLION payday in his sights - but here's why Briton's fate rests solely in the hands of his narcissistic American rival

‘Who ya like buddy?’ It’s the most asked question in casino-ville as the hours tick down to this Saturday’s world title fight between two angry young men.

One, America’s extravagantly gifted but troubled world welterweight champion. The other, the ever-persistent English challenger who never stops throwing punches whether they connect or not. As if in manic obsession with defeating not only opponents but also his demons and a sceptical outside world.

So, Ryan Garcia or Conor Benn?

When the denizens of this neon gambling Strip in the Nevada desert ask that question they don’t’ want to know which of these two combatants you like personally more than the other. It is their way of trying to find out who you might be betting on to prevail in the atmospheric T-Mobile Arena.

Their inquiries are even more numerous than usual on such occasions as this. Because neither the Americans nor the Mexicans who are thronging here in support of their blood brother by heredity know very much about Benn. Other than the fact he is the son of a fabled icon of the British ring.

On his two previous US visits Benn Jr made hard work of beating men who looked more like nightclub bouncers than professional boxers. Of his exploits back home only the pair of fights against Chris Eubank Jr evoked any interest whatsoever on either side of this border.

What they are aware of is the two positive tests for performance enhancing drugs and the protracted legal battle to technically clear his name which kept him out of the ring for months. Just as they know about Garcia’s conviction and suspension for a similar finding.

Conor Benn is locked in the battle of boxing's most unlikeable stars in Las Vegas

Benn is lining up a $10m payday after burning his bridges with promoter Eddie Hearn

So, what’s to like?

There can be no doubting Benn’s work ethic. He trains like a dervish to manufacture the maximum possible out of however much natural-born ability he inherited from Nigel the Dark Destroyer. Nor does he ever give up. Eubank Jr had to go beyond the normal limits of even this battle-hardened business to inflict the only defeat of Conor’s career thus far. A loss he avenged, albeit in partly contrived and contentious circumstances.

Eubank the Younger was perilously drained in the rematch by a clause in the contract which prevented him rehydrating fully after struggling to cut poundage to meet the agreed catchweight.

What goes around comes around. If not in a full measure of the irony. Benn has had to sweat and strain down by almost a stone from middleweight to make the welterweight championship limit of 147 lbs. As he puts it: ‘Five weeks in hell.’

To say his body looks shredded is putting it mildly. But he has not been subjected to rehydration limitations following his Friday morning visit to the scales.

Eubank was handsomely rewarded to put his health on the line, and now Benn has been lured into similar jeopardy by the fortune – some reports say ten million dollars – he is receiving from UFC boss Dana White to be one of the first poster boys for his venture into boxing.

Benn tells it otherwise: ‘I’m doing this because I relish challenges. Have always wanted to strap on the same green WBC belt my dad was so proud to wear. To start getting the world titles that will leave a legacy for my kids. And to prove wrong everyone who doesn’t give me a chance of winning. That puts all the pressure on him, not me.’

Hearn backed the British fighter during his controversial doping ban saga

Ryan Garcia stands in his way of the WBC title, who is the more talented of the fighters

WEIGH-IN VERDICT: After all the brouhaha Conor Benn made the weight with a full pound to spare After what he described as 'five weeks of hell' dieting down by two divisions he scaled 146 lbs in readiness to challenge world welterweight champion Ryan Garcia here this Saturday night. He did so with a told-you so smile. Throughout the speculation as to whether he could shed the best part of a stone in his training camp journey from middleweight Benn had assured one and all that he would be comfortable at his long-ago weight. Good as his word he came in only half a pound heavier than Garcia. Although he is leaner of hip the muscle is still there on arms and torso. Complete with a six pack as a reminder of his constant work ethic. The slightly taller part/Mexican great white hope of American boxing does look more natural at the weight. But Benn does not appear stressed from all his exertions. Even so Garcia is still a solid odds on favourite in the Vegas betting

Whether or not Benn can take in sufficient liquids and pasta before entering the ring, the dangers to him are greater than those with which Eubank struggled. Garcia, one year the younger at 28 but the riper in championships experience, has authentic one-hit-knockout power.

Benn goes into his first world championship fight reliant on the cumulative effect of his non-stop output. The problem with this is that King Ry is probably the best counterpuncher in the world right now and Benn’s headlong style will likely suit him nicely, thank you.

To complicate the evaluation, both have blotted their copybooks as people. Garcia, the handsome heartthrob, burnished his bad-boy rock-star image by trashing a five-star hotel room. He also needed his family’s help with overcoming mental problems aggravated by a passing fancy for social drugs and booze.

Benn invited mockery for claiming initially that he failed his drugs tests because of eating enough eggs to fill the shelves of all the Tescos in London. Then, in order to collect his bonanza from Mister UFC, he unceremoniously dumped his long-time promoter Eddie Hearn who had bankrolled his hefty legal costs and loaned him half a million quid to help sustain his flamboyant lifestyle through that crisis.

Not much to like there.

So, when it comes to the fight, who ya like? The answer is not Conor Benn’s to give. Because the real question is which Ryan Garcia turns up.

If it is the narcissist whose arrogant complacency has cost him a couple of big fights, it may not be totally beyond the bounds of possibility that Conor could pull off one of the major upsets by a British boxer abroad.

If it is King Ry fully prepared and ready to unfurl all the majesty then we can only hope the son of Nigel is not seriously hurt.

Sports.title: Ricky Hatton's mother recalls last hug with boxing champion three days before he took his own life a year ago as parents speak out for first time
Sports.content:
Ricky Hatton's mother recalls last hug with boxing champion three days before he took his own life a year ago as parents speak out for first time

Ricky Hatton's mother has recalled her last hug with him three days before he took his own life one year ago as his parents speak out for the first time.

Carol and Ray Hatton have urged people to tell their friends and family they love them before it's too late after the boxing champion hanged himself on September 14 last year.

One year on from Ricky's death, aged 46, his mother has revealed the last time she embraced her son.

Just days before he took his own life, the boxing champion had been in an argument with his parents but the family were 'building bridges'.

Carol decided to make an unplanned visit to his gym in Hyde and gave him a 'real proper hug'.

She told ITV News: 'I pulled up on the car park because I saw his car. He asked if everything was okay.

'I said "yeah, everything's fine". I said I'd like to see a bit more of him.'

Ricky's mother said he told her he wanted to see his father Ray the next week. However Ricky died three days later.

Former world boxing champion Ricky Hatton died by suicide in September last year aged 46

Ray and Carol Hatton (pictured at their son's funeral) have urged people to tell their friends and family they love them before it's too late

Ricky had previously opened up about his struggle with drug and alcohol addiction and had become estranged from his parents before the reconciled

She added: 'I'm so glad (I got to see him) because nobody knows when it's the last time you're going to see somebody.'

Ray, the boxer's father, said: 'You tell your grandkids how much you love them, you tell your wife how much you love them but I think, especially with men, don't ever be afraid of getting hold of your son and telling him you love him.'

Ricky had become estranged from his parents for around a decade before he reached out to patch up their relationship several years before his death.

He had survived previous suicide attempts and struggled with drug and alcohol addiction.

Ricky fell out with his parents over money and despite the dispute he still allowed Carol and Ray to see his newborn daughter Millie.

However the boxer became upset when his girlfriend Jennifer was not invited to a Christmas Day party.

Months later he received letters from his parents' lawyers saying they wanted to see their granddaughter.

But he told Manchester Evening News in 2013 that he responded by saying: 'I replied to my parents, through solicitors, and said we did not want them to have contact with Millie.'

Carol Hatton wipes a tear from her eye while reading a statement at her home after Ricky's death

Ricky had survived previous suicide attempts before he died in September last year

'We have never stopped them seeing her, as far as I was concerned they had just not been ******.

'I know that sounds harsh and I am sure they see it differently, but it is how I feel.'

He added that the situation 'was a mess', describing the family feud as 'bitter and horrible', referring to back-and-forth letters between his and his parents' lawyers.

This culminated in his father attacking him in a car park fist fight.

Angry about 'all that stuff you've written about your mum in that solicitor's letter', Ray then punched his boxing champion son in the face before Ricky hit back and his father then drove off.

But Ricky's parents are still struggling to come to terms with his death and Carol said the couple 'have to move forward' but will continue 'remembering him and loving him'.

Carol and Ray have now called for a statue of Ricky to be erected in Manchester, saying it would be a 'fitting tribute' to their son who 'brought a lot of pride' to the city.

Sports.title: Anthony Joshua vs Tyson Fury looks set for CARDIFF - at 2am: Welsh venue set to waive curfew to take boxing's biggest fight away from Wembley and New York
Sports.content:
Cardiff's Principality Stadium now looks set to be the unlikely winner of the venue war for boxing's biggest fight - by hosting Anthony Joshua vs Tyson Fury in the early hours of the morning.

The local authorities could today approve lifting the stadium's 10.30pm curfew to host the fight - stepping in after rows over holding it at Wembley Stadium or Madison Square Garden in New York.

Cardiff has history of hosting late-night boxing. Joe Calzaghe fought Mikkel Kessler at the Principality in 2007 at 2am. Fury and Joshua could fight at a similar time to satisfy broadcaster Netflix's huge audience in the United States.

Netflix had wanted the fight in New York to suit their prime timezones, while Joshua's promoter Eddie Hearn pitched Wembley to host under the guise that Britain's biggest fight of the century should be hosted in the UK - and he has refused to budge unless contracts are rewritten with upgraded financial offerings.

Cardiff now appears to be the compromise. The Principality Stadium has an 80,000 capacity and a retractable roof - unlike Wembley - which could be useful in late November or December. A date of Saturday, November 28 has been mooted.

The Times report a press conference is tentatively scheduled for next week pending the approval.

Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua could now be set to fight in Cardiff, Wales in November

Joshua and his camp wanted the fight in the UK - while broadcasters Netflix wanted a US host

Wembley looked an ideal venue for the fight but the strict 11pm curfew has been a sticking point, despite London mayor Sadiq Khan saying he wanted to ensure allowances were made to host the fight.

Boxing dealmaker Turki Al-Sheikh has been insistent on a start time of 2am.

Netflix have been running s for Fury-Joshua as recently as Thursday night, clearly confident an agreement will be struck.

The streaming giant has yet to sign off on Cardiff but American sportswriter Dan Rafael last night reported he had asked Netflix if they would approve, with a source telling him: 'I think they're OK.'

A spokesperson for the Welsh Rugby Union said: 'We'd be delighted to host this fight.

'We are very keen to attract more boxing to the stadium, which has a rich history in the sport, enhanced by its closable roof, unrivalled sight lines and unique city-centre location.'

Joe Calzaghe trains at the Principality Stadium before his 2am fight there in 2007

Joshua has fought in Cardiff twice previously, beating Carlos Takam and Joseph Parker in the Welsh capital in 2017 and 2018.

While Joshua has left Hearn to do the talking on his side of the deal, Fury has been publicly speaking and threatening that the heavyweight contest will be called off.

This week he suggested he will no longer be fighting Joshua in another social media rant as rows over the location and contract surrounding the fight continued.

'So it looks like AJ has s*** his pants yet again,' Fury said on social media on Sunday. 'After 11 years, he's finally s*** his pants yet again.'

Last week, Fury, who regularly takes to social media to express his views on potential opponents, was keen to make clear he feels Joshua is not motivated by a love of his country. Earlier this year Daily Mail Sport revealed Joshua had in fact quit the UK to move to Dubai – even as thousands tried to flee amid rising panic in the Middle East warzone.

And Fury, a tax exile to the Isle of Man himself, brought up a 2020 speech at a Black Lives Matter march, where Joshua read out a letter from his friend Reece Campbell to urge attendees to stop spending money with white-owned shops and businesses.

'Show them where it hurts', Joshua had said. 'Abstain from spending your money in their shops and economies, and invest in black-owned businesses.'

Fury re-posted the video of the speech, writing: 'This is the man who loves England, absolute s*** bag! Total piece of s*** bully with zero guts! Don't let them deceive you! & Living in Dubai.'

Provided Cardiff hits no further stumbling blocks, the Welsh capital may now offer the solution to get the fight on at last.

Sports.title: Russell's theory on his big hope for F1 2027 – and Antonelli's reply
Sports.content:
From being the 2026 Formula 1 pre-season title favourite to fighting to hold on to second place as Mercedes team-mate Kimi Antonelli accelerates into the distance, George Russell has endured a challenging few months. During that period he has been forced to question his entire approach to driving, owing to the peculiar requirements of the latest technical formula.

Most of the drivers on the grid have voiced reservations – or noisy complaints – about the unnatural driving style required to get the best out of the 2026 cars, but Russell belongs to a subset whose style appears to put them at a disadvantage compared with their team-mates. Most notably at Silverstone and Spa, Russell hit lower peak top speeds than Antonelli on key straights, explained by him using fractionally more electrical power to re-accelerate after scrubbing off more speed through preceding corners.

McLaren's Oscar Piastri is in a similar position.

Although F1's power units are shifting from a 55:45 ratio of internal combustion engine output and electrical power to 58:42 for 2027, this will not bring about a massive shift in performance characteristics. But there are other changes afoot, including a new family of Pirelli tyre compounds which have been developed through this year via testing with the current cars.

Asked in Baku ahead of this weekend's Azerbaijan Grand Prix whether this could promote a more natural style of driving, Russell suggested that it may.

"I think it's been clear this season that the tyres, front to rear, probably have not been well balanced enough," he said. "You look at some tracks that are clearly front-limited and the fronts have stayed pretty strong throughout. It could also be because of the extra power we've got coming off the corners, so the rear tyres are getting a harder time.

"It is quite interesting. I spoke with Antonio Giovinazzi, who drove this new generation of car for the first time a couple of days ago in Imola, and he said how impressed he was at the power of these new cars off the corner. And I think that has quite an impact on the rear tyres.

"Obviously, last year when we developed these tyres, they were with the previous generation of power unit, which had much less power off the corners. So, I don't think it's a big surprise the rear tyres are getting a harder time than we all anticipated."

Action-packed 2010 Canadian Grand Prix was the catalyst for the brief handed to Pirelli when it became F1's sole tyre supplier Photo by: Getty Images

When Pirelli became F1's exclusive tyre supplier in 2011 it was handed a brief to produce compounds which offered strong grip up to a certain point in their use cycle before falling off quickly. The trigger for this was the 2010 Canadian Grand Prix. Complaints about processional racing had been building for years until this point, where a combination of a freshly resurfaced track and mixed weather in the build-up to the event caused the usually robust Bridgestone tyres to degrade rapidly, and an unpredictable race ensued.

But Pirelli has often struggled to find an ideal compromise to fulfil what is a very challenging target. The tyres have often proved too sensitive to degradation, and when Pirelli has toughened them up in response to criticism, it has overshot – not helped by being restricted in terms of how much testing it can complete with relevant machinery. Whenever testing is performed with current cars, competitive paranoia arises as teams suspect each other of covertly evaluating performance upgrades.

While the focus on developing the 2027 tyres has been on ensuring greater lap time differences between compounds, it is understood that tweaking the balance between the front and rear axle has also been on the agenda. But would better balance alone help those drivers who have been losing momentum through rear sliding, then paying the price on the straights?

That is a complicated question to answer, since these changes – even if successful – won't happen in isolation. The FIA is also bringing in a package of aerodynamic changes to curtail the downforce gains teams have been finding through developments, as well as mitigating the straight-line demand on electrical power. What the teams have discovered in simulation is that these tweaks have greater effects than first anticipated – so much so, in fact, that those who had been planning to carry over their 2026 chassis to next year for cost-control reasons have changed tack.

George Russell, Mercedes Photo by: Sam Bloxham / LAT Images via Getty Images

Besides tidying up some of the loopholes around the rear wing, and making it shallower, the changes mandate fewer vortex generators on the floor leading edge, as well as a significantly shorter (from 900mm to 600mm) ‘tea tray', the section of the floor that extends under the driver's legs. This latter change opens up the possibility of teams adopting very different rake angles, hence the re-think on carrying over chassis designs.

For these reasons, Antonelli takes a slightly different view from his team-mate.

"I think the tyre, also this year the tyre changed completely," he said when Autosport asked for his opinion on the magnitude of the effect the new tyres will have.

"So I think on my side, you try to understand the tyre the best way you can, and you try to adapt. I think the tyres won't be so much different, probably the front tyre will change a little bit, and in terms of structure a little bit, we'll see what Pirelli decides.

"We've done some Pirelli tests and we've given the feedback, but of course we'll see what is going to be decided. But from what we heard, it shouldn't be much different to what it was this year.

"The car will be different – on the aero side the car is changing, especially around the bib area, there's going to be a big change, which is going to implement aero loss. Then the team for sure will find a way to recover that, but the car is going to be a little bit different next year for sure.

"The baseline will be the same I think, but maybe together with the tyre and the car evolving, it's going to feel a little bit different. It's all about adapting at the end of the day, so we'll see."

There's an understandable amount of equivocation here since Antonelli didn't want to publicly contradict his team-mate. But of the Mercedes drivers he is the one who has been adapting best to the requirements of the new regulations, which he is subtly pointing out.

And of course, the risk George runs if he pins his hopes on change is that Kimi will do so again.

Sports.title: How McLaren Hypercar test will help Norris in F1
Sports.content:
Lando Norris driving McLaren’s new Hypercar may seem inconsequential in the grand scheme of Formula 1 things, but the reigning world champion would disagree.

Norris took the wheel of the MCL-HY at Algarve last week, completing just 38 laps – enough to get a feel for the World Endurance Championship’s top machinery and provide feedback to McLaren ahead of the brand’s 2027 debut.

The 26-year-old was impressed with the depth of set-up options relative to F1 and insisted it was ‘still a quick car’ when asked by Autosport about his thoughts following the test.

“The level of detail that they go into is pretty crazy,” Norris said. “They have, in some situations, a lot more scope to do things with the car than what we're allowed to do in Formula 1.

“As much as you think Formula 1 is ‘you can do whatever you want’, it's not quite that. With how you can change the toys and set up the car itself, it’s actually quite a bit more limited than you can do with the Hypercar in terms of electronics and all of these things.

“So it's pretty cool to see what you could do. It's a bit more like old-school Formula 1, when it was a bit more just a free-for-all on what you could do, which is a good thing.

“Of course, it's a very different car, it's quite a heavy car, so adapting to that; obviously quite a bit less downforce, but it still feels like a quick car, so it's still exciting.”

As a reference, Peugeot’s Malthe Jakobsen took pole position in 2m00.653s at this year’s Spa-Francorchamps 6 Hours, where F1’s 2026 benchmark was Kimi Antonelli’s 1m44.361s while Rafael Camara topped F2 qualifying in 1m56.306s.

Norris was joined at the Portuguese track by two of McLaren’s 2027 drivers, Mikkel Jensen and Laurens Vanthoor, which provided the Briton with further learning opportunities.

“It was more, again, for me to try something and also to learn things,” he said. “Everything I do, really, even when I drive other cars, is always to try and learn things – understand different styles, learn from the other drivers that I met over there, and see what I can take onboard to help me drive better this weekend.

“So it's always a good opportunity, especially to stay within the McLaren family. It helps me learn and be more focused for doing my real job, which is Formula 1.”

Norris was adamant about that last part when the 2027 Le Mans 24 Hours was brought up, given the race doesn’t clash with F1 next year – only the Test Day does.

Lando Norris, McLaren Photo by: McLaren

“It's not something I've been thinking about, at all,” he insisted. “All my focus is still on F1, and will always be. I'll never sacrifice something in Formula 1 for something else.

“If there's a chance that things can work out, maybe, but I don't know if this is next year, the year after, three years, four years – I have no idea. Again, it's not something I've been thinking about at all, but it's something I would like to do in the future.”

Sports.title: What’s behind the delay in cancelling the Qatar and Abu Dhabi GPs?
Sports.content:
Given the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, for several months now it’s been assumed that the cancellation of the season-closing Qatar and Abu Dhabi Grands Prix is not just likely, but inevitable.

The commercial rights holder has been making contingency plans while outwardly maintaining that these races are still on. Many in the F1 paddock have followed suit: the hotels in the Imola vicinity are almost fully booked for the weekend occupied by the Abu Dhabi round.

Despite the assumption that Qatar and Abu Dhabi will inevitably be cancelled, the promoters of those races remain outwardly determined that they will go ahead as planned. Abu Dhabi has gone as far as announcing music acts including Zara Larsson, The Script, Imagine Dragons and Lewis Capaldi. Those who set store by what people say on social media will note that Larsson has subsequently claimed she will not be going.

This is all part of an ongoing dance over who would pick up the tab if those races were to be cancelled. Broadly speaking, when promoters cancel races, they are the parties who end up out of pocket since their contracts with F1 oblige them to pay the sanctioning fee anyway. If the commercial rights holder cancels the races, it forfeits those fees.

The sanctioning fees for Qatar and Abu Dhabi have been widely reported as $55million and $40million per year respectively, but it’s understood that these figures are highly speculative. Nevertheless, the sums involved are significant.

Contracts vary between promoters, especially those races which are backed by states rather than conventional commercial entities. But when events are cancelled and money is lost, there will always be a tussle over liability – especially when cancellations are enforced by outside circumstances.

Such is the commercial value of hospitality, trackside signage and other sponsorships that the potential financial fallout extends well beyond the sanctioning fees. That is why Bahrain is hosting its race in Malaysia, in effect renting the circuit so that both it and F1 can fulfil their contractual obligations.

F1 is going to Malaysia for the Bahrain GP this year Photo by: Peter J Fox / Getty Images

“We will take the decision at the right time,” said F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali at the end of July. “That moment will be not before the middle of September. For us today, the races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi are confirmed.



“By the way, they are already sold out. That is an incredible sign of how much the sport is bigger than the problem that our world is living. But of course, if the situation would not be clearer the way that we believe it should be, before the middle of September, we will take the decision.”

Besides showing a rather tone-deaf perspective on F1’s importance in relation to geopolitics, this pronouncement also muddied the picture of when the decision would be made: before or after the middle of September? Either way, this date has now passed.

Domenicali also confirmed that if the final two rounds were cancelled, the season would not end with a double-header in Las Vegas. Despite some sources still claiming such an event is likely, it is not. F1 already has to tread carefully around the other Las Vegas stakeholders and it is understood that holding back-to-back events there would definitely not be welcomed by the local business community. A double-header would also clash with the Thanksgiving holiday.

The requirement to find a home for a final round in the event of the Qatar and Abu Dhabi GPs not happening is also contractual. As it stands, if they were to disappear from the calendar, F1 would be left with 21 rounds. While this would enable it to fulfil the majority of its broadcast contracts, it’s understood that at least one stipulates 22.

Imola was viewed as a shoo-in for the season finale but, during the Italian Grand Prix weekend, it emerged that F1 has experienced significant pushback from Qatar and Abu Dhabi regarding the cancellation of their rounds. It is understood their position is one of business as usual, since they have not been targeted by Iran for several months.

Imola had been cued up to host an impromptu F1 finale Photo by: Steven Tee / Motorsport Images

Difficult days therefore lie ahead for the commercial rights holder, since it will be required to make a decision soon for logistical reasons. In its quest to reach net zero emissions by 2030, F1 now transports a great deal of equipment via sea. This naturally means longer lead times.

Beyond the timescales involved in sea-freighting infrastructure to the Gulf region, there is the practical question of it having to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, a chokepoint which opens and closes depending on the state of hostilities between Iran and the USA. Should the final rounds remain as presently scheduled, more freight would have to go by air, increasing costs as well as emissions.

And while this game of brinksmanship evolves between the commercial rights holder and the Middle Eastern promoters, the teams also have questions to ask. Should their respective governments' foreign offices advise against travel to the Middle East, they will not be insured.

But at the moment, the British government's advice is: "All British nationals currently in the Middle East should be prepared for possible flight cancellations, periodic airspace closures, and potential travel disruptions." The US Department of State says putative visitors to the region should "reconsider". Neither of these amounts to a warning not to travel.

As such, it's understood that the risk of cancellation for these final two rounds is receding.

Sports.title: "Free agent" Ocon talking to other teams with Haas yet to confirm F1 2027 line-up
Sports.content:
Esteban Ocon declared himself a "free agent" as Haas is yet to confirm its driver line-up for the 2027 Formula 1 season, but did not rule out potentially staying at the team.

Although the Frenchman has been enjoying much improved performances of late, which have gone largely unrewarded as Haas' performance has slipped away from its early-season points-scoring form, Ocon's seat has been under threat for some time.

Haas has been using its testing of previous cars (TPC) programme to identify a potential partner for Oliver Bearman next season, with Ferrari junior Rafael Camara, reigning F2 champion Leonardo Fornaroli, and current reserve Ryo Hirakawa in the frame.

Ocon confirmed that he was looking for other options for 2027, while Haas continues to assess its driver pairing for next year.

Recent rumours have surfaced suggesting that the team is leaning towards Camara - currently the reigning F3 champion and second in this year's F2 standings - although team boss Ayao Komatsu stated during the Spanish GP that he had "maybe five" drivers in contention.

"Yes, at the moment I am definitely a free agent for next year," Ocon stated. "There are things in discussion that are out of my control and there are certain topics that are out of my control. So I will keep pushing until the end of the year and see how it goes."

Asked if staying at Haas was an option, Ocon remained tight-lipped and responded: "Let's see."

Esteban Ocon, Haas Photo by: James Sutton / LAT Images via Getty Images

Ocon added that he was pleased with his performances of late, having suffered this season with an inconsistent car in the early stages of the season.

It is unclear if this is an aerodynamic sensitivity issue or a parts quality control problem; Komatsu has suggested both could be causes, and that the team is still investigating the issue at hand.

"We know it's been an ongoing issue," he said. "It's reassuring that I'm doing a good job. Obviously, my performance hasn't been an issue this year.

"I've performed every time I had the car. I've been the last one to score in Monaco. I was almost scoring in Madrid. There's been a lot of times where I've performed when the car was underperforming. It's been clear.

"Everybody in the team has been following that very closely, trying to fix the problem. We haven't been hiding from it. But it's been quite disappointing at times, obviously, to have these kind of problems."

Bearman was asked if he felt ready to step up as the team leader should Ocon depart, and the Briton stated that he'd learned a lot from his team-mate across the almost two years spent together as team-mates.

Esteban Ocon, Haas F1 Team, Oliver Bearman, Haas F1 Team Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

He pointed to Ocon's feedback in the engineering room as something that he'd taken inspiration from, along with his own improving performances on-track.

"I've been here for, well, this is my second year driving as a full-time driver, but also I've been one year as a reserve for Haas, also did a few races and FP1s the year before that, even in 2023, I did my first FP1. So I have a really good level of experience with the team," Bearman said.

"I feel like I've improved a lot in terms of my on-track performance, but also how I describe what I'm feeling in the car and things like that. And that's something I certainly learned a lot from someone who's very experienced like Esteban. So on that side, it's been really good learning for me.

"Even if I compare my feedback to 12 months ago, I'm not sure I would have the confidence to just rely on my own feedback. But I feel like I've made a good step in that regard, and it's just a normal learning process, really."

Sports.title: The initial plan for F1's next engine regulation in 2030
Sports.content:
Formula 1 stakeholders have reached an agreement on the main elements of the next engine rules cycle.

The FIA and F1 engine manufacturers have opted against a naturally aspirated option, partly because of noise restrictions at street circuits, with a smaller and simplified electronics package.

A push-to-pass overtake mode is also under consideration, along with a possible debut in 2030.

While discussions are still ongoing, the engine set to define the next technical cycle in F1 has largely taken shape. Meetings between the FIA and the manufacturers will continue to finalise the remaining details, but a substantial agreement has been reached on the key points with the focus on a simpler and lighter power unit, one that is considered closer to the traditional concept of a racing engine.

A return to V8 engines

F1 is set to move to 3.0-litre V8 architecture, but one of the issues that most divided the engine manufacturers was whether to retain the turbocharger.

The possibility of opting for a naturally aspirated engine was also on the table, a solution that would have delivered a sound particularly appealing to fans nostalgic for F1 in the early 2000s.

Fernando Alonso, Renault R25, leads Michael Schumacher, Ferrari F2005 Photo by: Motorsport Images

However, the turbocharger element will remain as part of the power unit configuration, but the reasons behind the decision go beyond purely technical considerations.

A naturally aspirated 3.0-litre V8 would have reached noise levels that would cause a major problem with some of the current F1 venues.

The issue concerns street circuits in particular: Melbourne, Miami, Madrid, Singapore, Baku and Las Vegas are venues where noise-emission restrictions are in place, and the arrival of cars significantly louder than the current generation could create major difficulties that would be impossible to overcome and potentially even put some events at risk.

This has led to the decision to retain a smaller turbocharger, a compromise that should still make it possible to achieve a considerably louder sound than that of the current power units, while keeping noise levels within limits applied at some F1 circuits.

Smaller electrical motor and lighter power units

The new V8 will not be completely detached from electrification either. The new rules look set to include a simplified 100kW electric motor, a considerably lower output than the 350kW current generation of power units.

The aim is to maintain a technological link with the automotive industry without replicating the complexity that has characterised the latest generation of power units. The direction emerging from the discussions is clear: electric power will remain part of F1, but with a less dominant role within the overall package.

Start action Photo by: Clive Rose / Getty Images

Another area where the lessons of recent years appear to have been taken on board concern the weight of the overall power unit. The target set for the new power unit is highly ambitious: to produce a complete unit weighing at least 50kg lighter than the current power units.

Push-to-pass and 2030 introduction being considered

Some aspects still need to be finalised. Among them is the system that will give drivers an additional power boost to assist overtaking manoeuvres.

There appears to be no intention to bring back the DRS used until the end of the 2025 season. The solution currently under consideration is closer to the push-to-pass philosophy adopted in IndyCar: a temporary increase in power that the driver could deploy under specific circumstances.

This will be one of the areas the FIA and the engine manufacturers still need to reach a definitive agreement on.

When the new regulations will be introduced in F1 also remains open, with the plan to debut the new rules in 2030 an option, which would bring forward the end of the current technical rules cycle that began by one year.

Reaching a decision will require all parties to find common ground, but the issues that have emerged with the current generation of power units have accelerated a broader discussion that goes beyond individual technical details. After pushing hard on technological complexity, F1 appears keen to return to a more traditional concept of a racing engine.

Sports.title: What would you like to ask Emerson Fittipaldi?
Sports.content:
On 24 September, two-time Formula 1 world champion Emerson Fittipaldi will join us in the Baku paddock to answer Autosport readers' questions ahead of the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.

In a remarkable career that span across three decades with even further outings, Fittipaldi not only clinched the F1 title with Lotus and McLaren in 1972 and 1974 but also won the IndyCar championship in 1989.

Sports.title: Hadjar to partner Verstappen at Red Bull for F1 2027
Sports.content:
Red Bull has confirmed it will field an unchanged Formula 1 driver line-up in 2027, with Isack Hadjar staying put alongside Max Verstappen.

Hadjar stepped up in 2026 after a rookie season at sister team Racing Bulls, and has impressed with his speed in what has historically been a difficult second Red Bull seat.

The Frenchman, who is making his return in Azerbaijan this weekend after missing three races through injury, will stay on board for another campaign in 2027 alongside Verstappen, who recently signed a contract extension to 2030.

"We’re very excited to continue our journey with Isack," said Red Bull team boss Laurent Mekies.

"Since joining us at the start of the year, he has been superb on and off track, especially considering this is only his second Formula 1 season, which made extending his contract an easy decision.

"From the very beginning, Isack immersed himself in the team, spending every minute at the factory with his engineers to develop the car, always eager to learn and improve.

"You could see from that first weekend in Melbourne that he handled the step up with remarkable composure and had earned his place in this seat."

Isack Hadjar, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

Despite sitting out Zandvoort, Monza and Madrid, Hadjar still holds eighth in the standings, boosted by a first Red Bull podium in Monaco to complement his maiden podium in 2025, as well as a streak of seven consecutive top six finishes in what has largely been F1's third or fourth quickest car.

"I am really excited to continue with Oracle Red Bull Racing," the 21-year-old said. "There are so many talented people at the factory, and you’re aware of the privilege of driving for such an incredible team alongside a four-time world champion like Max.

"From the moment I signed, I set out to dedicate myself to the team, and with the support of Laurent and everyone in Milton Keynes, I’ve been able to justify the faith they’ve had in me.

“I’m constantly looking to listen, learn and push myself further every single day, which only makes me more excited about what lies ahead."

Racing Bulls is yet to confirm its own driver line-up for 2027, with incumbents Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad having both impressed this season while the squad also has junior driver Nikola Tsolov waiting in the wings.

Sports.title: What were Leclerc's "other opportunities" before signing new Ferrari deal?
Sports.content:
Every time Ferrari and Charles Leclerc agree to extend their relationship in Formula 1, the news comes against a background of allusions to other suitors Charles has spurned to remain with his true love.

"For that, I'm also lucky to be in the position where I've got my manager," he said on a recent episode of F1's Beyond the Grid podcast when asked how seriously he had considered a life away from Ferrari.

"And my manager is here to let me know about what are the other opportunities, what's going on around. And so I didn't have any personal talks, but my manager did.

"I mean, it's his job to be honest with me and to give me the full picture of what's going on in the paddock and what opportunities we might have. So, yes, there were other opportunities. But at the end of the day, we sat down with Ferrari and we made it happen quite quickly."

If Leclerc has a special relationship with Ferrari, the same can be said of his manager, Nicolas Todt: son of Jean, the former rally co-driver who masterminded Peugeot's rally and endurance programmes before leading Ferrari to world domination in the Michael Schumacher era, then shifted into politics as FIA president for over a decade. Todt Jr also managed long-time Ferrari driver Felipe Massa and still superintends the affairs of James Calado, a Le Mans winner with the Scuderia. He has a great many drivers on his books at all stages of the career ladder, and is a consummate player in the paddock.

But what Todt Jr enjoys to a greater extent at Ferrari than anywhere else is the ear of influential figures further up the food chain than the team principal – although he is a key ally of Fred Vasseur, having co-founded the ART GP organisation with him over two decades ago. Indeed, it's understood that Todt was instrumental in the removal of former team principal Mattia Binotto and his replacement by Vasseur in January 2023.

Nicolas Todt and Fred Vasseur Photo by: Getty Images

Having a manager so plugged into the senior echelons of power enables Leclerc to get what he wants with plausible deniability, such as Binotto's departure at a time when Ferrari's recovery trajectory underwent a major wobble, and the peculiarly communicated removal of Xavier Marcos as Leclerc's race engineer early in the 2024 season. He would not have quite the same influence if he were to shift to another team.

Equally, his influence depends not just on his performance but also his market value. If Ferrari has Leclerc locked into a contractual "golden prison", as our Italian colleague Roberto Chinchero puts it, then threatening to go elsewhere is no longer a lever he can pull.

Nobody doubts Leclerc's speed or commitment. Arguably he often over-commits, especially if the car isn't good enough. If the Ferrari is only 90% or 95% as good as the frontrunning car, Charles will try to make up the shortfall himself in the form of risk. That's why the Tifosi place him in the same rarefied space in their hearts as Gilles Villeneuve.

In recent seasons Leclerc's prime options outside Ferrari have been with Mercedes, Red Bull and McLaren, whose leaders have had to weigh up the performance benefits Leclerc would bring against the change in equilibrium it would cause. Nicolas Todt has certainly been busy doing the rounds of those teams over the past couple of years, but there is a tendency in the F1 media to get rather too excited when a driver's manager is spotted in another team's motorhome.

Sometimes a casual chat is just a casual chat. Sometimes a deal may actually be in progress, though the likelihood of this happening in plain sight is quite low. Often such encounters are staged in public purely to suit each party's agendas: for the team principal, to show their drivers they have other options on the table; for the manager, to show his client has interest from elsewhere.

To manage the internal equilibrium when it announced in January 2024 that Lewis Hamilton would be joining the following season, Ferrari also signed Leclerc to a long-term deal that theoretically reached until the end of 2029 with options, but which was also understood to have included a break point in 2026. On Leclerc's side this was to cover the possibility of Ferrari making a mess of the new technical regulations.

Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton Photo by: Getty Images

Instead, a more complex picture has emerged in which Ferrari has engineered a competitive car, and has been able to add performance to it in the form of upgrades – which hasn't always been true in the recent past. But it has also suffered operational misfires and blown several chances to score more points.

The dynamic in the other leading teams has also changed, though. When Leclerc signed up for the long term in 2024, this was partially because Todt knew Hamilton's move was coming, and had approached Mercedes with a view to Charles filling that vacancy. But when the break clause came into view early this season, Mercedes was perfectly happy with its line-up. The same could be said of McLaren, where Todt is also understood to have held discussions on and off with leaders including Andrea Stella and Zak Brown. When Todt was doing the rounds late last season, McLaren had two drivers in contention for the world championship.

It's also understood that Aston Martin made an approach at the end of last year, but this was at a time of yet more underperformance and internal wrangling in that benighted organisation, when recently installed managing technical partner Adrian Newey had MD and team principal Andy Cowell ousted. Given a choice between Ferrari and a farrago, Leclerc wisely chose door number one.

"I don't want to give up on my ultimate goal, which is to become a world champion with Ferrari," Leclerc said.

"And I believe in the project. I believe in every single person of the team. I think we are in a year where we've been showing innovation. We are very aggressive also in the production plan and in the upgrades we are bringing and that gives me lots of hopes for the future.

"Fred is a big reason on why I have signed again as well. I believe in Fred 200%."

Next time his contract is up for renewal, Leclerc will be over 30. Will he still have as many other opportunities then?

Sports.title: Ocon confirms he is a “free agent” for 2027 as rumours link Camara to Haas | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Esteban Ocon looks set to leave Haas at the end of the season as the driver admitted he is a “free agent” for 2027.

The 30-year-old joined the team from Alpine last year. He was out-scored by rookie team mate Oliver Bearman last year and lies behind his team mate in the standings.

“At the moment I’m definitely a free agent for next year,” said Ocon in Baku. “[There are] all these discussions and there are certain topics in the background that are out of my control at this moment. So I’m focused on the track, trying to deliver the best I can and getting the result that this team deserves.”

Neither Haas driver has scored since Ocon’s ninth-place finish in Monaco.

Ocon said he’s been “really happy with my personal performance” lately. “I think I’ve been getting the maximum out of the car for quite a while now and we’ve never doubted about it.

“Of course, when the car is working, it helps [you] to get something better. When the inconsistencies of the cars are here, where you struggle more, you don’t look as good.

“But I know that I’m exploiting the maximum of the package that I have every single time. So that’s strong.

Ocon ran 10th at the last round in Madrid prior to his pit stop, but fell to 11th at the finish.

“I’m the last one to have scored for the team in Monaco, but it’s been a while. But we were [running] in the points in Madrid, we got both Audis at the start, and we lost it in the pit lane. So this is something we will get stronger on now. But it was a very strong weekend.

“I’m happy with my performance. So we need to keep going here, hopefully have another strong one. There’s usually things happening on this track so I’m looking forward to driving here.”

Ferrari junior driver Rafael Camara, who is currently second in the Formula 2 standings, has been linked to the team. Bearman is also part of Ferrari’s young driver programme.

Sports.title: Antonelli has “perfect driving style” for 2026 cars – Russell | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Andrea Kimi Antonelli is enjoying an extraordinarily successful second season in Formula 1 because his driving style works perfectly with the current generation of cars, says his team mate.

George Russell is Antonelli’s closest rival at the top of the championship standings, but the second-year driver is 81 points ahead. This is a sharp contrast to last year, when Russell out-scored Antonelli by 319 points to 150.

While Russell said Antonelli’s ability was clear before this season, he believes the reduction in aerodynamic downforce and grip this year has played to his team mate’s strengths.

“Of course Kimi is extremely talented,” said Russell. “He’s an incredible driver and has been fast in his whole career.

“I think his driving style is very similar to what he had last year and I think with just how things have fallen this year, it’s kind of the perfect driving style for these cars.”

Russell believes the same is true of other drivers, including Lando Norris, who is the only driver to have won more than one round this season.

“If you look last year, there are definitely trends,” said Russell. “If you look at Brazil last year, Kimi had a really strong race and Lando won in Brazil, and they’re two drivers who are always very strong on the low grip tracks and they’re two drivers who are arguably the best-performing drivers of this season.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“He’s an amazing driver and he was of course doing extremely well last year as well. Let’s see next year if it changes or not, but certainly his natural driving style suits very well for this regulation.”

Charles Leclerc echoed Russell’s view that Antonelli’s potential was clear despite his patchy rookie campaign last year.

“I wish I knew, but clearly he’s doing something that works very well,” said Leclerc. “But to be honest, it’s not that it comes as a complete surprise.

“If I look at Kimi going through the junior ranks, I think it was quite clear for everybody that he had something very special. If you look obviously at his first year in Formula 1, I think he probably faced challenges – it is not up to me to go into detail, I don’t know, but surely he had some struggles in the first year – but this year has been extremely impressive. I mean, from the first race to now, he’s been perfect and driving at a very high level against a driver that I rate extremely high as well, which is George. So he’s doing an incredible job.”

However Leclerc said there is only so much he can tell about Antonelli’s qualities from outside the Mercedes team.

“To [tell] you exactly why he’s so fast, and why he is outstandingly fast this year compared to last year, is very difficult for me. We are all here analysing the data of everybody but we can only go up to a certain amount of detail, then you really need the data of the actual car to dig into more detail.

“So it’s difficult. But his laps look a lot on the limit but somehow he manages to do the lap when it counts and that’s been very impressive to watch.”

Sports.title: Hadjar says injured wrist is “still going to be painful for a while” after comeback | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Isack Hadjar says he is still in pain from his injured wrist as he returns to racing this weekend.

The Red Bull driver, who has missed the last three rounds, said his wrist is “good enough to drive, so that’s all I need.”

He said no surgery was required on the injury and a pre-event simulator session indicated it is now strong enough for him to be able to drive.

“I have a small fracture on the outside of the wrist and it’s just quite a long process,” said Hadjar. “I didn’t need any surgery so it’s all natural and it takes some time.

“It’s still going to be painful for a while. It’s going to be six weeks.

“It says that it’s strong enough at the moment to resist the tensions. I had a test on the sim, it went well. I think it’s a similar environment as the cockpit. It’s actually, if anything, nearly identical. So if it’s fine on the sim, with the adrenaline on track and everything, I think I should be okay.

“It’s just been the training sessions have not been fun because I’ve been doing basically nothing with the left limb, so it’s been a bit boring.”

Hadjar confirmed he spoke to multiple Moto GP champion Marc Marquez, who has broken many bones during his career, notably in 2020 when he made an early return from one injury only to sustain another. Hadjar said Marquez told him: “Not to race.”

Red Bull confirmed today Hadjar will continue to drive for them next season. Hadjar said the news is “good, it is nice, but it is natural.”

“I’m not here to be hopeful,” he explained. “I’m here to show what I do on track and naturally, the rest comes, so it’s normal in a way.”

Sports.title: Excessive focus on battle between Ferrari drivers is “not fair” – Leclerc | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Charles Leclerc says too much attention has been paid to the on-track battle between him and his team mate, particularly since their clash at Monza.

The Ferrari driver has already admitted he went too far in his first-lap battle with Lewis Hamilton when he forced his team mate wide at turn two.

“Turn two in Monza is something that I’ve said repeatedly is not something that we want to see ever happen again,” said Leclerc. “And that [was] going too far on my side.

“But I’ve been through it already. I think it’s pretty clear that we don’t necessarily have to write [rules of engagement for] those things, I think it’s clear enough.

“But again, I feel like it’s being over-discussed and over-analysed when it’s about the red cars, and that’s not really fair.”

He alluded to incidents between the McLaren and Mercedes drivers during the final laps of the same race. “In Monza, if you look at the four top teams, three of them had fights like this with a car finishing in the grass, and at the end of the day, the only thing we are speaking about still now is the red car, which I don’t think is fair.”

Leclerc said both drivers have exceeded the limits of what is acceptable at times but he is happy with how they race wheel-to-wheel.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“Of course there’s been moments where I went too far, where Lewis went too far, but I think the key in that is to discuss,” he said. “I’ve been with Ferrari since 2019 now and I know how everything we do is over-analysed, over-discussed and very often the conclusions that are taken after those kind of fights are the wrong ones.

“We only need to speak with Lewis to understand, we’ve been doing that all our life. We both want to win and there’s competition but we also want to win as a team and to make Ferrari come out on eventually. So that is the priority.

“I enjoy fighting with Lewis and that’s what is exciting in Formula 1 is to be fighting against the best and Lewis is definitely up there. So for me it’s a big challenge, but I’m enjoying it.”

Sports.title: “Money fears” delay F1’s decision on whether Middle East races will happen – report | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Formula One Management is delaying its decision over whether to cancel the final two rounds of the season due to concerns over money, according to a report in The Times.

F1 will not receive its huge fees from the Qatar and Abu Dhabi grand prix promoters if it calls off the races. If the promoters make the decision to cancel, they will bear the costs.

But the longer F1 leaves the decision, the harder it may be to organise a replacement for either race. Cancelling a race would reduce the number of points available and could affect the championship situation, potentially even deciding it. Andrea Kimi Antonelli leads the championship by 81 points with 233 available.

Domenicali has indicated F1 has a plan to replace the Abu Dhabi finale if that cannot go ahead. This is believed to be a race at Imola in Italy.

F1 has already cancelled the Bahrain and Saudi Arabian grands prix as a result of the war. A replacement for the former, titled the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, will take place next week at the Sepang International Circuit.

Earlier this month FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem said the governing body will be guided by local promoters on whether the events could go ahead.

“Being from that part of the world, we can’t jump the gun and just say, that’s it, we are cancelling and then cancel,” he said.

“Are we going to allow our people, our staff, the drivers or the teams to go at risk? No, of course not. We will not. But we’ll have to also listen to the governments and to the local promoter there.”

Sports.title: Red Bull confirms Hadjar will remain as Verstappen’s team mate in 2027 | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Red Bull has given a vote of confidence to Isack Hadjar, extending his contract to drive for the team again next year.

Hadjar made his debut in Formula 1 last year with Red Bull’s second team, Racing Bulls, before being promoted to their leading squad this year.

“Since joining us at the start of the year, he has been superb on and off track,” said team principal Laurent Mekies, “especially considering this is only his second Formula 1 season, which made extending his contract an easy decision.”

Although Hadjar did not compete in the last three rounds due to injury, Hadjar made an impressive start to life at Red Bull, taking a podium finish in his sixth appearance in Monaco. Before being forced out due to injury he had scored 71 points to Verstappen’s 109.

Red Bull has struggled to find an effective team mate to pair Verstappen with. The team handed Sergio Perez a two-year contract extension during 2024 but dropped him at the end of the year for Liam Lawson. Perez’s replacement lasted just two rounds at the start of last year before Red Bull dropped him. Yuki Tsunoda, who replaced Lawson, ended the season with the largest points deficit to a team mate ever seen in F1, leading Red Bull to make another change.

Mekies said Hadjar performed well from the outset after moving up to Red Bull. He will race for the team this weekend in Baku for the first time since the Hungarian Grand Prix in July.

“You could see from that first weekend in Melbourne that he handled the step up with remarkable composure and had earned his place in this seat,” said Mekies. “The period since his injury has been a difficult one for Isack, but this extension is a testament to how much we believe in him and we can’t wait to see him back out on track.”

Hadjar said he is “really excited” by his new deal. “From the moment I signed, I set out to dedicate myself to the team, and with the support of Laurent and everyone in Milton Keynes, I’ve been able to justify the faith they’ve had in me,” he said. “I’m constantly looking to listen, learn and push myself further every single day, which only makes me more excited about what lies ahead.”
