Sports.title: Shakur Stevenson Stalls Zuffa Boxing As Layoff Drags On
Sports.content:
Shakur Stevenson says a fight announcement is coming. Nearly eight months after he beat Teofimo Lopez, the opponent matters more than the tease.

“Even my haters begging for a fight announcement 😂 I love yall it’s coming lol,” Shakur posted on X.

The Lopez win gave Shakur the strongest moment of his career. He controlled a major fight at Madison Square Garden and had the crowd’s attention afterward, when he brought Conor Benn into the ring and called him “food.” That confrontation made a Benn fight look like an immediate possibility. It went nowhere.

Shakur then spent months discussing a fight with WBO welterweight champion Devin Haney at 144 pounds. Haney’s side said it accepted the proposed weight, but no fight followed. Shakur holds a WBO title at 140, yet he sought a welterweight champion three pounds below that division’s limit while his own challengers waited. Fans are entitled to ask which division he actually intends to fight in.

Zuffa Boxing signed Shakur during the layoff. Dana White paid for a fighter whose win over Teofimo had made him more valuable, but Zuffa has yet to put him in one of its rings. Jose “Rayo” Valenzuela, another Zuffa fighter, called for the fight. Shakur rejected it.

The WBO has already indicated that a mandatory defense is due. It should follow through with a formal order and a clear timetable if Shakur’s next fight does not satisfy that obligation. A champion’s search for a bigger payday cannot leave the rest of the 140-pound division waiting indefinitely.

The Zuffa brass thought they were purchasing the premier American pound-for-pound star right after his masterclass against Teofimo Lopez. Instead, they bought eight months of dead air, endless social media bickering, and an asset that bleeds public interest by the week.

A luxury car loses thousands the minute you roll it off the dealer lot; Shakur Stevenson has been parked in the driveway collecting dust, losing resale value with every single tweet.

What must drive Dana White mad behind closed doors is the refusal to cooperate with company business. In the UFC model, in-house matchups are the lifeblood of the company. Jose Valenzuela stepped up to hand Zuffa a ready-made fight featuring a dangerous, aggressive puncher against their prized technician. Shakur turned him down. Turning down internal company fights while angling for safety catches against Devin Haney at 144 pounds shows an athlete trying to run matchmaking from his couch.

White and the executive room would be entirely justified in pulling the plug, swallowing their pride, and sending Shakur right back out to free agency to waste somebody else’s time and money.

Handing Shakur an ultimatum list is the exact kind of hardball Dana White needs to play. If Zuffa lets him dictate terms, negotiate catchweights, and cherry pick soft touches after an eight-month vacation, they surrender control of their own promotional venture. Giving him three names with a take-one-or-walk clause would instantly test his nerve.

Ernesto “Tito” Mercado belongs right at the top of that sheet. Mercado is a wrecking ball with legitimate dynamite in both hands, stopping 18 of his 19 opponents. He attacks the body with nasty intent, walks through fire, and possesses the kind of brute physical strength that makes safety-first technicians sweat through twelve rounds. The light welterweight division has become a ghost town filled with inactive beltholders and sparring partners, making Mercado the only genuine killer at 140 with the punch to crack Shakur’s defensive shell.

Shakur wants no part of a heavy-handed pressure fighter who will force him to run for his life. Dragging elite sharks up from 135 would apply maximum heat. Andy Cruz is pure agony for Shakur. Cruz boasts Olympic gold credentials, textbook Cuban ring craft, and the punch placement to neutralize Shakur’s potshotting style. Cruz represents the one fighter who can beat Shakur at his own game, outboxing him from the outside while forcing the pace.

Floyd Schofield brings the explosive athletic threat Shakur previously avoided when their scheduled Riyadh bout dissolved. Schofield possesses blazing hand speed, sharp combinations, and the hunger of a young lion with nothing to lose.

Forcing Shakur to sign against Mercado, Cruz, or Schofield would strip away the diva behavior in seconds. If he refuses all three, White can rip up the contract, write off the sunk cost, and show the boxing world that Zuffa refuses to be held hostage by fighters who prefer typing to throwing punches.

Sports.title: Filip Hrgovic Calls Daniel Dubois Easier Than Itauma
Sports.content:
Daniel Dubois stopped Filip Hrgovic in 2024, but Hrgovic believes a rematch would be easier for him than his recent win over Moses Itauma. His argument comes down to speed and stance. It leaves out what Dubois did after Hrgovic found him.

During their initial clash in 2024, Hrgovic discovered zero trouble finding Dubois with flush right hands. He landed them repeatedly, and it meant nothing. Dubois absorbed that punishment, marched forward through the artillery, and chopped Hrgovic down in the eighth round after ripping the Croatian’s face apart with heavy lacerations. Dubois proved that hand speed and southpaw angles mean very little when an iron-chinned puncher refuses to back down.

“I think fights against Kabayel and Dubois would be easier than this fight,” Hrgovic stated to talkSPORT Boxing. “Stylistically, speedwise, they will be much easier fights because they’re not so fast. They’re not southpaws. They’re easier to box.”

That is insane logic from an experienced fighter. Itauma faded badly down the stretch because he is a young fighter lacking professional mileage. Dubois operates as an entirely different animal. Dubois applies unrelenting physical pressure, throws heavy leather through the guard, and relishes violent exchanges. Hrgovic found the target in their first bout; he simply lacked the firepower to keep the bigger puncher off his chest. The damage Dubois inflicted on Hrgovic’s scar tissue will reopen in an instant if they share a ring again.

Hrgovic admitted he contemplated retirement in the immediate aftermath of his war with Itauma, showing the mental and physical toll of top-tier prizefighting. Heavyweights contemplating walking away are already feeling the wear on their tires.

Before Hrgovic can even daydream about a lucrative unification payday with Dubois, he must deal with mandatory challenger Frank Sanchez. The slick Cuban possesses the ring discipline and counter-punching ability to derail those stadium dreams in an instant. If Hrgovic treats dangerous contenders as mere stepping stones while chasing a Dubois rematch, he will quickly discover that getting demolished twice by the same man is a dreadful career strategy.

The IBF is historically ruthless about stripping champions who attempt to sidestep their mandatory obligations, and Frank Sanchez already took step-aside money once so Hrgovic and Itauma could contest the vacant title.

Sanchez and his team have zero incentive to sit on their hands again. They smell blood; they know Hrgovic absorbed heavy punishment to get that belt, and they want their shot. Treating Sanchez as an afterthought is dangerous matchmaking arrogance. Sanchez may lack the raw fanfare of Dubois, but the Cuban possesses real ring IQ, sharp counter-punching, fast hands, and defensive discipline.

He does not brawl recklessly or empty his gas tank in three rounds like Itauma did. If Hrgovic enters the ring sluggish, overconfident, or nursing physical mileage from his previous war, Sanchez will happily box circles around him, pile up rounds, and snatch that IBF belt before Hrgovic ever sniffs a unification payday. As for an Itauma rematch, Frank Warren and Queensberry are not foolish to take that risk. Itauma showed he is currently an explosive, three-round frontrunner who melted under sustained veteran pressure.

Throwing a 21-year-old right back into the same firefight that just broke him mentally and physically would be silly. Itauma needs rebuilding against mid-tier opposition to learn pacing and distance control before he ever shares a ring with Hrgovic again. That leaves Hrgovic in a bind. The Dubois rematch is where the massive payday is, but Dubois is tied up with his own business, and Hrgovic cannot legally get to that fight with the IBF belt around his waist unless he handles Sanchez first.

If Hrgovic tries to bypass Sanchez, he gets stripped, loses his leverage, and ends up walking into a Dubois rematch as a battered contender rather than a reigning champion. He has to take the dangerous, low-reward Cuban fighter, and if his head is already in a stadium fight with Dubois, Sanchez is exactly the type of technician to ruin the entire script.

Sports.title: Keith Connolly Says Conor Benn’s Comeback Pays 100% More Than Hearn Offered
Sports.content:
Conor Benn took a two-round thrashing from Ryan, yet his management still secured a lucrative deal for his next fight. Keith Connolly revealed Benn has a guaranteed purse for a return bout, a sum more than 100% higher than Eddie Hearn’s original offer for a Rolly Romero clash.

Connolly did not reveal either figure. His comparison still raises an awkward question for Zuffa: after paying Benn to face Garcia, what kind of fight justifies paying him substantially again?

“In the deal that we made for Conor, we have a substantial comeback number,” Connolly told talkSPORT. He said the payment was negotiated to give Benn a comeback fight in which he can get a win. Connolly also said Zuffa cannot drop Benn under the contract because of the Garcia defeat.

Connolly did his job for Benn. Give him an easy opponent, and he probably gets the win, but who’s going to be impressed after Ryan took him out in two rounds? Put him in with someone who can punch, and Zuffa risks paying a big guarantee to watch Benn lose again.

Benn can still sell a fight in Britain. He’s Nigel Benn’s son, he has a following, and there’s another Chris Eubank Jr. fight to make. But Ryan exposed the part of the sales pitch that said Benn belonged with the best welterweights. He’d looked poor in several fights since coming back; getting stopped in two rounds in his first world title shot made that much harder to sell his fights.

Connolly expects Benn to fight Chris Eubank Jr. a third time, and that’s Zuffa’s best chance of making money on his return. British fans know the family rivalry, even after Ryan stopped Benn in two rounds. Beating an easy opponent first might give Benn a win, but it won’t erase what happened against Garcia. Connolly made sure Benn gets paid either way.

Zuffa bought a circus act, and now they are stuck footing the bill for the cleanup. Dana White thought he was purchasing an elite British star with crossover appeal. Instead, Ryan took two rounds to turn Benn into an international laughingstock.

Now Zuffa holds a contract guaranteeing Benn millions for a return date, with nowhere left to hide him. They cannot put him in with an actual contender at 160 or 168 because any legitimate puncher will put him into retirement. They cannot put him on pay-per-view against an imported tomato can because fans will not pay fifty dollars to watch an unranked punching bag fall down in ninety seconds. That leaves Chris Eubank Jr. as the only escape route.

The promotional idea for a third fight between these privileged sons of famous British legends has completely changed. Nobody with working eyes believes this is a meeting of championship contenders. The athletic intrigue disappeared the moment Ryan landed his right hand, and Benn hit the deck.

The only angle left to sell is morbid curiosity. British boxing fans will tune in for one simple reason: to watch Benn get knocked out again. The novelty of the family rivalry is gone. It has turned into a pure demolition watch party. Eubank has every physical advantage, and he knows Benn cannot take a punch from someone with genuine power. If Zuffa pulls the trigger on the trilogy, they are selling tickets to an execution.

Benn-Eubank Jr. III can do strong business in the UK, but it will not generate the kind of money Zuffa needs to break even on the massive guarantees they handed out.

The British domestic market operates on nostalgia. UK ticket buyers will pack a stadium like Tottenham Hotspur again simply because of the family names. The problem is the pay-per-view numbers and international interest. Benn getting humiliated by Ryan inside two rounds destroyed any illusion that he is an elite global star. Overseas buyers in the United States will not pay sixty or seventy dollars for a domestic grudge match between an exposed welterweight and an aging middleweight.

Sports.title: WBC Orders Carlos Adames to Face Meiirim Nursultanov Next
Sports.content:
Meiirim Nursultanov was supposed to fight for an interim belt Saturday. Instead, he is going straight to Carlos Adames for the full WBC middleweight title.

The WBC ordered Adames to face his mandatory challenger next, Dan Rafael reported Tuesday. If the two sides cannot make a deal, a purse bid is scheduled for October 20. The winner must then fight interim champion Jesus Ramos Jr.

Nursultanov was set to face Ramos on Saturday’s PBC card before Ramos was hospitalized and withdrew with what PBC described as food poisoning. The WBC had previously said the winner of that fight would challenge Adames. Ramos had a sound reason to withdraw, but Nursultanov was ready to fight and should not have to wait for his title opportunity because the bout fell through.

The change gives Nursultanov more than a new opponent. He can fight for the full belt without first risking a loss to Ramos, and the WBC order gives him a deadline for negotiations. He still has to beat Adames, a difficult champion, but he no longer has another fight between him and the title shot he has sought.

Adames, meanwhile, has a mandatory to deal with rather than an open choice of opponents. Nursultanov offers a hard fight without the obvious payday of a marquee name. If the camps cannot agree on terms, the purse bid could also take control of the promotion out of their hands. That makes October 20 a meaningful date for both fighters, though an order is no guarantee the fight gets made.

Ramos keeps his claim to the winner, but his wait could stretch well beyond this fall. First, Adames and Nursultanov have to negotiate, fight, and recover. The WBC has given all three men a sequence; now it has to see that sequence through. Adames is completely trapped in boxing purgatory. He is the ultimate poster child for high risk, zero reward.

When Adames went to Riyadh and took Hamzah Sheeraz to school, he exposed the British fighter for everyone to see. He walked out of Saudi Arabia with a controversial draw while Sheeraz packed his bags and bolted straight out of the division to super middleweight rather than dare run that back. That fight cost Adames his golden ticket. If he had been given the decision he clearly earned, he would have commanded the massive purses and respect of an undisputed or marquee kingpin in Riyadh Season shows. Instead, he got left holding an empty bag.

Calling out Janibek Alimkhanuly and Osleys Iglesias was pure desperation to find someone with a pulse, but both routes were dead ends. Janibek has his own promotional mess and brings virtually no ticket sales or mainstream buzz to make the risk worthwhile for either side. Iglesias is a monster who punches like a mule and brings even less commercial appeal. Nobody with options wants to look in Adames’ direction because he is awkward, hits hard, possesses an iron chin, and cannot sell out an arena on his own name.

Now the WBC has boxed him into a corner. Instead of landing a lucrative unification or a recognizable name, Adames gets Meiirim Nursultanov. This is the classic who needs him scenario at its absolute worst. Nursultanov is a stone-cold Kazakh grinder with deep amateur seasoning who will make every second of every round physically miserable. If Adames wins a grueling decision, nobody outside the hardcore fanbase will care, and the casuals will not give him an ounce of credit. If he gets clipped or outpointed, his entire career plummets off a cliff.

Adames wanted the glory, the rematches, and the unifications. Instead, the boxing business did what it always does to guys without fanbases: shoved him into a basement fight against a dangerous mandatory where he has everything to lose and almost nothing to gain.

Sports.title: Gene Tunney Made Jack Dempsey Chase His Title
Sports.content:
Jack Dempsey’s left hook was most dangerous when he could weave inside and plant his feet. Gene Tunney spent their September 23, 1926, fight making both steps difficult. In the rain at Philadelphia’s Sesquicentennial Stadium, Tunney took the heavyweight championship by unanimous decision over ten rounds.

Dempsey had not defended the title since his 1923 knockout of Luis Firpo. Tunney had remained active and had already fought Harry Greb five times. The layoff invited questions about Dempsey’s timing, but Tunney gave him an immediate, practical problem: getting close enough to throw with full force.

Tunney watched Dempsey come forward and met him with straight punches. A right hand on one of the champion’s early rushes showed the danger of lunging in without making Tunney give ground first. When Dempsey tried again, Tunney changed his position and made him start the attack over. The champion was still dangerous at close range, but he could rarely keep Tunney there.

The rain made the canvas slippery for both men. It is tempting to blame Dempsey’s trouble closing the distance on his footing, yet the wet ring did not stop Tunney from punching and repositioning. Tunney’s timing was the more visible obstacle: he caught Dempsey on the way in, then denied him the stationary target his hooks needed. Contemporary accounts described the fighters slipping on the canvas as the rain grew heavier.

Tunney also refused to spend ten rounds merely fleeing. He stood his ground when he had the opening, drove Dempsey back at times and worked his body as well as his head. Dempsey’s attacks came in bursts, followed by pauses while he searched for another way through. That gave Tunney repeated chances to regain the distance he wanted.

By the final round, Dempsey’s left eye was badly swollen and he was still trying to force his way inside. Tunney continued to meet him with punches. Referee Tommy Reilly and judges Mike Bernstein and Frank Brown awarded the challenger a clear decision.

Dempsey’s three year absence may have cost him sharpness. The fight cannot measure how much. What it showed was Tunney denying him a sustained attack for ten rounds. Dempsey never stopped trying to reach him; Tunney kept making him pay for the attempt.

Stanley Weston / public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

Sports.title: Tim Bradley Backs O’Shaquie Foster to Pressure Emanuel Navarrete
Sports.content:
Tim Bradley is picking O’Shaquie Foster to defeat Emanuel Navarrete, but the call comes attached to an urgent reality check. Foster cannot spend thirty-six minutes waiting around for an immaculate counterpunch. Navarrete throws volume in bundles, keeps men moving in reverse, and steals rounds from guys who are content to admire their own defense.

The two meet October 24 in San Antonio with three super featherweight titles on the line.

Navarrete brings an unorthodox, lunging assault that presents a massive trap. He leaps into wide hooks, throws uppercuts from his knees, and squares his stance right in the line of fire. Foster owns the hand speed to slice Navarrete down the middle while those feet are still airborne. The opening vanishes instantly if Foster retreats instead of planting his feet to fire.

“You ain’t getting no points for no damn defense,” Bradley said on his channel when detailing the habit Foster has of letting opponents throw punches without paying an immediate tax.

Foster cannot afford to tuck behind a high shell while Navarrete clubs away at his elbows and shoulders. Those heavy thuds count in the eyes of ringside officials, particularly in Texas, where aggressive punch output always gets rewarded. Foster already tasted that bitter lesson during his robbery loss against Robson Conceicao, where he landed the cleaner counters yet gave away the visual contest.

The real blueprint involves ripping straight to Navarrete’s midsection and forcing him to drag his feet in reverse. Navarrete lacks the balance or footwork to operate on his back foot, but Foster must put hands on him early to make that happen. If Foster surrenders ring real estate and searches for single counters, he hands Navarrete the exact grinder bout he wants.

Sitting back and relying on defense against Emanuel Navarrete as the B-side is professional suicide. Navarrete is an established ticket seller, a fan favorite, and an all-action Mexican slugger fighting in front of a heavily pro-Navarrete Texas crowd. Every time Navarrete unleashes an ugly four-punch flurry that bounces off Foster’s gloves and forearms, ten thousand people in the arena are going to scream as if someone just got dropped. Judges hear that roar, see the constant forward march, and instinctively score the round for the aggressor.

Foster’s biggest flaw is that he falls in love with making guys miss by an inch without making them pay for it. He treats the sweet science like an academic exercise where simply not getting hit clean is enough to bank three minutes. It is not. That exact minimalist habit burned him against Robson Conceicao in Newark, where Foster clearly outboxed the guy on pure contact quality, threw far too little, and watched the belts get handed to the man who simply looked busier.

The similarities between Foster and Shakur Stevenson expose the exact problem. Shakur gets away with his safety-first style because he commands ring generalship with an authoritative, southpaw lead hand that physically dictates the distance. Shakur controls the geography of the ring so thoroughly that his opponents stop throwing because they feel stupid missing. Foster does not control real estate that way. He retreats in straight lines, covers up, and lets his opponents dictate where the action takes place while he waits for a clean counter window.

Against an awkward buzzsaw who throws 80 punches a round from his knees, his hips, and odd ceiling angles, waiting for the perfect counter means giving away forty seconds of every minute. Navarrete’s punches are heavy and crude. Even when they land on the shoulders, they physically push a retreating fighter back.

Foster does not need to get reckless and swing for the fences, but he absolutely must stand his ground and fire first. If he allows Navarrete to initiate every single sequence and just tries to slip and counter in spurts, he will walk back to his corner after twelve rounds feeling like a master boxer, only to hear the ring announcer read out scores that send him home empty-handed.

Sports.title: Rocky Marciano’s Greatest Win Almost Got Away
Sports.content:
Jersey Joe Walcott was ahead on the scorecards when Rocky Marciano caught him with a right hand in the 13th round on September 23, 1952. That punch made Marciano heavyweight champion. Seventy-four years later, the rounds before it offer a better way to judge him than his perfect record alone.

Walcott knocked Marciano down in the first. He was the older man, but he was also the reigning champion, and his skill gave Marciano trouble deep into the fight. Marciano kept pressing until Walcott made one mistake he could punish. It took him nearly thirteen rounds to find it.

The familiar criticism is that Marciano beat aging champions. There is truth in the ages: Walcott was 38 when Marciano took his title, and Joe Louis was 37 when Marciano stopped him in 1951. Louis was past his best. Walcott’s age, though, does little to explain a fight he was winning before Marciano knocked him out. Marciano gets too much credit if every famous name on his record is treated as a prime opponent. He gets too little if the Walcott fight is dismissed by reading a birth date.

Their rematch lasted one round. Marciano’s next title defense, against Roland LaStarza, took eleven. LaStarza had pushed him to a split decision before Marciano won the championship; in their second meeting, Marciano stopped him. Ezzard Charles then took Marciano the full fifteen rounds before losing their first fight. Three months later, Charles badly cut Marciano’s nose in the rematch, but Marciano finished him in the eighth.

Marciano’s final opponent, light heavyweight champion Archie Moore, dropped him early. Marciano got up and knocked Moore out in the ninth round on September 21, 1955. He retired after that fight with six successful title defenses and a 49–0 record.

The record tells us Marciano never lost. The Walcott fight tells us something harder to capture in a number: he was hurt, behind, and still dangerous enough to change the result with one punch.

Sports.title: Denzel Bentley’s Yoenli Hernandez Defense Heads to Purse Bid
Sports.content:
Denzel Bentley’s first defense as WBO middleweight champion is headed toward the fight he hoped to delay. Talks with mandatory challenger Yoenli Hernandez have failed, with a September 29 purse bid set to decide who stages the bout.

Bentley had a unification with IBF champion Aaron McKenna in reach. The WBO blocked it, ruling that its overdue mandatory obligation passed to Bentley when he was elevated to full champion. The sanctioning body also rejected a proposed title fight with Conor Benn. Bentley has the belt, but little freedom to choose what comes next.

Bentley has every reason to be frustrated. McKenna offered a UK fight with commercial appeal and, on paper, a more manageable opponent. Instead, he must face Hernandez, a highly regarded Cuban who brings far less name recognition and a serious risk of taking his belt. Bentley earned the interim title in the ring, but gained the full championship through elevation. If Hernandez beats him, there is no guarantee he finds another route to a world title. The McKenna unification and the bargaining power that comes with being champion would be gone.

Hernandez is a two-time amateur world champion, but Bentley has the deeper professional experience. He went twelve rounds with Janibek Alimkhanuly; Hernandez has yet to fight twelve as a professional. Bentley’s best chance is to close the distance with discipline, work to the body, and make Hernandez fight at a pace he cannot set himself entirely. Loading up on single punches would give the challenger time to move and score between Bentley’s attacks.

Hernandez’s August win over Francisco Daniel Veron offers a useful caution, though not a ready-made plan. Veron kept pressing and reached the final bell, but two judges gave Hernandez the fight by wide margins; the third scored it even. Pressure alone did not erase the Cuban’s cleaner work.

The purse bid adds another uncertainty. If a promoter outside Bentley’s camp wins, the champion may have to defend away from home. The WBO’s $200,000 minimum bid says where bidding starts, not what either fighter will earn.

Bentley wanted McKenna and a chance to add a second belt. Now he must beat Hernandez to keep the first one. For a champion who waited years for this position, that is a steep price for a fight with so little commercial upside.

Facing Yoenli carries massive tactical risk, but it remains the only move that preserves Bentley’s championship equity. Even if Hernandez outboxes him, Bentley at least collects a champion’s 75 percent purse bid share and goes down swinging with his career earnings maximized. If he vacates out of self-preservation, he surrenders the title for zero dollars, forfeits the McKenna unification anyway, and brands himself as a champion who ran from his mandatory.

In professional boxing, getting outpointed by a world-class Cuban amateur hurts, but surrendering the belt in a conference room without getting paid ruins a career far worse.

Without the WBO belt, Bentley reverts instantly to being a tough, high-risk, low-reward domestic gatekeeper. At thirty-one years old, clawing back up the sanctioning body rankings could take years, with no guarantee of ever receiving another title shot.

Ghana News.title: “I don’t see any rational basis” – Inusah Fuseini rejects proposed five-year term
Ghana News.content:
Former Tamale Central MP Inusah Fuseini has rejected the proposal to extend the tenure of the President and Members of Parliament from four to five years.

The proposal is contained in the report of the Constitution Review Committee chaired by Professor H. Kwasi Prempeh.

The government has accepted the recommendation, arguing that an additional year would give governments more time to formulate, implement and assess policies.

However, speaking at a press briefing on Wednesday, September 23, ahead of an Institute of Economic Affairs (IEA) seminar on the constitutional review, Mr Fuseini questioned the rationale for extending the tenure.

He argued that the current four-year term already provides sufficient time for an elected government to implement its policies.

“And if you are running four years, the last year is used for campaigning for re-election. Probably you can have three years if you have been re-elected a second time.

“So why do you say five? If the argument is that you have the first year to set up your government and the last year to run a campaign, what is the rationale for five? Because from that argument, you see that two years have been lost. So why five? I don’t see any rational basis for five,” he said.

Mr Fuseini also rejected the argument that a five-year term would improve policy continuity.

According to him, the 1992 Constitution already provides for continuity in governance through the Directive Principles of State Policy.

“Talk about continuity. The Constitution already anticipated that. That is why in the Directive Principles of State Policy, every succeeding President must, as far as possible, continue with ongoing projects,” he said.

He argued that the constitutional arrangement recognises that a President may not be able to complete all policy initiatives within a single term and that subsequent governments can continue or improve on existing projects.

“So the Constitution anticipated that a President might not be able to exhaust all his policy options and the government may improve the projects that it has undertaken. And I think the constitutional arrangement must be respected,” he added.

The former MP was speaking ahead of the IEA’s “Views and Reflections” seminar on the Prempeh Committee’s report and the government’s position on proposed constitutional reforms.

The IEA itself has rejected the proposed extension of presidential and parliamentary terms, arguing that four years is sufficient for an elected government to implement its programme

Ghana News.title: Constitution shouldn’t be amended simply because years have passed – IEA
Ghana News.content:
The Institute of Economic Affairs (IEA) has cautioned against amending Ghana’s Constitution merely because a certain number of years have elapsed.

The Institute said that while there are merits to the arguments on both sides of the constitutional review debate, there should be a continuous assessment of how the Constitution is functioning.

According to the IEA representative, such continuous examination does not necessarily mean that amendments must be made at fixed intervals.

“We should continuously examine how the Constitution is functioning. But that does not mean the Constitution must be amended simply because a particular number of years have passed. Constitutional maintenance should be continuous, even if constitutional amendments are occasional."

The comments come amid ongoing discussions over the process of reviewing Ghana’s 1992 Constitution and proposals for reforms to address identified gaps in the country’s governance framework.

The IEA maintained that the focus should be on ensuring that the Constitution continues to function effectively, rather than treating the passage of time as an automatic basis for amendment.

Ghana News.title: Access Bank, Visa launch ‘Visa Accept’ in Ghana
Ghana News.content:
Visa, a global leader in digital payments, in partnership with Access Bank (Ghana) Plc., today unveiled Visa Accept, a solution that allows micro, nano and small merchants across Ghana to accept contactless card payments directly on their smartphones, without the need for additional hardware.

Visa Accept helps to address a key challenge facing many of Ghana's smallest businesses.

While digital payment adoption continues to grow across the country, many micro and nano merchants have remained excluded from card acceptance due to the cost and complexity of traditional point-of-sale (POS) infrastructure.

Through Visa Accept, merchants can create a seller profile within the Access Bank mobile banking app and begin accepting payments within minutes.

Consumers can pay using a contactless card or mobile wallet, scan a QR code, or receive a secure payment link, eliminating the need for dedicated POS hardware. Funds are settled to the merchant's existing bank account in near real-time, while transactions benefit from Visa's security standards and consumer protections, including support for disputes and refunds.

" Consumer demand for digital payments in Ghana continues to grow, but acceptance among smaller merchants continues to face challenges. Visa Accept is helping close that gap by making it easier and more affordable for micro and small businesses to accept digital payments using the smartphones they already own. By expanding access to digital acceptance, we are helping more merchants participate in the digital economy while providing consumers with more ways to pay easily and securely." said Fabrice Konan, Country Manager, Visa Ghana.

Also speaking on the launch, Eugene Ocansey, Executive Director, Retail and SME Banking, Access Bank (Ghana) Plc, said “Access Bank is proud to be the first bank in Ghana to partner Visa on this solution. The bulk of businesses in our country are SMEs, and Visa Accept gives us an opportunity to start transitioning those who are informal into the formal economy. When a merchant has a tool that brings in their money and makes their cash flow visible, we can understand what the business does, and that is what makes the average SME bankable. Visa brings the technology; Access Bank brings the reach to put it in the hands of every merchant who needs it."

Visa Accept is now available to eligible Access Bank Ghana customers nationwide.

Merchants can enroll through the Access Bank mobile banking app or visit an Access Bank branch for assistance.

Ghana News.title: ‘Our young people must inherit story of what Africa created, not lost’ – Mahama
Ghana News.content:
President John Dramani Mahama has called for the restoration of Africa’s cultural heritage to help future generations reconnect with the continent’s history, achievements and identity.

He said young Africans should not inherit only the narrative of what the continent lost through conquest, colonialism and the removal of its cultural treasures, but should also have access to evidence of what African societies created and achieved.

Speaking at a High-Level Side Event on the Next Steps on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York, President Mahama said the return of African artefacts was important to how young people understand their history.

“Our young people must inherit more than the story of what Africa lost. They must inherit the story of what Africa created,” he said.

He said the presence of African artefacts on the continent would allow future generations to directly engage with tangible evidence of their ancestors’ achievements.

According to President Mahama, a young African visiting a museum on the continent should be able to see evidence that Africa’s history did not begin with subjugation.

“She learns that her history did not begin with subjugation. She learns that her ancestors built empires, mastered metallurgy, engineered complex political systems, and created sublime art.”

He said the restitution of cultural heritage was therefore not simply about returning physical objects but about restoring connections between African communities, their history and their identity.

President Mahama said Ghana’s campaign for reparatory justice was focused on building partnerships to address the consequences of historical injustices.

“Ghana does not come to this hall to assign guilt for the past. We come to forge a partnership with the present to repair the future.”

He said the ultimate goal was to ensure that Africa’s cultural heritage continued through its return to the communities and institutions from which it was taken.

Ghana News.title: Afreximbank, GIIF and 24-Hour Economy Authority pact marks real progress toward 24-hour economy agenda
Ghana News.content:
Amo Agyapong

Ghana’s 24-Hour Economy agenda has reached an important project-development milestone with the signing of a Joint Project Preparation Facility (JPPF) Framework Agreement between the African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank), the Ghana Infrastructure Investment Fund (GIIF) and the 24-Hour Economy Authority.

The significance of the agreement goes beyond the signing ceremony. For a country seeking to transform ambitious economic priorities into productive assets, industrial capacity, export opportunities and sustainable employment, project preparation is where vision begins to acquire financial and commercial credibility.

The JPPF is designed to accelerate the preparation of selected priority projects under Ghana’s 24-Hour Economy and Accelerated Export Development Programme (24H+). The wider 24Hour investment pipeline is currently valued at approximately US$11.5 billion, while Afreximbank and GIIF will each make an initial US$5 million contribution to finance eligible technical, financial, legal and advisory work.

This distinction is important. The US$10 million initial commitment is not US$10 million of construction financing for the US$11.5 billion pipeline. Rather, it is project-preparation capital intended to address the technical, financial, legal, commercial and structuring issues that can prevent potentially transformative projects from becoming bankable. Projects will be selected through joint screening and approval.

From Vision to Bankability

In development finance, one of the most persistent obstacles to infrastructure and industrial investment is not necessarily the absence of capital. It is the absence of well-prepared, properly structured and investment-ready projects. A project may have strategic importance and strong political support, but that alone does not make it financeable.

Investors and lenders require answers to fundamental questions: What is the project’s commercial model? What are its projected cash flows? Who bears which risks? What are the legal and regulatory arrangements? What is the market demand? What is the environmental and social impact? What are the construction and operational risks? How will foreign-exchange exposure be managed? What guarantees, offtake arrangements or revenue mechanisms are required? The JPPF addresses this critical upstream stage.

Afreximbank brings project-development and capital-mobilisation expertise; GIIF contributes local project origination and infrastructure-investment capabilities; while the 24-Hour Economy Authority is responsible for bringing forward strategic projects and coordinating relevant government stakeholders. The three institutions will jointly screen and prioritise projects for support. That institutional architecture matters. It creates a framework in which policy priorities, project development and investment expertise can converge before projects reach the market for financing.

The Real Test Is Project Delivery

For Ghana, however, the ultimate measure of success will not be the number of projects identified, feasibility studies completed or agreements signed. The real test will be whether projects move successfully through the project lifecycle—from concept, feasibility and structuring to financing, procurement, construction, commissioning and operations. This is where project governance becomes indispensable.

The country has no shortage of development ambitions. What Ghana needs is a stronger and more systematic capacity to convert those ambitions into projects that can withstand technical, financial, commercial, legal and institutional scrutiny. The JPPF therefore represents an opportunity to strengthen the project-development pipeline before billions of dollars of capital are committed. As Presidential Adviser on the 24-Hour Economy and Accelerated Export Development, Augustus Obuadum Tanoh, noted, the programme is delivered through transformational projects and projects must be properly prepared to attract capital. That principle should become central to Ghana’s infrastructure and development-finance culture.

Building a Bankable Project Pipeline

The sectors targeted by the facility demonstrate the breadth of Ghana’s economic ambitions. They include energy and infrastructure; logistics and digital connectivity; industrial parks; manufacturing and agro-processing; minerals beneficiation; tourism; creative industries; and healthcare. These are not isolated investments. Properly integrated, they can form interconnected economic corridors and productive value chains:

Energy supports manufacturing.

Infrastructure connects production centres to markets.

Logistics reduces the cost of moving goods.

Digital connectivity enables modern commerce and industrial management.

Industrial parks provide platforms for production.

Agro-processing creates value beyond primary agricultural production.

Minerals beneficiation can move Ghana higher up global value chains.

Tourism and the creative economy diversify sources of foreign exchange.

Healthcare contributes to human capital and economic resilience.

The project-delivery challenge, therefore, is to ensure that these investments are developed not as disconnected projects but as commercially coherent components of a national economic system.

GIIF’s Institutional Opportunity

One of the particularly significant aspects of the JPPF is that its benefits extend beyond individual projects. The arrangement includes training, knowledge transfer, capacity building and staff secondments designed to strengthen GIIF’s internal project-preparation capabilities. This is strategically important.

A country cannot sustainably depend on external advisers to prepare every major infrastructure transaction. Ghana needs institutions capable of originating, screening, appraising, structuring, negotiating and monitoring complex projects over the long term.

The capacity-building component can therefore help deepen GIIF’s institutional capabilities and contribute to the development of a stronger national project-preparation ecosystem.

GIIF Chief Executive Officer Nana Dwemoh Benneh has described the partnership as strengthening the Fund’s ability to move priority projects from concept to investment readiness, while giving its professionals access to Afreximbank’s project-preparation expertise. That institutional knowledge transfer may ultimately prove as valuable as the initial preparation funding.

From Preparation to Investment

Project preparation must not become an end in itself. Ghana must establish clear gateways through which projects progress from preparation to investment decision and then to implementation.

A robust project pipeline should distinguish between projects that are strategically desirable, projects that are technically feasible, projects that are financially viable and projects that are genuinely bankable and investment-ready. This requires disciplined project appraisal, realistic cost estimates, credible demand assessments, transparent procurement arrangements, appropriate risk allocation and strong governance. It also requires clarity on the source of the eventual construction and long-term financing.

The JPPF can prepare projects for financing, but each project will still require its own capital structure and investment case. The preparation facility should therefore be viewed as an upstream catalyst for much larger pools of public, private and institutional capital. This is where the partnership with Afreximbank becomes particularly relevant.

Afreximbank’s continental trade and capital-mobilisation mandate can help connect Ghanaian projects with a broader African investment and trade-finance ecosystem. The objective should be to ensure that projects emerging from the facility are capable of attracting financing beyond the initial preparation phase.

Infrastructure Must Deliver Economic Value

For Ghana’s project-delivery community, the central question should always be simple: What economic value will the completed project create, and how sustainably will that value be delivered? Infrastructure should not be measured only by the amount spent or the physical asset constructed.

The stronger measure is what the asset enables.

Does a logistics project reduce transportation costs?

Does an industrial park attract productive investment?

Does an energy project improve reliability and industrial competitiveness?

Does an agro-processing facility create value for farmers and expand exports?

Does digital infrastructure improve business productivity?

Does a healthcare investment strengthen access and service delivery?

These questions place project delivery within the wider framework of economic transformation.

A New Standard for Project Preparation

The Afreximbank, GIIF and 24Hour Economy Authority partnership also has the potential to establish a higher standard for how Ghana prepares major national projects. Every major project should have a clearly defined business case, economic rationale, financing strategy, implementation structure, risk framework, procurement plan, governance model and measurable outcomes before significant capital is committed. This is particularly important as Ghana seeks to attract private capital without placing excessive pressure on the sovereign balance sheet.

The 2026 Budget itself envisaged leveraging the 24-Hour Economy allocation with GIIF, the Development Bank Ghana and private capital, with the objective of keeping financing largely off the sovereign balance sheet. That approach places even greater responsibility on project sponsors and financiers to ensure that projects are commercially credible and properly structured.

The Opportunity Before Ghana

The JPPF comes at a time when Ghana is seeking to move from economic stabilisation towards accelerated production, investment and export growth. The opportunity is significant, but so is the responsibility. The US$11.5 billion 24H+ pipeline should not simply be viewed as a large number. It should be treated as a portfolio that must earn investor confidence project by project.

The immediate task is therefore to identify projects with strong economic and commercial fundamentals, prepare them rigorously, structure appropriate financing arrangements and move them efficiently through the investment and implementation cycle.

If that discipline is maintained, the JPPF can become more than a project-preparation mechanism. It can become an important institutional bridge between Ghana’s development priorities and the capital required to deliver them. For Ghana’s project-management, infrastructure and development-finance professionals, this is the moment to focus on execution.

The country does not need another generation of projects that remain trapped between policy announcements and implementation. It needs projects that are properly conceived, rigorously appraised, professionally structured, responsibly financed and successfully delivered. The Afreximbank, GIIF and 24Hour Economy Authority pact is an important step in that direction.

The real measure of progress, however, will ultimately be what Ghana builds, what those assets produce, how efficiently they operate, and the jobs, exports, businesses and economic opportunities they create.

That is where the promise of the 24-Hour Economy must finally become measurable project-delivery reality.

Ghana News.title: IMANI, Local Government Ministry discuss reforms on sanitation, local revenue and urban infrastructure
Ghana News.content:
Sanitation reform, local revenue mobilisation, urban mobility and the redevelopment of major markets have featured prominently in policy discussions between policy think tank IMANI Africa and the Ministry of Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs.

The discussions took place on September 18, 2026, during an engagement involving the Minister, Chief Director, the Chairperson of Parliament’s Committee on Local Government and representatives of IMANI Africa.

The meeting considered a range of proposed interventions aimed at improving urban management, strengthening local government institutions and increasing internally generated funds for municipal development.

New approach to sanitation and waste collection

On sanitation, the discussions focused on reorganising waste collection in the Greater Accra Region into three operational blocks, with dedicated disposal infrastructure intended to reduce the distance waste collection trucks travel.

The proposals include using geospatial mapping to divide the operational blocks into smaller zones, with transfer stations located within approximately five-kilometre areas.

Under the proposed system, smaller collection vehicles, including tricycles, would deliver waste to the transfer stations, where it could then be loaded onto larger trucks.

A two-bin system was also discussed, with households expected to separate organic and non-organic waste at source.

The proposals envisage digital monitoring of compliance, including possible automated penalties for households that mix waste.

The discussions also included plans to mobilise financing for sanitation infrastructure and procure self-loading and self-tipping electric tricycles to improve residential waste collection.

Another proposal is to restrict the movement of large waste trucks to nighttime hours to reduce their impact on daytime traffic.

The meeting also considered a cashless waste collection system under which fees would be paid through mobile money platforms, with charges potentially linked to the quantity of waste delivered and recorded through weighing systems.

Digital property-rate collection

Local revenue mobilisation was another major focus.

The participants discussed a centralised digital platform for property-rate collection, with the aim of reducing reliance on manual collection and limiting opportunities for leakages and middlemen.

The proposed system would link property and spatial data from several public institutions, including the Electoral Commission, Ghana Statistical Service, Ghana Post and security-related agencies.

The discussions also considered using digital systems to prevent partial payments and automatically capture statutory property rates.

A further proposal is for a substantial proportion of property-rate revenue — between 60% and 70% under the proposal discussed — to be channelled back into municipal infrastructure such as roads, drains, pavements and streetlights.

The approach is expected to strengthen the link between local taxation and visible community development while potentially creating a foundation for future municipal financing instruments.

Contraflow lanes for peak-hour traffic

Urban mobility also featured prominently, with discussions around the use of contraflow arrangements on selected major corridors during peak periods.

The proposal involves temporarily using an opposing lane to give high-capacity public buses a dedicated route through congested areas.

Routes identified for consideration include Madina, Amasaman, Kasoa, Tema and Legon.

The engagement also considered expanding the high-capacity bus fleet, with a proposed pipeline of 120 buses as part of a broader 240-bus target.

Motorbikes for traffic enforcement and security teams were also proposed to help manage the contraflow corridors during peak periods.

The idea follows a proposal publicly raised by Local Government Minister Mahama Ayariga earlier in September to dedicate a peak-hour contraflow lane to Ayalolo buses. He said the proposal would require discussions with the Interior Ministry and the Inspector-General of Police.

Agbogbloshie redevelopment

The meeting further considered the redevelopment of the Agbogbloshie enclave, including the dredging of the lagoon and removal of accumulated waste.

The proposal involves clearing the area over an extended period and relocating unauthorised settlements as part of efforts to restore the environment.

The discussions included the possible use of government machinery, private-sector support and Common Fund resources to support the clean-up operation.

Plans were also discussed for developing industrial and housing zones on recovered land, with a focus on industries such as textiles and garments that could provide employment opportunities for young people.

One of the more unconventional proposals involves using upcycled shipping containers to develop low-cost housing close to employment centres.

The concept would involve working with the Ghana Ports and Harbours Authority and shipping companies to acquire containers that could be converted into housing units.

Technical input from professional bodies, including engineers and surveyors, is expected to inform the designs if the proposal is pursued.

Strengthening local government capacity

The engagement also explored measures to give Metropolitan, Municipal and District Assemblies a stronger economic development role.

One proposal is the appointment of regional economists to support district planning officers and help assemblies track indicators such as economic growth, job creation and infrastructure development.

The discussions also called for stronger collaboration among assemblies, national security agencies and other state institutions on spatial planning, building regulations and community safety.

The deployment of security camera networks along major routes and in selected neighbourhoods was also discussed.

Another proposal is to give local assemblies greater scope to develop or manage local water-distribution systems in areas where national water utilities are unable to adequately meet demand.

Regular regional training sessions and an annual conference for Metropolitan, Municipal and District Chief Executives were also proposed, with sessions focusing on areas including housing, energy, water and economic transformation.

Kejetia Phase II financing

The stalled Kejetia Market Phase II project also featured in the discussions, with the engagement considering ways to reduce costs and secure financing for completion.

The project was originally contracted at €248 million in 2018 and has faced delays following the suspension of work. The Local Government Ministry has previously said the cost has risen because of suspension claims and other associated costs.

Current discussions around the project include exploring alternative approaches to financing and construction, including greater use of locally produced materials where technically feasible.

The meeting also considered concerns about intermediaries benefiting from market spaces at rates significantly higher than the amounts paid to the Kumasi Metropolitan Assembly.

A proposed alternative would involve the state dealing more directly with traders and capturing a greater share of rental and goodwill payments to support the financing of market infrastructure.

Recent discussions by the Local Government Ministry have similarly focused on having traders pay market-value charges directly to the state to help finance completion of Kejetia Phase II.

Next steps

Following the September 18 engagement, IMANI team members are expected to develop thematic policy areas covering urban transport, urban housing, urban water and economic transformation.

Further working sessions are expected to review the proposed policy frameworks, develop data requirements and coordinate possible implementation strategies.

The participants are expected to reconvene in about two weeks for a further briefing and review of the work produced by the respective task teams.

The proposals discussed at the engagement represent areas for further policy development and implementation planning rather than a confirmation that all the measures have been formally adopted by government.

Ghana News.title: Ghana’s international reserves drop to US$11.04 billion in August as BoG pushes for significant build-ups in coming months
Ghana News.content:
Ghana’s international reserves have dropped to US$11.4 billion, ending August 2026, representing 4.2 months of import cover.

This marks a US$1.9 billion decline from the about US$12.94 billion that the country recorded at the end of June 2026.

Bank of Ghana governor Dr. Johnson Asiama revealed this international reserves data when he opened the 132nd Meeting of the Monetary Policy Committee of the Bank of Ghana on 23 September 2026.

Dr. Asiama also disclosed that Ghana’s current account is projected to record a deficit in the third quarter as gold shipments slowed and service payments increased.

However, fresh data that JOY BUSINESS has picked up from the Summary of Economic and Financial Data report released by the Bank of Ghana today showed that Ghana's international reserves, as of September 22, 2026, stood at US$12.04 billion.

The Bank of Ghana Governor went on to explain that, based on this development, “Rebuilding net foreign assets must therefore remain the priority heading into the fourth quarter."

“The weaker current account, the decline in reserves, and the pause in gold exports by GoldBod since mid-August call for a careful look at our buffers ahead of the usual rise in foreign exchange demand in the fourth quarter,” the governor added.

He also went on to state that "rebuilding reserves will be a key priority for the Bank in the coming months."

Data from the Bank of Ghana showed that, in February this year, Ghana’s international reserves reached a historic high of US$14.5 billion, representing 6 months of import cover.

What will shape the policy rate review?

In his address to the members of the Monetary Policy Committee, the Bank of Ghana Governor noted that the Committee faces some critical issues and key domestic risks that it must weigh carefully going forward.

“These issues," the governor noted, "will shape their discussions during the meeting, each carrying its own risk," Dr. Asiama stated.

The governor stated that "some of these issues will be the fact that headline inflation has been rising, going up from as low as 3.2% to 5% in August this year."

He, however, added that even the "level remains well below the lower bound of the target band, but the direction has been upward, and the question before the Committee is whether the expected rise over the coming months will be a one-off adjustment to higher energy prices and administered tariffs or the start of more persistent pressure that could unsettle expectations."

The governor also highlighted that the fiscal development in the rest of the year will be very important, adding that “Spending is set to rise, the share of short-term domestic debt is rising, and completion of the external debt restructuring will raise debt service obligations, each with implications for liquidity and the exchange rate."

Ghana News.title: Four years enough for any government to deliver – IEA rejects five-year term
Ghana News.content:
The Institute of Economic Affairs (IEA) has rejected a proposal to extend the tenure of Ghana’s President and Members of Parliament from four to five years, arguing that the existing four-year mandate provides sufficient time for governments to implement their programmes.

Former Chief Justice and IEA Fellow, Justice Sophia Akuffo, said there was no compelling evidence to justify extending the current term.

She made the remarks at a press briefing ahead of an IEA seminar under its “Views and Reflections” series, which is examining recommendations of the Prempeh Committee and the government’s position on proposed constitutional reforms.

The Prempeh Committee recommended extending the presidential and parliamentary terms from four to five years.

The government has accepted the proposal, arguing that an additional year would give governments more time to formulate, implement and assess policies.

The IEA, however, maintains that governments should be sufficiently prepared to begin implementing their programmes immediately after assuming office.

Justice Akuffo said political parties and prospective governments should undertake the necessary preparations before taking office rather than using a significant portion of their mandate to establish their administration.

“Four years you prepare before you come into office. In fact, you prepare before you even vie for power, so that on the day you come to power, from that day you’re on your feet and running,” she said.

She also criticised delays in appointing ministers and other key officials, saying such delays reduce the time available for governments to execute their programmes.

“It shouldn’t take six months to appoint ministers and people into key positions as has been our experience in times past,” she said.

The IEA said the debate over the proposed five-year term should take into account the need to balance effective policy implementation with democratic accountability.

While proponents of a longer mandate argue that an additional year would provide more time to implement long-term programmes, opponents maintain that shorter electoral cycles strengthen citizens’ ability to hold elected officials accountable.

The institute said a key issue for consideration is whether policy discontinuity is genuinely caused by the four-year electoral cycle or is instead the result of weak institutions, inadequate planning and successive governments abandoning or redesigning programmes initiated by their predecessors.

The IEA further said the proposed extension should be considered alongside efforts to strengthen the National Development Planning Commission (NDPC).

It argued that a credible long-term national development framework could enable successive governments to implement substantial programmes within four-year mandates while contributing to a common national development direction.

World.title: Trump pleads not guilty to 34 felony counts
World.content:
News outlets will not be allowed to broadcast former President Donald Trump’s arraignment on Tuesday in a New York state court, a judge said Monday night, but he will allow some photographers to take pictures in the courtroom before the proceedings formally begin.

Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan rejected the request by several media organizations, including CNN, for permission to broadcast the historic proceedings. Trump’s arraignment — like most arraignments in the Manhattan courthouse — is a public proceeding, but news cameras are not usually allowed to broadcast from inside the courtroom.

However, the judge is allowing five pool photographers to take still photos at the beginning of the proceedings “until such time as they are directed to vacate the jury box by court personnel.”

Earlier on Monday, Trump’s lawyers urged the judge to reject the media’s request for live cameras in the courtroom. The Manhattan District Attorney’s office told the judge they didn’t have a position.

The media outlets that tried to get cameras into the courtroom argued that “the gravity of this proceeding … and, consequently, the need for the broadest possible public access, cannot be overstated.”

Trump is now in Manhattan ahead of the arraignment. A grand jury indicted the former president last week.

The arraignment is also expected to bring the unsealing of the criminal charges against Trump, which have not yet been seen by his lawyers or the public.

The indictment stems from Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s investigation into hush-money payments, made during the 2016 presidential campaign, to women who claimed they had extramarital affairs with Trump, which he denies.

Trump denies all wrongdoing and his lawyers said last week that they’ll fight to get the charges dropped.

World.title: Russian authorities detain suspect over St. Petersburg cafe blast
World.content:
A Ukrainian tank is seen near the frontline area amid the Russia-Ukraine war, in Bakhmut, Ukraine, on April 02. (Muhammed Enes Yildirim/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images)

The Ukrainian military has reported little change to the front lines but heavy fire from Russian forces at various parts of the front line in the Donetsk region.

The General Staff said that more than 45 enemy attacks had been repelled over the past day, with the focus on Lyman, Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Mariinka.

It said there were 17 air strikes and more than 20 strikes by multiple launch rocket systems.

“In the Bakhmut direction, the enemy is trying to take full control over the city of Bakhmut and continues to storm it,” the General Staff said.

West of the city, Ukrainian defense forces repelled about 20 enemy attacks, according to the General Staff.

Oleksandr Syrskyi, commander of Ukrainian Land Forces, posted on Telegram that in Bakhmut he had met with “soldiers and commanders who destroyed the myth of invincibility of the Wagner fighters and Russian paratroopers.”

“The enemy is weakening and trying to cover up its failures with new fakes about the capture of Bakhmut,” Syrskyi said.

Syrskyi referenced the possibility of a future counter-offensive, saying that “the forward movement of our entire army depends on what every soldier is doing right now on their section of the front.”

Some of the most intense fighting is to the northwest and west of the city of Donetsk – as the Russians continue months-long efforts to dislodge Ukrainian defenses in Avdiivka and Mariinka. The General Staff said that some 20 assaults had been repelled.

“There are also some operational successes of our military in the Donetsk area. Our military have taken some positions. They have taken a more strategic and favourable position,” said Oleksii Dmytrashkivskyi, spokesperson for the military in that zone.

He also noted that Russian special forces had been introduced in the area.

“The enemy is trying to attack our positions between Avdiivka and Marinka. These attempts do not stop. It should be noted that the enemy has suffered quite significant losses,” Dmytrashkivskyi said.

He also claimed that the Russians “don’t have the same amount of equipment and, as they themselves say, they are on a ‘diet’ of ammunition for assaults.”

Social media video showed both sides engaged in heavy fire in the Avdiivka area, which the Russians have surrounded on three sides.

Denis Pushilin, the leader of the self-declared Donetsk People’s Republic, claimed that Russian forces were still advancing in the Avdiivka direction.

“It is still premature to speak of encirclement, but the situation is being created, if not critical, then extremely difficult for the enemy… After clearing Kamianka, our units are moving further. There are difficulties both with the terrain, which must also be overcome, and there are also similarities with weather conditions. But these difficulties are mutual — both for the enemy and for us,” Pushilin said.
