Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

The Ecuador curfew now running in four coastal provinces comes from a security decree signed on 15 September 2026. A separate energy order, issued a week later, asks 185 large industrial users to draw less power.

Two orders, two ministries, two reasons

The Ecuador curfew was signed by President Daniel Noboa. The electricity order came a week later from the Ministry of Environment and Energy.

No official statement connects them. Neither authority has said that one measure caused the other.

The two do overlap on the map. Most affected factories sit in Guayaquil and Durán, in Guayas, which is also under the night rule.

What the Ecuador curfew covers

Executive Decree 498 was signed on Tuesday 15 September 2026 at the Carondelet Palace in Quito. It declares a state of exception for grave internal unrest, lasting 60 days.

That declaration covers eight provinces and three cantons. The night movement ban is narrower and applies only in El Oro, Guayas, Los Ríos and Manabí.

The restriction runs each day from midnight to 05:00. It started at 00:00 on Thursday 17 September and ends at 23:59 on Wednesday 30 September 2026.

The stated reason is organized crime. Reports behind the decree counted 107 intentional homicides in those provinces between 16 August and 10 September 2026.

This is the third such night restriction ordered in Ecuador this year. The earlier two ran in March and May 2026.

The arrest figure and where it comes from

Interior Minister John Reimberg gave a first-week tally on Wednesday 23 September 2026, in a radio interview. He said police had held at least 1,225 people since 17 September.

Of those, 901 were held for offences such as extortion, contract killing, weapons charges and drug trafficking. The other 324 were held for breaking the night restriction itself.

The minister also reported 650 operations and 506 checkpoints across the four provinces. Police seized more than 187 firearms, and the minister put drug seizures at about six tonnes.

The electricity order and what caused it

The Ministry of Environment and Energy published its statement on Tuesday 22 September 2026. It told 185 companies in the AV1 and AV2 segments to cut their grid use one day a week.

The target is a saving of about one gigawatt-hour, or 1,000 megawatt-hours, of energy a day. Firms may cut load, run their own generators or move production to other days.

The legal basis is ARCONEL Regulation 004/25, the rule on running the grid when generation falls short. ARCONEL is Ecuador’s electricity regulator.

The trigger was hydrology, not demand or transmission. CENACE, the national grid operator, warned on 15 September that covering demand had become high risk.

The Mazar reservoir feeds the Paute Integral complex, which can supply up to 30 percent of national demand. At 07:00 on 22 September it stood at 2,138.46 metres above sea level, 14.54 metres below its maximum.

What AV1 and AV2 mean, and who is spared

AV1 and AV2 are voltage bands in Ecuador’s national tariff schedule, not a list of the biggest firms. AV1 covers supply above 40 kilovolts and up to 138 kilovolts.

AV2 covers supply above 138 kilovolts, the level of the transmission system itself. Only industrial users in those bands are named in the order.

Energy Minister Juan Carlos Blum said on 18 September that Mazar would otherwise run dry by late October. The aim is to stretch it to December, when rain is expected.

The ministry says the order is for industry alone. It says no household or commercial disconnections are planned under this arrangement.

A separate decree gives AV1 and AV2 users until 15 December 2026 to install their own generation.

Ecuador has rationed power before

This is not new ground for the country. Ecuador rationed electricity from 27 October to 19 December 2023, during a change of government.

A worse round followed from 23 September to 19 December 2024. Outages reached 14 hours a day and averaged about eight hours over 87 days.

El Universo counted 691 hours without power in that 2024 stretch. That is the equivalent of 28 full days in the dark.

Officials say the current order is meant to avoid a repeat. That claim has not been tested through a full dry season.

Why this matters if you live in or invest in the region

Ecuador uses the US dollar, so every figure here is already in dollars. That removes the currency risk found in Brazil, Argentina or Colombia.

For residents, the Ecuador curfew is the more visible rule. Movement stops between midnight and 05:00 in the four named provinces until 30 September.

For investors, the energy order matters more. Firms that keep drawing at full rate may have to buy costly emergency barge power.

Several things are not known. The government has not published which weekday each company takes, nor an end date for the energy order.

Both orders are reversible, and both turn on conditions nobody controls. Rain at Mazar and homicide counts on the coast will shape what comes next.

Frequently Asked Questions

Are Ecuador’s curfew and its power measure connected?

No official statement links them. The Ecuador curfew comes from a security decree; the power order comes from the energy ministry.

Will homes lose electricity under the new order?

The Ministry of Environment and Energy says no. It states the measure is for industrial users only.

When does the night restriction end?

It is due to end at 23:59 on Wednesday 30 September 2026. Any extension would need a new decision.

Connected Coverage Ecuador Army Rocket Strikes Target Illegal Mining in Imbabura

Sources: Executive Decree 498, signed 15 September 2026; Ministry of the Interior briefing by John Reimberg, 23 September 2026; Ministry of Environment and Energy statement, 22 September 2026; ARCONEL tariff schedule; El Universo, Primicias, Expreso, El Comercio, Extra and Radio Pichincha.

World.title: Costa Rica Airport Warns Drone Incidents Are Disrupting Flights
World.content:
Reports of drones flying near San Jose’s Juan Santamaría International Airport have increased sharply this year, prompting airport officials to warn that unauthorized flights can force takeoffs and landings to be temporarily stopped and potentially delay hundreds of travelers. AERIS, the company that operates Costa Rica’s main international airport, said reports of drones near the terminal have roughly doubled compared with last year.

The devices pose their greatest danger when commercial aircraft are taking off, approaching the airport or preparing to land. The problem has already affected airport operations. When a drone is spotted in an area that could interfere with aircraft, the control tower and airport authorities may temporarily restrict or suspend takeoffs and landings while they determine whether it is safe to continue operating.

For passengers, that can mean delayed departures, arriving aircraft being asked to remain in holding patterns and, in more serious cases, flights being diverted to another airport. Airport officials say even a relatively small drone can create a serious problem if it collides with a passenger aircraft traveling at high speed. Engines, cockpit windshields and other parts of the aircraft could be damaged in a collision.

Costa Rica already has restrictions designed to prevent that situation. The General Directorate of Civil Aviation (DGAC), prohibits drone operations within 8 kilometers, or about 5 miles, of an airport unless the operator has received specific authorization. Anyone who needs to fly a drone inside that restricted area must request permission in advance and provide information including the location, reason for the flight, planned altitude, operating area and the dates and times when the drone will be used.

Aviation authorities then decide whether the flight can safely take place and what coordination is required. People who fly drones without the required authorization can face administrative proceedings and penalties under Costa Rican aviation rules. The warning is particularly important around Juan Santamaría, where aircraft continually approach and depart over populated areas west of San José.

AERIS said drone operators should check the rules before flying rather than relying solely on the restrictions shown in a drone’s mobile application. The airport operator is asking recreational and commercial drone pilots to stay outside restricted areas unless they have received permission, arguing that a short, unauthorized flight can have consequences far beyond the person controlling the drone.

For anyone traveling by air, the issue adds yet another potential cause of unexpected delays at our busiest airport: if a drone is reported close enough to an aircraft’s flight path, safety takes priority and airport operations can be stopped until authorities determine that the airspace is clear.

World.title: Costa Rica Proposes 15% Tax on Certain Foreign Income
World.content:
Costa Rica has proposed a new 15% tax on certain types of income earned outside the country, a change that could affect residents who receive money from foreign investments, rental properties and other assets abroad. The proposal was presented to the Legislative Assembly yesterday and would apply to five main types of foreign income: interest, dividends, royalties, rental income and capital gains.

The legislation would apply to people and companies considered tax residents of Costa Rica, including individuals who do not operate a business here. The proposal is not yet law and it must go through the Legislative Assembly, where lawmakers can approve it, reject it or make changes before it reaches a final vote.

If approved in its current form, the legislation would mark an important change in the way Costa Rica taxes some money earned outside the country. Costa Rica has traditionally followed what is known as a territorial tax system. In simple terms, that generally means the country taxes income generated inside Costa Rica rather than income earned elsewhere.

The new proposal would keep that general system but create a broader exception for certain types of passive income coming from abroad. Passive income generally refers to money generated from investments or property rather than a salary earned from working. For example, a Costa Rican tax resident who owns a rental property in another country and receives rental income from it could potentially fall under the proposal.

The same could apply to someone receiving dividends from foreign investments, interest from money held abroad or profits from selling certain assets outside Costa Rica. However, the proposal should not be interpreted as a 15% tax on every dollar a person receives from another country.

The bill specifically focuses on foreign interest, dividends, royalties, rents and capital gains. That distinction will be particularly important for foreign residents living in Costa Rica, many of whom receive money from overseas. The legislation as presented does not simply state that all pensions, salaries, retirement income or other money coming from abroad would automatically be subject to the new tax.

The exact treatment of individual sources of income would depend on how they are classified under Costa Rican tax law. Another important issue is tax residency. Being a legal resident of Costa Rica for immigration purposes does not necessarily answer every tax question. Tax residency is determined under tax rules, and people with income abroad would need to determine whether those rules apply to their individual situation.

The proposal also includes a system intended to reduce the possibility of paying tax twice on the same income. If a person has already paid or had a similar tax withheld in another country, that amount could be taken into account when calculating what is owed in Costa Rica.

The exact calculation would depend on the amount received and the foreign tax already paid. For example, a person receiving dividends from investments in the United States may already have taxes withheld there. Under the proposal, those foreign taxes would be considered when determining the taxable amount in Costa Rica.

The government says the change is intended to create more equal treatment between people earning passive investment income inside Costa Rica and those earning similar income from assets located abroad. The issue has been debated in Costa Rica for several years. In 2023, lawmakers changed the income tax rules while Costa Rica was working to resolve concerns raised by the European Union over its treatment of foreign income.

The law that emerged from that process generally kept Costa Rica’s territorial tax system and limited taxation of foreign passive income to specific circumstances involving certain multinational companies. The government opposed parts of that legislation at the time, arguing that it left too much foreign investment income outside the Costa Rican tax system.

The new bill would go considerably further. Instead of concentrating mainly on multinational groups, the proposal would use tax residency as one of the central tests for deciding who could be required to pay. That means individuals, companies, trusts, investment funds and other legal structures based in Costa Rica could potentially fall within the new rules if they own assets or rights abroad that generate the types of income covered by the legislation.

The bill would also change the treatment of some tax credits related to investment securities, although that part of the proposal is likely to have less direct impact on most individual residents. The foreign-income proposal was presented alongside a separate bill that would overhaul the way Costa Rica manages tax exemptions and eliminate some existing exemptions.

Both measures now begin the legislative process. For residents with money or property outside Costa Rica, the most important point for now is that nothing has changed yet. Foreign interest, dividends, rent and capital gains are not suddenly subject to a new 15% tax because the proposal was introduced.

The Legislative Assembly will first have to debate the bill, and its wording could change substantially before any final approval. The proposal nevertheless deserves close attention from people who are tax residents of Costa Rica and receive investment or property income from abroad because, if approved, it would broaden Costa Rica’s ability to tax foreign passive income beyond the rules currently in place.

World.title: Costa Rican Lawmakers Reject Minute of Silence for Man Who Died in ICE Custody
World.content:
Costa Rica’s Legislative Assembly yesterday rejected a motion to hold a minute of silence for Carlos Josué Marchena, a Costa Rican man who died last week while in the custody of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in Louisiana. The motion failed 28 to 25, with lawmakers from the governing Pueblo Soberano party voting against it.

In a statement issued after the vote, the Pueblo Soberano caucus extended its condolences to Marchena’s family and said its vote did not reflect indifference to their grief. The caucus said it was awaiting clarification of the circumstances of the death and argued that the motion sought to bring a debate over U.S. immigration policy onto the Assembly floor.

Hours before the vote, the political committee of the opposition Frente Amplio party called on the government to open a formal and transparent investigation into the deaths of two Costa Ricans in ICE custody. The party also asked the Foreign Ministry to provide consular support to Costa Ricans detained in the United States.

ICE confirmed the death in a statement released Monday. According to the agency, Marchena was found unresponsive on Sept. 18 at Winnfield Correctional Center, where staff called a medical emergency and began life-saving measures. He was taken to Winn Parish Medical Center, where a physician pronounced him dead at approximately 8 a.m. ICE said the official cause of death remains pending a medical examination.

The agency’s statement gave Marchena’s age as 36 and described him as a “criminal illegal alien.” ICE said his record included convictions for retail fraud and malicious destruction of personal property, along with separate arrests for second-degree retail fraud and assault. His family puts his age at 37. His sister, Franciny Araya Marchena, told local media that he had been held by immigration authorities since Jan. 14 and was moved from Michigan to California and finally to Louisiana.

Araya said her brother had diabetes and required medication and a controlled diet, and that the family received confirmation of his death through Costa Rica’s Foreign Ministry. She said that hours before he died, he told relatives he was experiencing chest pain. The family has alleged that Marchena had difficulty obtaining adequate food and medication after he was transferred out of Michigan. Araya has said those assessments are her own conclusions and that the family does not know the exact circumstances of his death.

A cousin, Bryan Marchena, said Carlos had lived in the United States for about five years, held a work permit and had begun the process of regularizing his immigration status. He said Marchena had been denied bond and voluntary departure on several occasions. Relatives said they had expected him to be deported to Costa Rica within one or two weeks and had already bought him clothes for his return. The family is now seeking financial help to repatriate his remains.

Marchena’s death follows the case of Rándall Gamboa Esquivel, who returned to Costa Rica gravely ill last year after about 10 months in ICE custody. Gamboa, 52, died weeks after his return, and his family said he had been held in poor conditions. Autopsy results are expected to determine the cause of Marchena’s death. The case has renewed questions in Costa Rica about medical care for detainees in U.S. immigration custody and about the consular support available to Costa Ricans held abroad.

World.title: Seprod surges 20% as company seeks approval for 5-for-1 stock split
World.content:
The Seprod Group headquarters in Kingston.

SEPROD Limited’s share price surged nearly 20 per cent Wednesday after the manufacturing and distribution group announced plans to restructure its share capital, including a proposed five-for-one stock split and a resolution authorising the company to raise fresh equity.

The stock was trading at $77.99, up $12.86, or about 19.7 per cent, with 166,914 shares changing hands.

The movement follows Seprod’s announcement that it has called an extraordinary general meeting for shareholders to vote on three proposals: increasing the number of shares the company is authorised to issue, splitting every existing share into five, and giving its board authority to issue new shares in the future, including through an additional public offering, or APO.

Seprod already has about 910.9 million shares in issue against its current authorised limit of one billion shares, leaving relatively little room to issue additional stock under its present structure.

The first proposal would therefore increase the number of shares Seprod is authorised to issue from one billion to 1.9 billion.

Based on approximately 910.9 million shares currently in issue, the five-for-one split of the shares already held by investors would increase that number to roughly 4.55 billion units.

Importantly, that does not by itself make an investor five times richer. Someone holding 100 Seprod shares before the split would instead hold 500 shares afterwards, while retaining the same percentage ownership of the company immediately following the split. The market price of each share would normally adjust lower to reflect the much larger number of shares in circulation.

At Wednesday’s price of $77.99, for example, a straight five-for-one adjustment would put the theoretical share price at about $15.60, assuming nothing else changed.

So an investor with 100 shares worth $7,799 before the split would have 500 shares worth roughly the same $7,799 immediately after it. The practical effect is that Seprod shares would be available in smaller denominations, potentially making individual units more affordable to investors who may find the current price relatively high.

Further, the split itself would not provide Seprod with any new money. But that’s where the third resolution becomes important.

Seprod is also seeking shareholder approval to allow its board to issue new shares in the future, including through an APO. Seprod has not said that an APO is imminent or disclosed how much it might seek to raise. The proposal instead gives the board the ability to issue new equity should it decide additional capital is required.

Chairman P B Scott said the measures are intended to give the company more room to strengthen its finances and pursue further growth.

“Over the past four years we have built the Caribbean’s largest integrated manufacturing and distribution platform for food, pharmaceuticals and premium beverages. We are now focused on integrating our businesses and strengthening our balance sheet,” Scott said in a press statement.

He added that the resolutions would provide Seprod with “greater flexibility” as it pursues those objectives and future growth opportunities.

The proposals come as Seprod continues to work through softer sales but improved profitability.

For the six months ended June 30, group revenue declined three per cent to $72.93 billion from $75.18 billion a year earlier, while net profit climbed 62 per cent to $2.34 billion. The company said the result included a gain from the disposal of International Biscuits Limited.

During the April-to-June quarter alone, revenue fell three per cent to $36.51 billion, largely due to weaker demand from Jamaica’s tourism sector as some hotels continued to operate with reduced room availability or delayed reopening following Hurricane Melissa.

Despite the lower sales, quarterly net profit increased 16 per cent to $688 million, compared with $592 million in the corresponding period last year.

The group has also been reducing debt. Seprod said cash flow generated during the first half allowed it to cut debt by more than $3 billion while declaring $551 million in dividends.

Its financial statements show long-term liabilities declining to approximately $38.1 billion at June 30, from $41.1 billion at the end of December, while stockholders’ equity increased to $50.52 billion from $49.71 billion.

The company has said its priorities for the remainder of the year include debt reduction, regional integration, improving operations and completing capital projects at its manufacturing plants.

Shareholders will vote on the proposed changes at a virtual extraordinary general meeting scheduled for October 12 at noon.

– Karena Bennett

World.title: Dr Gabrielle Henry sues Miss Universe organisation over 2025 fall
World.content:
Miss Universe Jamaica 2025 Gabrielle Henry .

Former Miss Universe Jamaica Dr Gabrielle Henry has filed a lawsuit against the Miss Universe Organisation and two of its parent companies, nearly a year after she fell from the pageant stage during the 2025 Miss Universe competition in Thailand.

PEOPLE magazine reported that Henry filed the lawsuit on Monday, September 21, in Delaware Superior Court, bringing five claims against the defendants, including negligence, premises liability, negligent hiring, retention and supervision, and negligent and intentional infliction of emotional distress.

According to the complaint, Henry was following rehearsed choreography during the preliminary competition on November 19, 2025, when she fell about five feet through an “unmarked and uncovered opening in the stage”. The suit alleges that the opening contained lighting equipment and concrete.

Henry also alleges that intense lighting directed towards her during her rehearsed walk impaired her visibility and contributed to the fall.

According to the lawsuit, Henry lost consciousness upon impact and suffered a traumatic brain injury, including acute subarachnoid haemorrhage, frontal lobe haemorrhagic contusion and subdural haemorrhage. She was hospitalised from November 19 to December 10, 2025.

The complaint describes the incident as the “most traumatic moment” of Henry’s life and alleges that the media attention surrounding the fall caused continuing emotional distress in addition to the effects of her physical injuries.

READ: Miss Jamaica Universe withdraws from pageant after suffering head injury in fall

Henry, who was practising as an ophthalmologist at the time, alleges that her injuries prevented her from resuming her medical residency and have resulted in ongoing neurological and cognitive symptoms requiring continued care, rehabilitation and follow-up.

The lawsuit further alleges that other contestants had raised concerns about the lighting and staging conditions. It claims that following Henry’s fall, the stage was modified to add bright white lights along its edge, PEOPLE reported.

In a statement to PEOPLE, the Miss Universe Organisation said it had not been served with, nor received, any lawsuit, claim, demand letter or subpoena from Henry or anyone acting on her behalf and therefore could not comment on claims it had not seen.

The organisation said the host and production entities, Miss Grand International (MGI) and Miss Universe Thailand, under the direction of Nawat Itsaragrisil, were responsible for producing the 74th Miss Universe competition, including the venue, stage, and on-site safety.

It also said it had paid Henry’s hospital expenses after the incident, despite having no obligation to do so, and later covered her treatment at a specialised hospital in Jamaica following her return home.

The organisation said it had not received any further request for medical expenses and had also offered Henry a position as a goodwill ambassador on the Miss Universe team. According to the organisation, she had not responded to the offer.

Henry’s lawsuit also names MGI, which she alleges was responsible for the staging, lighting and safety arrangements for the event. It further alleges that the Miss Universe Organisation retained and exercised control over those aspects.

The complaint alleges that MGI’s failure to oversee stage safety contributed to Henry’s injuries.

According to PEOPLE, Henry also alleges that the Miss Universe Organisation failed to maintain a safe stage by leaving an opening unguarded, unmarked and unbarricaded, and by failing to identify what she describes as MGI’s unsafe staging and production practices.

The lawsuit comes nearly a year after the incident sparked public speculation about the circumstances surrounding Henry’s fall.

At the time, Miss Universe Haiti Melissa Sapini told PEOPLE that following the incident, the remaining contestants were gathered for a meeting where she alleged a staff member appeared to blame Henry for the fall.

“I don’t know that they handled that correctly,” Sapini told PEOPLE at the time, adding that the first comment made was that Henry had not been paying attention.

The Miss Universe Organisation did not respond to PEOPLE’s requests for comment on Sapini’s claims at the time.

In a December 8, 2025 statement, the organisation said it had assumed all related expenses, including accommodation, airline rebooking, transportation and support for Henry’s family.

MGI, meanwhile, told PEOPLE at the time that the incident occurred primarily because Henry had missed her blocking and may not have been looking at the runway while walking. However, the organisation said no one from MGI had blamed her.

The representative also said the runway was more than five metres wide and had clear, oversized white borders, adding that no other contestant had experienced an accident on the runway.

The Miss Universe Organisation has previously rejected suggestions that Henry was responsible for the incident, saying such claims were inaccurate, unfounded and did not reflect the facts.

World.title: Chilling confession
World.content:
Murder victim 64-year-old domestic helper Hyacinth Rose Johnson, who was also called June.

FRANKFIELD, Clarendon — Police here say a 15-year-old schoolboy has been charged with murder after he confessed to using a screwdriver to fatally stab his 64-year-old neighbour then dragged her body to hide the gruesome crime.

The victim, Hyacinth Rose Johnson, a domestic helper, was killed in Union district, Grantham, north-west Clarendon in July.

“The police continued their investigation, which led them to the arrest of this young man. He was arrested on Saturday and on Monday, while being interviewed in the presence of his mother and two justices of the peace, he confessed to using a screwdriver to stab the female to death. He indicated that he was not provoked by the female, and that he doesn’t know why he [killed] her. The incident occurred at his home, which is in front of the home of the deceased,” a police source told the Jamaica Observer Tuesday.

Police dispelled rumours that Johnson, also called June, had been sexually assaulted by her killer. Police said the teen, who is a student at a prominent high school, confessed to moving the woman’s body to the back of her house.

“We have no evidence that she was sexually assaulted. Her clothing was found in a certain position; that is why persons were of the view that she was sexually molested. She was drawn by him, in a bid to hide the crime, from his premises to another premises. In the process [her underwear] were pulled down to her ankles,” the police source said.

A police report outlined that about 7:00 am on July 1 residents of Union stumbled upon Johnson’s body at the back of her house. Police said the body had stab wounds to the chest. Five days later, placard-bearing residents dressed in red and black marched through the community, protesting Johnson’s gruesome murder.

Member of Parliament for Clarendon North Western Richard Azan said Johnson was a mother of four who lived alone.

“People are outraged about it, because June was not a person who gave trouble. June went around washing and cleaning [homes] for people. She was a hard-working churchwoman. I said it at the funeral [on August 29], and I said it at a community meeting. I said we have to find this one; that was clear in my mind and we arranged community meetings and all of that with the police and everybody,” said Azan.

“I am so disappointed that a young person could be able to [allegedly] commit a crime on someone in a community who gave service to the same community by helping other persons. She could be the grandmother of the person [accused of] committing the crime,” added Azan.

World.title: Royal Caribbean Group and Sandals Resorts announce landmark partnership
World.content:
Royal Caribbean Group Chairman and CEO Jason Liberty (left) and Sandals Resorts and Beaches Resorts Executive Chairman Adam Stewart sign the partnership agreement.

Royal Caribbean Group and Sandals Resorts on Wednesday, September 23, 2026 announced the signing of an agreement to form a partnership in the all-inclusive resort space with a 50 per cent investment from Royal Caribbean Group.

“Building on Sandals and Beaches Resorts’ more than four decades of leadership in Caribbean hospitality, the joint venture will create new opportunities for continued resort growth while broadening the experiences across Royal Caribbean Group’s vacation platform,” both entities said in a joint news release.

The partnership brings together two of the travel industry’s most celebrated vacation companies, pairing Sandals and Beaches’ all-inclusive resort expertise with Royal Caribbean Group’s vacation platform, including industry-leading brands — Royal Caribbean, Celebrity Cruises and Silversea — a portfolio of private destinations, new river cruising offering, and an industry-first loyalty programme.

“United in a shared history in the Caribbean and connected by a love for their communities, the companies will offer travellers an unparalleled collection of cruise, private destination and resort experiences, serving guests across more vacation occasions and establishing their undisputed leadership in Caribbean vacations,” the release added.

“The joint venture expands Royal Caribbean Group into an adjacent vacation category, growing its participation in the approximately US$2 trillion global vacation market, and meets the growing global demand for Sandals and Beaches Resorts by accelerating their expansion,” the release stated.

“The partnership will include Sandals and Beaches’ collection of premier all-inclusive properties across the Caribbean, and the companies will explore opportunities to broaden distribution, deepen guest engagement, and make it easier for travellers to discover vacation experiences offered across both portfolios,” they added.

“For nearly 60 years, we’ve reimagined what a vacation can be, constantly expanding the ways we inspire our guests to explore, connect and create lifelong memories,” the release quotes Royal Caribbean Group Chairman and CEO Jason Liberty.

“We have been building a vacation platform that brings joy to millions of people around the world and creates meaningful relationships that last with our guests. Our partnership with Sandals and Beaches Resorts is an important next step on that journey, bringing together two iconic leading vacation companies to further strengthen and grow one of the most admired resort portfolios in the world,” Liberty said.

“The Stewart family has created powerful and beloved brands, and we are honoured to build on that legacy. Together, we see tremendous opportunity to expand the reach of Sandals and Beaches Resorts and continue turning the vacation of a lifetime into a lifetime of vacations,” he added.

“My father, Gordon ‘Butch’ Stewart, founded Sandals Resorts with the belief that a company built in the Caribbean could stand on the world stage alongside the most respected names in hospitality. Today is proof of how far that vision can go,” said Sandals Resorts and Beaches Resorts Executive Chairman Adam Stewart.

“This partnership is the natural next step in building on that conviction. It gives us the ability to grow faster with a partner that shares our values of exceptional hospitality, long-term investment, and the power of enduring brands. Together, we will introduce more guests to Sandals and Beaches Resorts while creating even more extraordinary experiences for those who have made our resorts part of their lives for decades.” Stewart added.

“As we continue to grow, we will remain true to what has always defined us: delivering authentic vacations that exceed expectations while creating opportunities for our team members, travel advisor partners and the communities we call home. The future has never been brighter, and I know this moment would make my father incredibly proud,” Stewart said.

The joint venture will be governed by a board under the shared leadership of Stewart and Liberty. Stewart will maintain a leadership role in guiding the company’s long-term strategic growth as executive chairman of Sandals and Beaches Resorts. Existing reservations, loyalty programmes, resort operations, and cruise operations will continue as usual, with the partnership bringing additional resources to support future opportunities.

Under the terms of the agreement, Royal Caribbean Group will acquire a 50 per cent equity interest in Sandals and Beaches Resorts for approximately US$3 billion, representing a forward EBITDA multiple of approximately 10x.

Royal Caribbean Group has secured committed debt financing from Morgan Stanley to fund the investment. The transaction is expected to close in early 2027, subject to customary approvals and closing conditions, and is expected to be accretive to earnings next year.

BofA Securities and PJT Partners acted as financial advisors, and Latham & Watkins and Jones Day acted as legal advisors to the Sandals Group. Perella Weinberg Partners and Morgan Stanley acted as financial advisors and Kirkland & Ellis LLP acted as legal advisor to Royal Caribbean Group.

World.title: NROCC to fix Catherine Hall flood woes
World.content:
Councillor Dwight Crawford with a team from the St James Municipal Corporation cleaning drains in Catherine Hall Monday.

MONTEGO BAY, St James — The agency executing the Montego Bay Perimeter Road project has rejected often-made suggestions that the ongoing work is to be blamed for flooding now plaguing the Hurricane Melissa-battered communities of West Green and Catherine Hall in St James. The National Road Operating and Construction Company (NROCC) has also promised a long-term fix for the issue, while the local authorities work on short-term solutions.

“The flooding in Catherine Hall and West Green is not related to the project,” NROCC Managing Director Stephen Edwards told the Jamaica Observer Tuesday morning.

“West Green and Catherine Hall have a history of flooding; the drains are inadequate,” he added.

His comments came a few hours after residents staged a protest to call attention to the water logged area. It was brief but caused significant disruption to traffic which was already moving at a snail’s pace.

The area has had periods of heavy rain since last week, resulting in flooding that brought back memories of last October’s Category 5 storm and fresh agony for some homeowners who have had to place furniture on blocks to keep them dry. Some residents insist that the ongoing roadwork has clogged drains which were never fully cleared after Melissa.

However while NROCC’s Edwards agrees the drains are clogged, he maintains the debris in them is unrelated to the perimeter road project and solely to debris from the storm. He pointed out that the drains being installed along the roadway, as part of the project, have been operating well so far.

“They are wide enough where a bobcat can drive through and so it can manage the water levels,” Edwards explained.

Although the two flood-prone communities do not fall directly under NROCC’s remit, he said the agency has a plan for the area.

“We are mobilised in the area, for the Montego Bay Perimeter Road Project, and we have engineers in the space; we have a contractor in the space and we’re going to take a look at it… as part of the comprehensive drainage study that we’re doing,” he promised.

The hydrological and drainage study, Edwards said, is expected to cover the wider parish in an effort to mitigate flooding challenges. However, he noted that the process would take time and requires proper preparation to ensure communities receive the best support possible.

“We’re going to do something that is going to alleviate the problem not only in the short term but the long term as well, but it needs a proper plan,” Edwards insisted.

“[Residents] are traumatised and they have been going through it; even from before Melissa that place would flood,” he added, noting that project contractors have been helping to clean drains in the two communities.

Councillor Dwight Crawford (Jamaica Labour Party, Spring Garden Division) has also been doing his part by leading a team from the St James Municipal Corporation.

“I was there on Sunday, I was in about eight inches of water but we managed to alleviate the challenges. We are employing all kinds of different avenues so we managed to alleviate the challenges in that area,” he told the Observer Tuesday.

According to Crawford, the team made significant headway in removing silt build-up from sections of the drains in Catherine Hall, allowing water that had accumulated after recent rains to run off.

However, he stressed that the flooding is not widespread.

“I know naturally when persons hear Catherine Hall and they hear floods, they think that the whole place is under water; the whole place is not under water. There are some areas where the drains are giving us some challenges. There are about three areas, two of which I think we have managed to remedy,” Crawford said.

“I know [residents] are traumatised but I wanted to show them that we are here with them, working for them to ensure that the challenges are alleviated,” he assured.

World.title: Kevin Downswell leads Sterling Gospel Music Awards noms
World.content:
Kevin Downswell.

Kevin Downswell tops the list of nominees for the 2026 Sterling Gospel Music Awards.

The full list of nominees was revealed on Monday via the event’s official Instagram page.

The acclaimed gospel recording artiste, minister and producer received six nominations in the multiple categories including Male Artiste to the Year, Collaboration of the Year, Local Hit of the Year, and Local Hit Producer of the Year.

Johnmark Wiggan and Gilead Collective followed with five nominations each, while Prince Saj received four.

Rondell Positive, Trinidadian gospel/reggae artiste Positive, Sherwin Gardner, Rhoda Isabella, Jermaine Edwards, Levy’s Heritage and broadcasters Jucal Dyer and Mical Forsythe picked up two nominations a piece.

For its 2026 staging, Sterling Gospel Music Awards (SGMA) will see a change of format from a physical, live ceremony to a national television broadcast on Television Jamaica (TVJ) on Sunday, October 18 during the Heroes’ holiday weekend.

“So this year we’re not having a physical staging… we’ll be doing a television broadcast on TVJ that will also stream via TVJ’s YouTube platform as well as Sterling YouTube channel. It will also be available regionally and worldwide to the international market,” Basillia Barnaby Cuff, organiser and founder of the awards told the Jamaica Observer.

She added: “We are seeking to expose the brand Sterling to a much wider audience and for year 10 we decided to pivot and more in that direction.”

This year will see the introduction of a Digital Impact Award. The winner will be voted on by the public. The nominees in that category are Monique McLeggon, Samijo, Stephen The Christian, Kyleon Thomas, and Sheena Lyn Hanson.

Said Barnaby Cuff: “This award is an award for persons in the faith-based community who have been making an impact online, whether its through fashion, social media, comedy, or content. We wanted a category that moved with the times, like Sterling always does.”

The eligibility period for the 2026 Sterling Gospel Music Awards for submission of songs, albums and music videos is January 1, 2025 to December 31, 2025.

Katrina Grant D’Aguilar is the group marketing and communications manager for the Jamaica Co-operative Credit Union League. It is the second year that her organisation has partnered with the event.

“Year one was amazing and a rewarding experience. The feedback, even from our members, the moment they realised that we were connected to the Sterling Gospel Music Awards, persons were reaching out to say kudos to the credit union. And so we continue to build communities, we believe in helping people, and we are happy to be a part of the Sterling family. We are pleased about the returns of the association,” said D’Aguilar.

For nine years, Restaurants of Jamaica through its KFC brand, has been a major sponsor for the event. The company salutes the veterans in gospel music through its Big Deal Awards.

“It’s gonna be another Big Deal Year, the Big Deal Awards of excellence, and we’re paying tribute to the veteran broadcasters who have helped to ensure the voices of gospel music are heard. Sterling [Awards] is one of those platforms that allow us to connect to the community and our audience,” Andrei Roper, marketing manager for KFC told the Observer.

Roper continued, “We’re celebrating those stalwarts, those pioneers, and those persons who have helped to move the gospel fraternity forward and, overall, we’re just celebrating excellence in the fraternity.”

Below are some of the nominations in the 2026 edition of the awards:

Album of the year:

Doxalogii Vol 1 – Rhoda Isabella;

The Triad – Levy’s Heritage;

Local hit of the year:

World.title: SLOW RESPONSE
World.content:
BANK of Jamaica (BOJ) researchers are questioning whether policymakers react too slowly when global food costs surge, after finding that increases tend to last longer but draw a slower response than oil price shocks.

The finding comes ahead of the BOJ’s next monetary policy decision on September 28, with inflation at 7.9 per cent in August, above the central bank’s four to six per cent target range.

The study, prepared by BOJ economists Calvin Grant, Ashaud Shirley, and Reneisha Craig, looked at how changes in global food, oil and alumina prices affect inflation, economic activity, interest rates and the exchange rate in Jamaica. It used quarterly data from June 2000 to March 2025.

The researchers found that when oil prices jump, monetary conditions tend to tighten sooner. Food price shocks, however, are more likely to be allowed more time to work through the economy before a stronger response comes.

For instance, after four quarters, a one-percentage-point food-price shock was associated with a small decline in the real interest rate, while the same-sized oil shock was associated with a small increase. The researchers said this suggests monetary authorities may initially choose to “look through” food price shocks.

In simple terms, interest rates may not rise as quickly as inflation when food prices start climbing, leaving monetary conditions relatively easy even as price pressures build.

That would matter less if food price increases faded quickly. But the study, which the authors cautioned does not necessarily represent BOJ management or its board, found the opposite.

After four quarters, a one-percentage-point shock to global food prices produced a cumulative increase of about 0.95 percentage points in Jamaica’s quarter-on-quarter annualised inflation. The comparable increase was 0.21 percentage points for oil and 0.14 percentage points for alumina.

Even after eight to 12 quarters, the effect from food remained much larger than the others, at roughly 0.9 to one percentage point, compared with 0.2 to 0.3 percentage points for oil and less than 0.1 percentage point for alumina.

“The evidence shows Jamaica’s monetary response differs across commodity shocks and sometimes is misaligned with their relative persistence: oil shocks prompt faster tightening, while more persistent external food shocks initially face accommodative real rates,” the researchers said.

The issue is especially significant in Jamaica, where food accounts for about 33.3 per cent of the consumer price index basket, compared with approximately 14 per cent in the United States. Processed food, which is more directly exposed to imported prices, makes up about 27.2 per cent, while energy and transport-related items account for a combined 16.8 per cent.

The study found that food becomes a bigger driver of inflation the longer the shock lasts. By the end of the near-term period examined, global food price shocks accounted for 21.8 per cent of the variation in domestic headline inflation, compared with 7.6 per cent for oil and 2.3 per cent for alumina.

The researchers described food as the “single most important external driver of inflation uncertainty”.

Still, oil has the quicker initial effect. On impact, a one-percentage-point oil price shock raises domestic inflation by 0.05 percentage points, compared with 0.02 percentage points for food.

The researchers said food can take longer to show up fully in local prices because distributors and producers may absorb some of the increase before passing it on to consumers. Once those higher costs begin filtering through, however, the effects tend to last much longer.

The issue is particularly timely as oil prices remain volatile. Brent crude moved above US$100 a barrel earlier this month as supply concerns intensified in the Middle East, although prices have since eased somewhat. At the same time, local inflation has been pushed higher by rising food prices, with Statin reporting food as the main driver of the increase in August.

The study suggests that those two pressures do not affect Jamaica in the same way and may not require the same response.

Further, the researchers argue that monetary policy should take more account of what is driving inflation instead of treating all commodity shocks alike.

“A refined policy reaction function could formally test whether policy should vary with the source of inflation,” they said.

The paper also found that global food price shocks affect more than what consumers pay at the supermarket. By the eighth quarter, they accounted for about 9.2 per cent of variation in Jamaica’s output gap, compared with 5.7 per cent for oil and one per cent for alumina.

“External food price shocks explain 9.2 per cent by the eighth quarter, making them the most important commodity price driver of real activity,” the researchers said. Food shocks also accounted for 17.3 per cent of variation in the domestic real interest rate gap, compared with 5.1 per cent for oil.

The authors ultimately argue that monetary policy should distinguish more clearly between different types of commodity shocks rather than treating commodity-driven inflation as a single problem.

World.title: HOME, SWEET HOME
World.content:
Reggae Boyz midfielder Courtney Clarke celebrating after scoring on his debut in a 2-0 win over India at the Unity Cup in London in May.

ENGLISH-born midfielders Courtney Clarke and Brandon Cover say they’re looking forward to playing in Jamaica for the first time as they gear up for the start of the Reggae Boyz campaign in the Concacaf Nations League this weekend.

Interim Head Coach Rudolph Speid could hand the pair their home debuts at the National Stadium when the national men’s team take on Guatemala on Friday and Honduras on Monday in their first two of four games in their group-stage campaign.

Clarke, a 23-year-old midfielder who plays for Walsall FC in England’s fourth tier, earned his first caps for Jamaica at the Unity Cup in London in May. He also scored his first goal in the 2-0 semi-final win over India.

Clarke, whose parents are Jamaican, says representing the country was a memorable experience.

“That was a special day for me and my family. I’ve always dreamed of that,” he said. “It was just perfect timing. I don’t really score many goals but I’m still adding it into my catalogue. That was a big moment and it was just the best timing for me. I’ve got to thank my family and God for the best timing.”

Cover, 22, plays for Rotherham in England’s fourth tier, and has a longer history with the national team than Clarke, having made his debut during a friendly international against Jordan in 2023. He also played for Jamaica at the Central America and Caribbean Games in El Salvador that year.

Cover, whose father is Jamaican, earned a recall at the Unity Cup, playing the full 90 minutes in the win over India and the 3-0 loss to Nigeria in the final.

He is hoping to be a mainstay in the team similar to veteran centre back Damion Lowe.

“I just want to keep racking them up [appearances] for Jamaica. I want to be like Nana [Lowe], I want to get the 80 caps, the 100 caps. I just want to keep fighting for more, striving for more,” he said.

“I’ve really enjoyed it, I just want to thank Coach Speid for giving me the opportunity to play for Jamaica because that’s all I’ve wanted to do since I was a youth and now I get to do it. I want to repay my faith in him, my family and everyone.”

Clarke and Cover have been to Jamaica before but have never played a competitive game on the island.

They’re looking forward to playing in front of the local support at the National Stadium in the coming days.

“It’s going to be even more special being at home. Seeing my family that’s watched me grow over the years, that’s watched me from when I was younger to now seeing me play for the nation, it’s just a really special moment for me,” Clarke said.

“I just love the way Jamaicans are so passionate about football and I just want to show them that they’ve got a new player here that’s going to excite them and get them off their feet and show that we can do this and go further.”

Cover said, “It would mean everything. I think I’ve got loads of family coming as well, I’ve got 20 plus people coming so, I just want everyone to come to the stadium and support us and it’ll mean the whole world to me. I expect the stadium to be loud and supportive and I’m just ready to go really for the first game versus Guatemala.”

After the home games against Guatemala and Honduras, the Reggae Boyz travel to El Salvador next Friday before closing out the group away to Honduras on October 5. Jamaica need to finish top two in the group, which also consists of Suriname and Martinique, to advance to the quarter-finals where they will face one of the top four teams in Concacaf, Mexico, USA, Canada or Panama.

Clarke and Cover say the team fully understand the importance of the matches.

“The aim is really to win all of them and that’s what we’re going to do,” Clarke said. “We’re going to try to do our best but we just have to go in with the mentality of ‘we are Jamaica’ and no one will stand in our way to win so we’re all going to work together and train hard this week and prepare right.”

“We’ve got to climb up in the FIFA rankings, but it’s one game at a time so we’ll focus on Guatemala first,” Cover said. “Hopefully, we get that win, play really well and then on to the next so [I’m] really looking forward to it.

World.title: Poland scrambles jets after Russian helicopter breaches its airspace
World.content:
A Russian Mi-8 helicopter flies toward Novosibirsk in Russia during a Victory Day parade rehearsal in May 2020. | Rostislav Netisov/AFP via Getty Images

Warsaw said the incident was another test of its defenses.

A Russian Mi-8 helicopter briefly violated Polish airspace near the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad on Wednesday, prompting Warsaw to scramble its fighter jets.

The Operational Command of Poland’s Armed Forces said in a statement on X that the helicopter had entered Polish airspace at 11:08 a.m. from Kaliningrad in the country’s north, remaining there for 42 seconds.

“The flight of the machine was observed by the radio-location systems” of Poland’s military, the command said in a statement, adding that ground forces remained on standby. “The nature of the incident indicates that Russia is once again testing the readiness of our air defense.”

World.title: A huit mois de la présidentielle, les comptes de campagne déjà sous surveillance
World.content:
"Beaucoup de questions portent sur l'utilisation des réseaux sociaux et sur leur inscription dans les comptes", rapporte l’ancien magistrat à la Cour des comptes, passé par la direction de l’Agence nationale pour l’emploi. Pas plus tard que le 22 septembre, la Commission a répondu à Renaissance, le parti de Gabriel Attal, qui voulait des précisions sur le statut des interviews avec des créateurs de contenu.

"La liberté, qu'elle soit d’expression, d’opinion, d’information, est là. C’est compliqué d’incriminer un influenceur qui fait un podcast avec un candidat, s’il n’y a pas de contrepartie financière derrière", acte le haut fonctionnaire. A l’inverse, si le créateur de contenu est payé pour réaliser une interview, l’opération doit être imputée dans les dépenses. Une telle transaction sera d’ailleurs interdite à partir du 1er octobre, date à laquelle la publicité politique est prohibée.

Prévention… et vérifications

Autre signe d’un changement d’époque, sur fond de craintes des ingérences étrangères : les candidats sont invités à faire preuve d’une "extrême vigilance" sur l’origine des fonds qui permettent de faire campagne. Pour les dons aux candidats, ils doivent être faits par des personnes résidant en France ou de nationalité française. Les prêts bancaires ne pourront, eux, provenir que d'une banque située dans l'espace économique européen.

Christian Charpy aura une vigilance toute particulière sur l’origine des prêts de personnes privées, qui constituent un moyen de se financer en plus des dons ou des ressources de son parti. "Est-ce que les prêteurs sont réels, ou sont-ils des prête-noms ? C’est une question qui peut se poser", pointe-t-il.

En cas de doute, le gendarme des comptes de campagne saisit le service de renseignement financier Tracfin pour remonter l’origine de fonds douteux, ou dialogue avec Viginum, l’agence de l’Etat chargée de lutter contre les ingérences numériques, en cas d’opération de déstabilisation "caractérisée".

Lors des dernières municipales, deux candidats LFI avaient fait l’objet d’une attaque extérieure sophistiquée. Le sujet est d’autant plus sensible que certaines formations, comme le RN, peinent à trouver un prêt. Et ce, alors que l’initiative de Matignon de créer un "pool bancaire" pour éviter cette situation a été abandonnée, comme l’a révélé

POLITICO.

World.title: EU’s Ribera joins push for first woman to lead UN
World.content:
Grynspan topped the latest informal Security Council poll, while Argentina’s Rafael Grossi, Senegal’s Macky Sall and Uganda’s Olara Otunnu are also in the field. All nine previous U.N. secretaries-general have been men.

Ribera’s intervention echoes that of Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, who said on American comedian Jon Stewart’s podcast Wednesday that “after 80 years of this multilateral order, I think it’s important, it’s fair that we choose a woman, the first woman, leading the U.N. as secretary-general.” Sánchez also called himself a “feminist politician.”

The race is unfolding as U.S. President Donald Trump pressures the U.N. to overhaul its finances and structure. Trump reportedly floated FIFA President Gianni Infantino for the job in July, though the U.S. has not formally nominated him.



The next U.N. chief will inherit an organization facing funding shortfalls and pressure to overhaul its structure, with the U.S. State Department saying in a statement that candidates must “get the U.N. back to basics and publicly commit to the changes we require.”

“The U.S. is not walking away, we’re not turning out the lights, but we are demanding reform,” U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz said last Sunday.

The Security Council must recommend a candidate with at least nine votes and no veto from its five permanent members before the General Assembly can appoint the next U.N. chief, according to organization rules.

World.title: Burnham set to join King Charles at high-stakes Commonwealth summit
World.content:
Some government officials have long suggested that conversations around the U.K. prime minister’s attendance at CHOGM are guided closely by the monarch’s wishes. Burnham and his wife had an audience with King Charles at Balmoral, his Scottish castle, earlier this month. Royal officials say plans are led and decided by the Commonwealth Secretariat and its secretary-general.

The king would have good reason to want backup, as the politics of this year’s summit looks destined to be particularly fraught.

It is being held in Antigua and Barbuda in the Caribbean, many of whose island nations are leading a charge for Britain to pay reparations for its historical role in the slave trade. Last week, Caribbean nations met in Barbados for a conference on reparatory justice.

Calls for reparations dominated the last CHOGM on the Pacific island of Samoa, where Burnham’s predecessor, Keir Starmer, insisted the issue was not on the table before other nations confronted him with a communique that mentioned reparations directly.

While U.K. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband is also due to attend CHOGM, one of the three people cited at the start of this article said attending personally would allow the prime minister to “lead from the front” rather than watching the debate unfold in his absence.

However, Downing Street’s line on reparations has changed little since 2024. Burnham’s spokesperson said on Sept. 7 that “the U.K. does not and will not pay reparations,” adding: “The transatlantic slave trade was abhorrent, and of course it’s right that we acknowledge the wrongs of the past, but we’ll continue to face forward and work with other countries on our current shared challenges.”

World.title: German police official Jürgen Ebner selected to lead Europol
World.content:
He beat two other senior police officials in the race: Alicia Malo, head of international cooperation at Spain's national police, and Linas Pernavas, director of Lithuania's main anti-corruption law enforcement agency.

Ebner began his career with the German police in 1988 and went on to hold several operational positions at the Federal Criminal Police Office, or BKA, eventually serving in the office of its president.

He moved to Europol in November 2019 after being appointed as deputy executive director responsible for governance. His portfolio has included legal and institutional matters, and he has also served as Europol's security coordinator.

His selection does not quite finish the process.

Ebner will now appear before the European Parliament's civil liberties committee, known as LIBE, which can issue a non-binding opinion on his candidacy. The Council of the EU will then formally appoint Europol's next executive director.

He is set to take charge at a pivotal moment for the agency. The European Commission has proposed significantly expanding Europol's role, resources and technological capabilities as Brussels seeks a stronger response to organized crime, cyberattacks and hybrid threats.

World.title: Vater, Mutter, Kinder – Alice Weidel und das Familienbild der AfD
World.content:
Share on LinkedIn

Share on WhatsApp

Share on X

Share via email

Alice Weidel lebt in einer gleichgeschlechtlichen Partnerschaft mit Kindern – ein scharfer Kontrast zum traditionellen Familienbild der AfD. Wie reagiert die Parteichefin, wenn Spitzenkandidaten wie Ulrich Siegmund ihr Lebensmodell öffentlich abwerten und Parteikollegen gegen sexuelle Minderheiten hetzen? Pauline von Pezold und Frederik Schindler analysieren einen internen Kulturkampf, in dem Weidel zunehmend ins Visier der eigenen Leute gerät.

Trotz historischer Wahlerfolge in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern und Berlin brodelt es hinter den Kulissen gewaltig. Ein brisantes internes Strategiepapier des Wahlkampfmanagers Daniel Fiß rechnet gnadenlos mit dem Spitzenkandidaten Leif-Erik Holm ab und fordert einen radikaleren Kurs. Die Recherche zeigt, wie extreme Kräfte die Gunst der Stunde nach der Wahl nutzen, um unliebsame Funktionäre aus dem Weg zu räumen.

Ein Blick nach Österreich offenbart zudem tiefe Risse im europäischen Rechtsaußen-Bündnis. FPÖ-Chef Herbert Kickl inszeniert sich plötzlich als israelfreundlich und erntet dafür heftigen Gegenwind von AfD-Politikern, die von „Schuldkult“ sprechen. Zudem ordnet die Folge eine bemerkenswerte Geschichtsumdeutung ein und klärt, warum Alice Weidel Adolf Hitler öffentlich als „Linksradikalen“ bezeichnet.

„Inside AfD“ ist der POLITICO-Podcast über die umstrittenste Partei des Landes. Trotz Radikalisierung und Beobachtung durch den Verfassungsschutz wächst die AfD weiter. Wie ist das möglich? Was treibt ihre Anhänger, Strategen und Gegner an? Wie funktioniert das Innenleben der Partei? Und was bedeutet ihr Aufstieg für das politische System Deutschlands?

Antworten liefern immer mittwochs Pauline von Pezold von POLITICO und Frederik Schindler von WELT — unaufgeregt, aber kritisch.
