World.title: Live: Albanese says OpenAI took three months to report Medicare breach
World.content:
Greens Senator Sarah Hanson-Young says the government needs to put an immediate stop to the growth of AI in Australia, following the hack.

"Australians are rightly worried and concerned about the power of this technology and the lack of regulation and lack of guardrails," she told News Breakfast.

"We know that it's a technology that is expanding rapidly....we've got big AI like OpenAI – this exact company – in talks with governments to set up their big data facilities here in Australia.

Sarah Hanson Young has been chairing a parliamentary inquiry into AI and data centres.

"I urge the Prime Minister to not waste this moment. Big AI needs regulation. And it's not there yet. And we should put a pause, put a moratorium, before we let them run loose here in Australia.

"She said news of the hack was "extraordinary, but somewhat expected."The Senator also questioned why it took Open AI three months to alert the government about the incident.

World.title: First Nations workers in Australia paid 16pc less per hour, report finds
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

A landmark report into the First Nations pay gap has revealed Indigenous workers are on average paid 16 per cent less per hour than the average Australian worker.

The report by the University of Technology Sydney's Centre for Indigenous People and Work (CIPW) and Indigenous Business Australia (IBA) found Indigenous workers earned 84 cents to every dollar earned by Australian workers on average.

CIPW director Professor Nareen Young said the size of the pay shortfall was equivalent to losing a lifetime of superannuation payments or working nearly two months every year for free.

"Nobody would accept that in a contract and no one should have to accept this gap," she said.

Australia's gender pay gap is smaller, with women on average earning 11.2 per cent less than men.

"Obviously we still have a problem but [the gender pay gap] is getting much better because of policy interventions," she said.

"But this research shows that Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people are on average getting paid a lot less for doing the same jobs."

Indigenous women had the greatest pay disparity, earning an average of $41 an hour compared to $52 for all Australian men.

Professor Nareen Young says Australia needs a discussion about "the value of Indigenous work". (Supplied)

Pay disparities across range of professions

The report found that across all eight major occupation groups, from managers to labourers, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander workers earned on average less per hour.

The largest hourly pay gap was recorded amongst professionals at 19.5 per cent.

IBA chief economist Dr Siddharth Shirodkar said it showed higher-paid or highly skilled occupations were not immune from pay inequality.

"If you've got a post-grad qualification … and you're First Nations, you've got a higher employment rate than non-Indigenous people, but the average annual income for Indigenous people with those qualifications is generally lower."

Dr Shirodkar said the pay gap existed across almost every age category as well.

"That points to systemic issues, structural issues and indeed bias and discrimination," he said.

Dr Siddharth Shirodkar estimates the pay gap will amount to $170 billion in lost income by 2050. (Supplied)

The report analysed data from 227 occupations and found in three quarters of occupational groups, Indigenous workers earned less per hour than all workers in the same role.

The size of that gap varied, from 34 per cent for environmental scientists to 6 per cent for truck drivers.

"The dominant pattern is persistent underpayment, not isolated anomalies," the report said.

Teachers and machinery operators/drivers stood out as exceptions, earning close to pay parity on hourly wages or even slightly reversed hourly pay gaps.

Dr Shirodkar estimated the pay gap would amount to $170 billion in lost income by 2050, which would have broader impacts on the Australian economy.

"That's not taking into consideration the compounding effect of lower superannuation, lower savings, lower rates of wealth creation as well," he said.

Pay gap attributed to structural racism

The study examined the factors typically given as reasons for pay gaps — such as hours worked, occupation, age and education — and found these could not fully explain the pay gap.

The study found differences in the numbers of hours worked by Indigenous people could only explain about 2 per cent of the gap.

And while Indigenous workers were somewhat more likely to work in lower-paying occupations, the authors said this could only explain 27.5 per cent of the total gap.

Professor Young said that left 70 per cent of the Indigenous pay gap "unexplained".

"We've been told for years that this is about education, about experience, about the sorts of jobs our mob end up in, and we've tested every one of those explanations," she said.

"So what is left is structural racism in the way work is valued and paid.

"What we need to have as an Australian community is a big discussion about the value of Indigenous work."

The report said the gap likely reflected factors such as the legacy of historically discriminatory wage setting, racial bias in recruitment, and limited power for First Nations workers to negotiate salaries and pay increases.

These factors were not directly measured in the report but were identified as potential contributors.

While the report measured pay gaps using average hourly earnings, the authors found strong correlations when examining median pay gaps across occupations as well.

The authors said this meant their findings were unlikely to be skewed by a small number of unusually high or low-income earners but reflected broader differences across occupations.

They said their estimates of hourly earnings were economy-wide figures and should not be interpreted as "like-for-like comparisons of otherwise identical workers".

Employers urged to prevent racial discrimination

The report made several key recommendations aimed at creating fairer pay and employment structures.

The most significant was to place a positive duty on employers to prevent racial discrimination, in the same way they must prevent sex discrimination.

Other recommendations included improving Indigenous employment data collection, and for cultural skills to be valued properly when wages are set.

World.title: Why this beach was named Sydney's cleanest
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Water quality at the state's beaches has improved slightly, but one of Sydney's most popular swimming spots has received a "poor" grade for the fifth year in a row.

Ninety seven per cent of the state's monitored ocean beaches received a rating of "good" or "very good" in this year's State of the Beaches report, up from 95 per cent in 2025.

Avalon was Sydney's cleanest beach, while on the Central Coast, Birdie Beach, Frazer Beach and Forresters Beach shared top honours.

Birdie Beach is named one of the cleanest swimming spots on the Central Coast. (Supplied: Central Coast Council)

One Mile Beach was the Hunter's highest-scoring swimming spot, while the Shoalhaven's cleanest was Warrain Beach.

Wollongong City Beach and Shellharbour Beach were the Illawarra's cleanest beaches in 2026.

However, the report also highlighted continued water quality issues at some swimming spots, including Coogee Beach, which received another "poor" rating.

It hasn't received a "good" rating since 2021.

Dr Meredith Campey, manager of the NSW government's Beachwatch program, said Coogee was "more susceptible to stormwater impact" than other beaches.

"In dry conditions, it's usually suitable for swimming," Dr Campey said.

"But when it rains, it gets a lot of stormwater which comes through a large stormwater drain at the north end of the beach," she said.

Narrabeen Lagoon, Rose Bay Beach, Frenchmans Bay and Yarra Bay were among the 40 sites to receive "poor" grades.

Foreshores Beach, Gymea Bay Baths and the Blue Mountain's Minnehaha Falls all received "very poor" grades.

How were swimming spots graded?

Beachwatch did not assess every swimming spot, but graded 229 sites on a scale from "very good" to "very poor."

As well as ocean beaches, they included estuarine, lake, lagoon and freshwater sites.

The sites were given a sanitary inspection to assess the likelihood of faecal contamination.

Stormwater drains, sewage outflow points and swimmers themselves could all contribute that risk, Dr Campey said.

Coogee Beach, which received another "poor" rating. (Supplied)

Regular water quality testing was also undertaken, measuring the levels of enterococci — a bacteria found in faeces.

Overall, 79 per cent of swimming spots received "good" or "very good" gradings, a slight improvement on last year's result of 76 per cent.

Dr Campey said many parts of the state received average to below-average rainfall during the 2026 reporting period, which had a positive effect on water quality results.

"Rainfall is the major driver of pollution to recreational waters, because it generates stormwater runoff and also triggers discharges from the wastewater system," she said.

Bondi vs 'Pondi'

Mona Vale Beach, another improver this year. (Supplied: Northern Beaches Council)

While the blue water and golden sand of Bondi Beach are internationally recognised, the report shows 'Pondi' — Penrith Beach — enjoys the same "good" grade as the famous landmark.

Mona Vale and Dee Why both improved their grades to "very good" in 2026.

Manly's Shelly Beach improved its performance, as did Double Bay's Murray Rose (Redleaf) Pool, which both moved from "poor" to "good".

North Avoca and MacMasters beaches were among several Central Coast swimming spots that received improved results in 2026.

Shelly Beach in Manly improved on its performance. (ABC News)

On the north coast, Air Force Beach, Evans Head Main Beach and Shark Bay all ascended into the "very good" category.

Water quality at Sydney's Maroubra Beach declined in the 2026 reporting period and it was downgraded from "very good" to "good".

Surf Beach at Kiama also went backwards, receiving a "poor" grading in this year's report.

NSW Environment Minister Penny Sharpe said the report was backed by "good science."

"Through decades of consistent monitoring, Beachwatch provides the robust data needed to track water quality trends and give swimmers confidence in the information they use," she said.

World.title: 'Cheeky' 95yo celebrates another birthday jumping out of a plane
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Betty Gregory doesn't know any other 95-year-olds who celebrate their birthday the way she does — by jumping out of a plane.

This year marked the sixth time Ms Gregory has been airborne on her birthday, after she first took flight at age 80.

Even a recent move to a nursing home couldn't keep the great-great grandmother grounded.

"I thought, 'You only live once and 95 is just a number, so why not make the most of it?' And that's what I'm trying to do," Ms Gregory said.

"I just live one day at a time and anything I feel like doing, I do it."

Betty Gregory airborne for her 95th birthday. (Supplied: Gold Coast Skydive)

Ms Gregory said she decided to downsize after living alone in her high-rise apartment for the past 26 years.

"It was right on the beach and I had a beautiful view from the balcony up to Surfers Paradise and I was really happy with that view," Ms Gregory said.

" But the point is, as you get to 95 you begin to be able to do less and less, competently anyway. "

Ms Gregory now has daily assistance with personal care and uses a walking frame to get around her new home.

Betty Gregory recently moved into aged care. (ABC Gold Coast: Danielle Mahe)

However, getting older won't stop her from jumping out of a plane for her birthday again next year.

"My friends are used to me doing things that are rather unconventional," Ms Gregory said

" I'm not your usual 95-year-old, I'm afraid to say. I'm rather cheeky. "

Melinda Griffiths, general manager of the southern Gold Coast facility where Ms Gregory now lives, said she was proof that life doesn't stop when someone moves into residential care.

"I think it just shows that there is so much more that actually happens in aged care than what people maybe believe or have misconceptions about."

Melinda Griffiths runs the facility Betty now calls home. (ABC Gold Coast: Danielle Mahe)

Ms Griffiths said elderly people, especially those in aged care, should be encouraged to do what they love.

"This is just the start of another journey … and it's important for us to take the opportunities to try new things, to make sure that we're still involved in the community, understand what they like, what their passions are," she said.

" We go to the football, we go to the AFL … it's about living their best life. "

Ms Gregory's son, Jim Gellately, 70, said his mother has been active her whole life and is always open to trying new things.

"We've got video after video after video of her doing different things, entertaining people," he said.

"And although she's not doing too much of that now, she gets all this notoriety from jumping out of the plane. Everybody speaks to her, which she loves."

Back down to earth, after Betty Gregory landed safely on Kirra beach. (Supplied: Gold Coast Skydive)

Mr Gellately said he and his two sisters would happily support their mother to go skydiving again, as long as she received medical clearance.

"We've got no worries. We've never tried to talk my mum out of it.

"Honestly, if the doctor says it's all right to do it, let them do it.

"So I figure, as long as you can just lift your knees up when they land, that's about all you've got to do, really."

World.title: Breaking: OpenAI agent hacked Medicare portal, PM says
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has revealed an AI agent hacked into an Australian Medicare data portal earlier this year.

Speaking in New York, Mr Albanese said the Open AI agent gained unauthorised access to the Medicare statistics reporting service portal administered by Services Australia.

The AI agent accessed both public and non-public files.

The agent was conducting research into public medical spending when it found a way to break through privacy protections.

Mr Albanese said it took three months for OpenAI to admit the breach, which he said was unacceptable.

"Today I spoke with the CEO of OpenAI, Sam Altman, to express Australia's extreme concern about this incident," he said.

"And I also expressed my disappointment that it took the company way too long to inform the government what had occurred.

"The nature of the way that the notification occurred as well was unacceptable."

He said there was no evidence any individual personal information had been accessed, but an investigation aided by the Australian Signals Directorate was now underway.

Defence Minister Richard Marles, who is currently acting prime minister while Mr Albanese is in New York, said he had been advised "the impact to our systems is very minor".

"That said, what we are seeing here is an unauthorised access that has occurred via an AI model," he said.

"That is completely unacceptable. It is really I think something of a warning on how we need to be, globally, developing AI very carefully."

World.title: 'Anomalies' in images could prompt further search for young Gus Lamont
World.content:
When the lead detective in the investigation into the disappearance of four-year-old Gus Lamont spoke of the "unwavering commitment" of police, he couldn't stop a waver from briefly entering his voice before he regathered his composure.

"They are working their arses off, on this job, sometimes thanklessly," Superintendent Darren Fielke said of his fellow detectives on the case.

" They live and breathe this every day. "

Superintendent Fielke, who is the officer in charge of SA Police's Major Crime Investigation Branch, made those comments at a media conference on Wednesday, on the eve of the first anniversary of Gus being reported missing from his outback home near Yunta.

It has been almost a year since Gus Lamont was reported missing on Saturday, September 27, 2025. (Supplied: SA Police)

Seasoned senior police officers are not in the habit of being publicly unrestrained in their feelings — the requirements of the job perhaps dictate against anything other than dispassionately professional demeanour.

But Superintendent Fielke's moment of emotion underlined the fierce determination of police.

"We're going to continue to thoroughly and meticulously investigate the disappearance of Gus until we get a resolution," he insisted.

Loading...

Wednesday's media conference was the setting for two significant developments — a video appeal from Gus's grief-stricken parents, and the announcement of a reward of up to $1 million for information leading to a conviction over the boy's disappearance or to "the location of his remains".

"A reward is a legitimate strategy that we use in police investigations," Superintendent Fielke said.

"In the past 12 months we've paid out a significant amount of money for rewards, for cold case matters, that wouldn't have been resolved without a reward being offered, so we know they work.

"One million dollars is a life-changing amount of money for someone. Now is the time to come forward."

Strategically the right time

An incentive of that magnitude is not unprecedented in the history of South Australian policing.

Superintendent Fielke said there had been, in total, 17 missing children's cases that had prompted million-dollar rewards, and added that the latest one had been sought by police from the SA government "in the last few weeks".

Footage of Gus riding a bike was released earlier this year. (Supplied: SA Police)

Criminologist Xanthe Weston told the ABC she thought the timing of that move was right.

She said in the immediate aftermath of Gus's disappearance, police were inundated with information — "but clearly they need a push now".

"They've thought this through very carefully," Dr Weston said.

"It feels like it's been a long time, but actually, strategically, I don't think it would have worked earlier in the investigation.

"[Initially] the police were receiving a lot of information from the public that they certainly followed up."

Xanthe Weston says she suspects police had very carefully considered the timing of the reward. (ABC Newcastle: Romy Stephens)

Dr Weston cautioned that rewards were double-edged swords, and had the potential to elicit not just legitimate intelligence but false information.

"If somebody is involved in Gus's disappearance, it's likely they've talked to somebody. People generally don't keep these things totally secret to themselves," she said.

"What the police need is genuine information — what they don't need is people calling with theories and guesses."

'Anomalies' could prompt further search

The challenge presented by misinformation is one police are acutely aware of.

"We need people to come forward with information that will help drive this investigation forward," Superintendent Fielke said.

"Theories and conspiracies are not what we're looking for."

But police have multiple irons in the fire.

The early days of the search for Gus on Oak Park Station. (Supplied: SA Police)

While the media conference was mostly focused on matters other than the strictly investigational, the chief detective's comments nevertheless offered a glimpse of a potential fresh line of enquiry.

Superintendent Fielke said detectives from Taskforce Horizon — the police unit established to investigate Gus's disappearance — had recently completed "a painstaking, methodical, forensically detailed manual" scouring of imagery gathered during aerial searches above Gus's home, Oak Park Station.

"As a result of that manual searching, we have identified some anomalies in the imagery that has been provided to us," he said.

" These anomalies are now being further reviewed and depending on how that review will plays out will determine whether we return to Oak Park Station and conduct further searching. "

A map released earlier this year showing the search areas undertaken around Gus's home. (Supplied: SAPOL)

Asked to elaborate on what those anomalies are, Superintendent Fielke was reluctant, citing investigational reasons.

But he was adamant that, as the first anniversary of Gus's disappearance approaches, police are as "focused and determined" as ever.

World.title: OpenAI agent breached Medicare, Albanese reveals
World.content:
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has revealed that an artificial intelligence agent developed by OpenAI infiltrated an Australian government website in June, accessing public and non-public files. Speaking to reporters in New York, Albanese said the incident involved an OpenAI agent gaining unauthorised access to the public-facing Medicare Statistics Reporting Service portal, administered by Services Australia. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese speaking from New York. Nine “This incident occurred in June this year, and involved an OpenAI agent gaining unauthorised access into the public-facing Medicare Statistics Reporting Service portal, which is administered by Services Australia,” Albanese said. He said the agent accessed publicly available files, as well as material not intended for public access.



“Evidence currently available is there is no broader compromise to the Services Australia network. Nonetheless, this situation is obviously unacceptable,” he said. “And today, I spoke with the CEO of OpenAI, Sam Altman, to express Australia’s extreme concern about this incident. And I also expressed my disappointment that it took the company way too long to inform the government what had occurred, and the nature of the way that that notification occurred as well was unacceptable.” OpenAI chief Sam Altman. Bloomberg News of the breach comes two days after Albanese urged other world leaders to unite on efforts to protect people from the risks of artificial intelligence, saying in a speech that no country can manage the technology’s growing risks alone. Australia was among 22 signatories calling for new international safeguards on AI at the United Nations on Monday, amid warnings from scientists and industry executives that the rapid development of powerful systems could outpace governments’ ability to control emerging risks.



Related Article AI ‘Could kill us all’: Anthropic insiders say AI has more than 10% chance of ending humanity – soon The prime minister joined colleagues, including Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz to call for mandatory safety testing, independent evaluations and greater international oversight of so-called frontier AI models. US President Donald Trump has rejected calls for slowdowns and restrictions on AI growth, comparing it to the Industrial Revolution, and warning that any self-imposed guardrails would give China a dangerous advantage. Trump will meet China’s President Xi Jinping at the White House later on Thursday. It is not yet clear whether OpenAI was testing the agent or someone was using it when it got into the Medicare portal. OpenAI was contacted for comment.



Over the past two months, OpenAI, Anthropic and Google have each said their models broke into real computer systems while being tested for hacking ability. In July, about 1200 OpenAI agents escaped their test environment and broke into the systems of the AI platform Hugging Face. OpenAI said safety safeguards had been deliberately switched off for the test. In August, it announced it would slow development of its models and paused one stage of its training for two weeks. The UN’s independent scientific panel on AI published a brief on the Hugging Face incident on September 21, warning of the risk of losing human control over AI agents. Anthropic, which makes the Claude chatbot, said on July 30 that its models had gained unauthorised access to three organisations’ systems during cybersecurity tests, while Google said on September 19 that one of its Gemini models had accessed three outside companies’ systems during testing in May. More to come Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: FBI hacked: Cyber gang claims it has sensitive data of agents and operations
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaCybersecurity FBI hacked: Cyber gang claims it has sensitive data of agents and operations Raphael Satter and AJ Vicens September 24, 2026 — 6:24am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington - FBI data allegedly stolen by the hacking group ShinyHunters carries granular detail about scores of bureau officials’ job assignments, including sensitive work against Chinese spies, Russian intelligence, drug cartels, and more, Reuters has found. The 5000-line spreadsheet – said by the hackers to represent only a small piece of their claimed two- to-three-terabyte trove – includes names, addresses, telephone numbers, dates of birth, social security numbers, and emergency contact details for what they claimed were thousands of FBI employees. The Department of Justice (DOJ) seal on the J. Edgar Hoover Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) building in Washington. Bloomberg It also includes details of assignments to specific field offices and, in some cases, to units engaged in high-stakes intelligence, security, or counterespionage work. In a statement, the FBI said it was aware of “a cyber-criminal enterprise group claiming a compromise of the FBIJobs.gov portal and alleged impact to FBI employee personally identifiable information”.



The bureau said the cause of the breach was still undetermined, but that it was “actively and aggressively investigating the matter.” Related Article Updated

Trump's White House FBI says it thwarted plot to use explosive drones, snipers to attack White House UFC event The hackers said on Tuesday (Washington time) that they had breached the FBI, stealing data on a large number of current and former FBI employees. ShinyHunters said it is holding the data hostage until the bureau rescinds an unflattering statement about the group issued in May. Former FBI counterintelligence operative Eric O’Neill said the data allegedly stolen by ShinyHunters was “a foreign intelligence service goldmine.” “China would be incredibly interested to know the individuals who are working against it,” said O’Neill, founder of the cybersecurity company Nexasure AI, after his stint at the bureau. He predicted that other hostile intelligence services would be eager to get their hands on the data, along with disgruntled extremists in the United States.



“If I were on that list I would be very concerned,” he said. ShinyHunters said in a statement on Wednesday that it was trying to keep the personnel information from circulating widely in the meantime. “If the 5000 sample data records leak, it’s not because of us,” the group said. Although Reuters has not been able to authenticate the entire spreadsheet, it has been able to individually verify the details of more than 22 people by cross-referencing information in the hacked data with credit records and previous data leaks carried by the dark web intelligence platform District 4 Labs. The FBI building in Washington. The bureau said the cause of the security breach was still undetermined Bloomberg Some of the assignment details in the ShinyHunters’ data are indistinguishable from what employees themselves might say publicly, noting agents at field offices in Baltimore or Newark, New Jersey, for example.



But in some cases, the data referred to FBI units or initiatives that were sensitive or whose existence has not previously been disclosed. The data names 14 staffers focused on China-related matters, including members of the “China criminal enterprise unit,” the “China tech transfer analysis unit,” and the “China intelligence

section.” Nine others are listed as serving in Russia-related roles, including two in the “Russia Operations Section” and one working on “Russia Critical Infra and Tech Threat.” Three people are listed as working in Iran- or Hezbollah-focused intelligence roles. ‘You don’t have to look far to find examples of undercover agents being harmed when their cover is blown.’ Trevor Hilligoss, chief intelligence officer for cybersecurity company SpyCloud Eighteen others are listed as working with “data intercept” or “telecom intercept” technologies, or in the FBI’s “clandestine technical operations” unit, or its “covert access section,” or in video, audio, or electronic surveillance roles.



A further 11 FBI staffers are listed as working in HUMINT, or human intelligence, jobs, including several listed as working in the “Humint program management section.” Related Article Cybersecurity Ransom ‘paid’ to hackers who crippled online learning in Australia Trevor Hilligoss, a former Army investigator who worked with the FBI, said the information tying specific named people to human intelligence work was particularly troubling. “You don’t have to look far to find examples of undercover agents being harmed when their cover is blown,” he said. Hilligoss, now the chief intelligence officer for cybersecurity company SpyCloud, said his concerns were

heightened by the inclusion of emergency contacts – often spouses or children – “who may have less operational security knowledge than their relative that works in a sensitive field.”



Reuters could not verify that all the job assignments were authentic or up-to-date, but it was able to match the career details or titles of eight people whose data was leaked to information in court filings, news articles, or public profiles on LinkedIn or to online posts on sites such as Instagram. ShinyHunters previously claimed credit for the purported theft of millions of business records from video game developer Rockstar Games, the maker of Grand Theft Auto, and an intrusion focused on the education tool Canvas that ⁠triggered widespread ​disruption across US schools. In May, the FBI said ShinyHunters sometimes used “exaggerated claims of access to sensitive or personal information to prompt payment from victims.” ShinyHunters said its “threats and claims are very real”, adding that the FBI’s statement was why it targeted the bureau. Reuters has not been able to verify what else the hackers are holding. ShinyHunters previously said they obtained files related to the vetting of employees and applicants, the contracting of background investigations, and agents’ sensitive medical data, but said on Wednesday it would not release any further data.



O’Neill, the former FBI operative, cautioned against drawing conclusions about what the hackers hold. “They’re really trying to scare the hell out of the FBI,” he noted. Reuters

World.title: Chinese carmaker’s new EV battery will charge in under five minutes
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesElectric vehicles Chinese carmaker’s new EV battery will charge in under five minutes Tom Haynes September 24, 2026 — 6:18am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Volvo’s Chinese owner has unveiled an electric car battery that can charge in just four-and-a-half minutes. Geely said the time needed for its new battery to go from 10 per cent to 70 per cent, an industry benchmark for a reasonable charge, was the fastest in the industry. Geely tested the battery on a Zeekr 001 model. The company said the time needed for its new battery to go from 10 per cent to 70 per cent, an industry benchmark for a reasonable charge, was the fastest in the industry. Getty It has shaved 20 seconds off the next best battery, developed by China’s biggest electric carmaker BYD, which has also been pouring money into so-called “flash charging”. BYD unveiled a system earlier this year capable of charging a battery from 10 per cent to 97 per cent in nine minutes, and announced plans for 90,000 charging stations by 2028.



Geely said its new system could charge a battery from 10 per cent to 97 per cent in eight minutes and 40 seconds, using a charger capable of delivering up to 2.2 megawatts (MW) of power. Related Article Energy EVs are taking over as Australians flee the bowser. What happens next? The one-upmanship underlines the pace of innovation among Chinese carmakers in the cut-throat EV market. Zhang Dewang, a Geely executive, said the speed of charging was “approaching the physical limit”. “The marginal gains from pursuing even faster speeds in the future will become increasingly small,” he told Reuters at a launch event in China.



Geely has bested BYD by using a higher voltage system. Its new battery uses an 800-volt electrical system and the higher voltage allows more electricity to be pushed into the battery at once, helping to cut charging times. The 2.2 MW peak output is also above the power available from most conventional public chargers. Tesla’s latest Supercharger technology, for example, is rated at up to 500 kilowatts, making Geely’s claimed peak power more than four times as high. Geely has bested BYD by using a higher voltage system. Its new battery uses an 800-volt electrical system and the higher voltage allows more electricity to be pushed into the battery at once, helping to cut charging times. Getty Images The Galaxy E5, an electric SUV, will be the first Geely model to use the new technology when it goes on sale in China later this year. Geely, which also owns Lotus and has stakes in Polestar, is among the Chinese groups expanding rapidly overseas. It sold 1.42 million vehicles in the first half of this year and has raised its target for exports to 920,000 vehicles in 2026.



In the UK, Geely currently sells its EX5 electric SUV and the Starray EM-i hybrid. The new Galaxy E5 is a Chinese-market model and is not currently sold in Britain, although the E5 is badged as the EX5 for the UK market. Related Article Energy ‘The shift is now absolute’: China’s BYD says Australia just passed its EV tipping point China produced almost 75 per cent of the world’s electric cars last year, while exports of Chinese-made EVs more than doubled to a record 2.5 million vehicles. Chinese-made EV sales in Europe also jumped by almost 50 per cent in 2025. The charging battle is part of a wider shift in the Chinese car industry, where manufacturers are now competing on battery range, charging speeds and driver-assistance technology rather than simply price. World.title: Seismic switcheroo: Peter V’landys quits Racing NSW for unprecedented NRL job
World.content:
Analysis NationalNRL 2026 Seismic switcheroo: Peter V’landys quits Racing NSW for unprecedented NRL job Bevan Shields September 24, 2026 — 5:45am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

As far as soft landings go, the one Peter V’landys has just orchestrated for himself is about as good as they come. The 66-year-old sporting administrator – easily one of the most powerful figures in Australian sport, media and politics – has resigned as chief executive of Racing NSW following 22 years at the helm. V’landys is due to be unveiled as the NRL’s new executive chairman – an unprecedented role for the game and the man himself. Seismic? Yes. Surprising? It shouldn’t be. This has been in the works for a good six months. The catalyst for the switcheroo was the mid-season departure of Andrew Abdo as NRL chief executive. The big-vision loving V’landys and the details-focused Abdo and were a good yin and yang, but the latter jumped at the chance to become Tennis Australia boss and have a breather from his unpredictable and demanding chairman. Peter V’landys has dominated Sydney’s racing scene for more than two decades. Tim Bauer A worldwide search would have ordinarily found a new chief executive to lead the booming NRL into the 2030s. But wouldn’t you know it, the search ended up settling on V’landys, who will combine the role with his existing duties as Australian Rugby League Commission chairman. There is talk he may be paid up to $3 million a year – roughly double what Abdo was banking.



V’landys has told friends he feels a genuine emotional pull about leaving Racing NSW. Fair enough. While things have become tricky of late – V’landys and the organisation found themselves in far too many legal and political scraps – his impact on the industry is undeniable. “He will go down as one of the best, if not the best, sporting administrators in Australian history,” says champion trainer Chris Waller. “When he came in he promised to double the prize money and introduce this and that, and everyone thought ‘what a load of nonsense’. And I was very sceptical. But everything he said, he did. Sure, he may have made a few mistakes over the time, but overall his impact has been quite amazing.” Peter V’landys during a trip to Royal Ascot in 2022. Getty The best indicator of V’landys’ success in pulling NSW racing out of its doldrums is the ferocious way in which Victorian racing authorities responded to new events in Sydney like The Everest, now the world’s richest turf race and attracting a new generation of racegoers. The stuffy Melbourne establishment still hates it – something V’landys has taken great delight in.



His willingness to go to court to secure a 1.5 per cent tax on online wagering operators that take bets on races in NSW has delivered annual fees of at least $150 million. The windfall allowed V’landys to act as a generous benefactor, throwing cash around like confetti and winning friends and allies in the process. Racing NSW says V’landys’ initiatives as chief executive since 2004 have delivered $3.5 billion in new funding, with total new recurring annual revenues nudging the $375 million mark. Saturday metropolitan prize money is up from $45,000 in 2004 to $160,000 now, and country TAB prizes up from $5000 to $27,000. V’landys’ right-hand man, chief operating officer Graeme Hinton, is in the box seat to take over. V’landys also secured a big federal government rescue package during the equine influenza outbreak of 2007. Related Article Exclusive

NRL grand final Fallout with star leaves NRL with no pre-game entertainment for grand final But it has not all been sunshine and rainbows. V’landys arguably stayed too long. He was sometimes too eager for a fight. There has been much speculation about what a review into the laws governing racing in NSW, led by former health minister Brad Hazzard, might say. The report is sitting on the government’s desk. What’s in it depends on who you ask. Some believe Hazzard has stuck to his brief and merely scrutinised the Thoroughbred Racing Act. Others reckon it could make some pointy observations about corporate culture at Racing NSW. V’landys is known to be a bit of a tyrant in the office and a notorious cheapskate. Staff at the racing regulator required permission to print a colour photocopy, and catching cabs was banned if a meeting venue was within the CBD.



That approach has made its way to the NRL’s Sydney headquarters, with biscuits in the kitchen cut back and indoor pot plants banished and replaced with footballs. “You don’t have to water the footballs,” he explained. Staff who had great affection for Abdo are much more cautious about how V’landys does business. As chair of the game, his big thinking was chaotic but at least good fun. As a nuts and bolts manager, some say he is just chaotic. V’landys’ critics believe the embarrassing collapse of talks with singer Tones and I over a performance for the league’s October 4 grand final could be a sign of things to come. The debacle means there will be no major act at the game. The singer’s management says an offer was only presented on September 5 – one month before the big day. Once V’landys gets his racing farewell out of the road on Thursday morning, he and the ARLC commission will need to start answering questions about how this NRL leadership experiment is going to work. Former NRL chief executive Andrew Abdo and ARL Commission chairman Peter V’landys. Nick Moir V’landys once thought the idea was a shocker. Amid speculation in 2020 that V’landys might have a stab at combining the chief executive and chairman roles, he said: “There needs to be a segregation between the board and management. I’ve always believed in proper corporate governance, so it would be hypocritical to do anything other than that.”



Putting so much power in the hands of one man provides real potential for things to go wrong. What are the safeguards? Appointing a couple of commissioners to mediate in disputes with internal or external stakeholders isn’t enough – particularly when most of the members of the commission are diehard V’landys loyalists. He is likely to be appointed on a contract of three years, which would take him close to 70 years of age. V’landys may have faults, but a lack of energy and focus on work isn’t one of them. Once he’s landed in the big chair at Driver Avenue, he might be able to stay as long as he likes. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: ‘I’ve got 10 years left as a sexual person’: Inside Sharon Horgan’s hilarious new show
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Sharon Horgan can’t quite remember the quote. “The title for this came from something I read. What was it … this saying about 50 being the old age of youth. No, the youth of old age. Yeah, that was it, 50 is the youth of old age,” she says triumphantly. It’s a line from French novelist Victor Hugo, which shows you that one, Horgan – the most acclaimed female comedy writer of her age – is a big reader, and two, she’s a pragmatist. Related Article ★★★★★

Review Sharon Horgan’s five-star comedy is for every woman stuck in the ‘sandwich generation’ “Because I also thought that ‘50 is the Youth of Old Age’ is too long for the title of a TV show. So I just went with Youth.” It turns out that Youth is the perfect title for her new HBO comedy because it’s as much about a 50-year-old woman, played by Horgan, as it is about her son, a teenager played by Aran Murphy (son of Cillian). And her ostensible love interest, Patrick (Rupert Friend, Homeland), is also someone who can’t quite leave his youth behind. “He’s described by Sharon as, ‘an institutionally single man-child’,” Friend says. “He’s just in his mid-to-late 40s and he hasn’t considered things like families and commitment. Not in a dastardly, caddish way, just in a kind of Peter Pan way: he never grew up.” Rupert Friend co-stars as the roguish Patrick, a former boyfriend of Horgan’s Alex. HBO Max



Youth is all about growing up, even for so-called grown-ups. In the case of Horgan’s character, literary agent Alex, she’s embarking on growing up for the third time. She has a marriage behind her that didn’t work, she’s very close with her son, but he’s now off to college and so Alex is left doing the things we all do in our 20s – except that she’s 50. On reflection, it’s a life stage that seems to have been largely overlooked in storytelling. “It’s about this particular time in a woman’s life, but also it’s the sandwich generation thing,” says Horgan, referring to the modern predicament of middle-aged parents looking after their children and their own ageing parents at the same time. Aran Murphy, son of Cillian, stars in Youth alongside Horgan. HBO Max I meet Horgan and Friend on set in the London suburb of Clerkenwell, where they’ve taken over an 18th century courthouse, now a fashionable restaurant and members’ club. Today, it doubles as the office of Alex’s publishers: she works alongside her best friend and boss, Sam (Sharlene Whyte), doing things like trying to break it to Damian Lewis, in another Homeland nod, that maybe his book isn’t the next big thing. The real story of Youth, however, is Alex herself, and as with much of Horgan’s work it’s personal. When Horgan talks about her character, she does it in the first person – “I” do this, then “I” do that, which suggests how much of the story comes from her own life. Her youngest daughter, for example, is currently sitting her A-levels when we meet. She will soon go to university, leaving Horgan, also a divorcee like Alex, in a similar predicament: with her baby moving out, she thinks that at 50, now’s the time to get her life back. With a child moving out of home, Horgan says “it”s just this sudden feeling of f---ing freedom”. HBO Max “I mean, I’m still desperately sad that he goes,” she says of on-screen son Ruari’s departure, “but for me it’s just this sudden feeling of f---ing freedom. The character has this sort of epiphany. She gets arthritis in her jaw and she’s like, ‘Is this the start of a general decline? I’ve got 10 years as a sexual person tops, you know, I need to find someone now’.”



Naturally, things soon fall apart. Ruari is forced to move home again in a matter of weeks. “So the show is me navigating that,” Horgan says, “trying to find the final part of my story … to find happiness and not die alone. But life decides something else.” ‘I feel like I don’t know how to write something that isn’t hopefully going to f--- you up a bit.’ Sharon Horgan On the page, this could all be desperately sad. But on the screen it’s also achingly funny. It’s the gut-wrenching, bittersweet combination that has become a hallmark of Horgan’s writing, through modern classics like Pulling, Catastrophe and most recently Bad Sisters. “I feel like I don’t know how to write something that isn’t hopefully going to f--- you up a bit,” she says. “I mean, my dream is that the first episode takes you somewhere really funny, and then really slaps you around the head at the end.” The events of Youth could all be desperately sad. But on the screen it’s also achingly funny. HBO Max Much of the head-slapping in Youth comes from Horgan’s interactions with her son, who is a most challenging of challenging adolescents, and then with Patrick — an equally bamboozling on-off boyfriend. As with Rob Delaney’s character in Catastrophe, or even Claes Bang’s “The Prick” in Bad Sisters, Horgan is as adept at writing men as she is women.



After all, as she says, “It’s not just women – especially now – who reach a point in their life where they feel like, ‘What am I doing?’ Men are also feeling the ticking clock in a way, asking what’s expected of you as a man and what you’re supposed to bring to the world. I hope that that’s what [Friend’s] character is representing because I’m really interested in that as well.” ‘I wanted to avoid the notion of jumping on some kind of bandwagon to talk about menopause.’ Sharon Horgan The abstract Rupert Friend, an actor best known for scowling and subterfuge, might not have been the obvious choice. “I wanted Rupert to do it because he’s so f---ing funny,” says Horgan. “He’s so funny. I mean obviously people would mainly know Homeland, but he’s a really great comic actor. And his bullshit detector is on a par with mine. When we’ve been on set together, if something doesn’t feel authentic or real, he’s on it.” There’s nothing much more authentic and real than having your character drunkenly consider eating a burger off the floor of the bus. HBO Max Friend duly appears, bullshit detector active to the extent that he immediately spots my light bewilderment that he’s got the role at all. “Patrick’s actually not a cad or a player, which I know means the fact that I’m playing him is a surprise,” Friend says, laughing. “Neither does he have a knife under his bed nor any extra expertise with guns. He’s not that guy at all. He can barely boil an egg, and that’s one of the things that was so exciting when Sharon asked me to do it.”



Horgan picked Friend for the role and called him out of the blue. He says he has long admired her comedy and her acting, but most of all her writing. Editor's pick Streaming Wild, profane and heartbreaking: A guide to Anthony Bourdain’s best TV “One of the things I love in this is that every time that we sort of enter a Richard Curtis film, Sharon subverts it. Even within a scene we will look at each other and go, ‘Is this getting schmaltzy? Is there like a spotlight coming on?’ and if it is, then we’ll dodge it. Because frankly, real life isn’t like that. You might find the person of your dreams but as you get older, there’s always a big conversation to have.” In other words, Youth isn’t just about women of a certain age, it’s about everyone at a certain age. “I didn’t want to write anything that had middle-aged female tropes and I wanted to avoid the notion of jumping on some kind of bandwagon to talk about menopause,” Horgan says. “I just wanted to write about what I know and what I’ve learned at this particular point in my life. And to show through a comic lens … how hard it is.” Youth in streaming on HBO Max now.

World.title: OpenAI agent breached Medicare, Albanese reveals
World.content:
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has revealed that an artificial intelligence agent developed by OpenAI infiltrated an Australian government website in June, accessing public and non-public files. Speaking to reporters in New York, Albanese said the incident involved an OpenAI agent gaining unauthorised access to the public-facing Medicare Statistics Reporting Service portal, administered by Services Australia. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese speaking from New York. Nine “This incident occurred in June this year, and involved an OpenAI agent gaining unauthorised access into the public-facing Medicare Statistics Reporting Service portal, which is administered by Services Australia,” Albanese said. He said the agent accessed publicly available files, as well as material not intended for public access.



“Evidence currently available is there is no broader compromise to the Services Australia network. Nonetheless, this situation is obviously unacceptable,” he said. “And today, I spoke with the CEO of OpenAI, Sam Altman, to express Australia’s extreme concern about this incident. And I also expressed my disappointment that it took the company way too long to inform the government what had occurred, and the nature of the way that that notification occurred as well was unacceptable.” OpenAI chief Sam Altman. Bloomberg News of the breach comes two days after Albanese urged other world leaders to unite on efforts to protect people from the risks of artificial intelligence, saying in a speech that no country can manage the technology’s growing risks alone. Australia was among 22 signatories calling for new international safeguards on AI at the United Nations on Monday, amid warnings from scientists and industry executives that the rapid development of powerful systems could outpace governments’ ability to control emerging risks.



Related Article AI ‘Could kill us all’: Anthropic insiders say AI has more than 10% chance of ending humanity – soon The prime minister joined colleagues, including Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz to call for mandatory safety testing, independent evaluations and greater international oversight of so-called frontier AI models. US President Donald Trump has rejected calls for slowdowns and restrictions on AI growth, comparing it to the Industrial Revolution, and warning that any self-imposed guardrails would give China a dangerous advantage. Trump will meet China’s President Xi Jinping at the White House later on Thursday. It is not yet clear whether OpenAI was testing the agent or someone was using it when it got into the Medicare portal. OpenAI was contacted for comment.



Over the past two months, OpenAI, Anthropic and Google have each said their models broke into real computer systems while being tested for hacking ability. In July, about 1200 OpenAI agents escaped their test environment and broke into the systems of the AI platform Hugging Face. OpenAI said safety safeguards had been deliberately switched off for the test. In August, it announced it would slow development of its models and paused one stage of its training for two weeks. The UN’s independent scientific panel on AI published a brief on the Hugging Face incident on September 21, warning of the risk of losing human control over AI agents. Anthropic, which makes the Claude chatbot, said on July 30 that its models had gained unauthorised access to three organisations’ systems during cybersecurity tests, while Google said on September 19 that one of its Gemini models had accessed three outside companies’ systems during testing in May. World.title: FBI hacked: Cyber gang claims it has sensitive data of agents and operations
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaCybersecurity FBI hacked: Cyber gang claims it has sensitive data of agents and operations Raphael Satter and AJ Vicens September 24, 2026 — 6:24am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington - FBI data allegedly stolen by the hacking group ShinyHunters carries granular detail about scores of bureau officials’ job assignments, including sensitive work against Chinese spies, Russian intelligence, drug cartels, and more, Reuters has found. The 5000-line spreadsheet – said by the hackers to represent only a small piece of their claimed two- to-three-terabyte trove – includes names, addresses, telephone numbers, dates of birth, social security numbers, and emergency contact details for what they claimed were thousands of FBI employees. The Department of Justice (DOJ) seal on the J. Edgar Hoover Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) building in Washington. Bloomberg It also includes details of assignments to specific field offices and, in some cases, to units engaged in high-stakes intelligence, security, or counterespionage work. In a statement, the FBI said it was aware of “a cyber-criminal enterprise group claiming a compromise of the FBIJobs.gov portal and alleged impact to FBI employee personally identifiable information”.



The bureau said the cause of the breach was still undetermined, but that it was “actively and aggressively investigating the matter.” Related Article Updated

Trump's White House FBI says it thwarted plot to use explosive drones, snipers to attack White House UFC event The hackers said on Tuesday (Washington time) that they had breached the FBI, stealing data on a large number of current and former FBI employees. ShinyHunters said it is holding the data hostage until the bureau rescinds an unflattering statement about the group issued in May. Former FBI counterintelligence operative Eric O’Neill said the data allegedly stolen by ShinyHunters was “a foreign intelligence service goldmine.” “China would be incredibly interested to know the individuals who are working against it,” said O’Neill, founder of the cybersecurity company Nexasure AI, after his stint at the bureau. He predicted that other hostile intelligence services would be eager to get their hands on the data, along with disgruntled extremists in the United States.



“If I were on that list I would be very concerned,” he said. ShinyHunters said in a statement on Wednesday that it was trying to keep the personnel information from circulating widely in the meantime. “If the 5000 sample data records leak, it’s not because of us,” the group said. Although Reuters has not been able to authenticate the entire spreadsheet, it has been able to individually verify the details of more than 22 people by cross-referencing information in the hacked data with credit records and previous data leaks carried by the dark web intelligence platform District 4 Labs. The FBI building in Washington. The bureau said the cause of the security breach was still undetermined Bloomberg Some of the assignment details in the ShinyHunters’ data are indistinguishable from what employees themselves might say publicly, noting agents at field offices in Baltimore or Newark, New Jersey, for example.



But in some cases, the data referred to FBI units or initiatives that were sensitive or whose existence has not previously been disclosed. The data names 14 staffers focused on China-related matters, including members of the “China criminal enterprise unit,” the “China tech transfer analysis unit,” and the “China intelligence

section.” Nine others are listed as serving in Russia-related roles, including two in the “Russia Operations Section” and one working on “Russia Critical Infra and Tech Threat.” Three people are listed as working in Iran- or Hezbollah-focused intelligence roles. ‘You don’t have to look far to find examples of undercover agents being harmed when their cover is blown.’ Trevor Hilligoss, chief intelligence officer for cybersecurity company SpyCloud Eighteen others are listed as working with “data intercept” or “telecom intercept” technologies, or in the FBI’s “clandestine technical operations” unit, or its “covert access section,” or in video, audio, or electronic surveillance roles.



A further 11 FBI staffers are listed as working in HUMINT, or human intelligence, jobs, including several listed as working in the “Humint program management section.” Related Article Cybersecurity Ransom ‘paid’ to hackers who crippled online learning in Australia Trevor Hilligoss, a former Army investigator who worked with the FBI, said the information tying specific named people to human intelligence work was particularly troubling. “You don’t have to look far to find examples of undercover agents being harmed when their cover is blown,” he said. Hilligoss, now the chief intelligence officer for cybersecurity company SpyCloud, said his concerns were

heightened by the inclusion of emergency contacts – often spouses or children – “who may have less operational security knowledge than their relative that works in a sensitive field.”



Reuters could not verify that all the job assignments were authentic or up-to-date, but it was able to match the career details or titles of eight people whose data was leaked to information in court filings, news articles, or public profiles on LinkedIn or to online posts on sites such as Instagram. ShinyHunters previously claimed credit for the purported theft of millions of business records from video game developer Rockstar Games, the maker of Grand Theft Auto, and an intrusion focused on the education tool Canvas that ⁠triggered widespread ​disruption across US schools. In May, the FBI said ShinyHunters sometimes used “exaggerated claims of access to sensitive or personal information to prompt payment from victims.” ShinyHunters said its “threats and claims are very real”, adding that the FBI’s statement was why it targeted the bureau. Reuters has not been able to verify what else the hackers are holding. ShinyHunters previously said they obtained files related to the vetting of employees and applicants, the contracting of background investigations, and agents’ sensitive medical data, but said on Wednesday it would not release any further data.



O’Neill, the former FBI operative, cautioned against drawing conclusions about what the hackers hold. “They’re really trying to scare the hell out of the FBI,” he noted. Reuters

World.content:
BusinessCompaniesElectric vehicles Chinese carmaker’s new EV battery will charge in under five minutes Tom Haynes September 24, 2026 — 6:18am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Volvo’s Chinese owner has unveiled an electric car battery that can charge in just four-and-a-half minutes. Geely said the time needed for its new battery to go from 10 per cent to 70 per cent, an industry benchmark for a reasonable charge, was the fastest in the industry. Geely tested the battery on a Zeekr 001 model. The company said the time needed for its new battery to go from 10 per cent to 70 per cent, an industry benchmark for a reasonable charge, was the fastest in the industry. Getty It has shaved 20 seconds off the next best battery, developed by China’s biggest electric carmaker BYD, which has also been pouring money into so-called “flash charging”. BYD unveiled a system earlier this year capable of charging a battery from 10 per cent to 97 per cent in nine minutes, and announced plans for 90,000 charging stations by 2028.



Geely said its new system could charge a battery from 10 per cent to 97 per cent in eight minutes and 40 seconds, using a charger capable of delivering up to 2.2 megawatts (MW) of power. Related Article Energy EVs are taking over as Australians flee the bowser. What happens next? The one-upmanship underlines the pace of innovation among Chinese carmakers in the cut-throat EV market. Zhang Dewang, a Geely executive, said the speed of charging was “approaching the physical limit”. “The marginal gains from pursuing even faster speeds in the future will become increasingly small,” he told Reuters at a launch event in China.



Geely has bested BYD by using a higher voltage system. Its new battery uses an 800-volt electrical system and the higher voltage allows more electricity to be pushed into the battery at once, helping to cut charging times. The 2.2 MW peak output is also above the power available from most conventional public chargers. Tesla’s latest Supercharger technology, for example, is rated at up to 500 kilowatts, making Geely’s claimed peak power more than four times as high. Geely has bested BYD by using a higher voltage system. Its new battery uses an 800-volt electrical system and the higher voltage allows more electricity to be pushed into the battery at once, helping to cut charging times. Getty Images The Galaxy E5, an electric SUV, will be the first Geely model to use the new technology when it goes on sale in China later this year. Geely, which also owns Lotus and has stakes in Polestar, is among the Chinese groups expanding rapidly overseas. It sold 1.42 million vehicles in the first half of this year and has raised its target for exports to 920,000 vehicles in 2026.



In the UK, Geely currently sells its EX5 electric SUV and the Starray EM-i hybrid. The new Galaxy E5 is a Chinese-market model and is not currently sold in Britain, although the E5 is badged as the EX5 for the UK market. Related Article Energy ‘The shift is now absolute’: China’s BYD says Australia just passed its EV tipping point China produced almost 75 per cent of the world’s electric cars last year, while exports of Chinese-made EVs more than doubled to a record 2.5 million vehicles. Chinese-made EV sales in Europe also jumped by almost 50 per cent in 2025. The charging battle is part of a wider shift in the Chinese car industry, where manufacturers are now competing on battery range, charging speeds and driver-assistance technology rather than simply price. World.title: Seismic switcheroo: Peter V’landys quits Racing NSW for unprecedented NRL job
World.content:
Analysis NationalNRL 2026 Seismic switcheroo: Peter V’landys quits Racing NSW for unprecedented NRL job Bevan Shields September 24, 2026 — 5:45am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

As far as soft landings go, the one Peter V’landys has just orchestrated for himself is about as good as they come. The 66-year-old sporting administrator – easily one of the most powerful figures in Australian sport, media and politics – has resigned as chief executive of Racing NSW following 22 years at the helm. V’landys is due to be unveiled as the NRL’s new executive chairman – an unprecedented role for the game and the man himself. Seismic? Yes. Surprising? It shouldn’t be. This has been in the works for a good six months. The catalyst for the switcheroo was the mid-season departure of Andrew Abdo as NRL chief executive. The big-vision loving V’landys and the details-focused Abdo and were a good yin and yang, but the latter jumped at the chance to become Tennis Australia boss and have a breather from his unpredictable and demanding chairman. Peter V’landys has dominated Sydney’s racing scene for more than two decades. Tim Bauer A worldwide search would have ordinarily found a new chief executive to lead the booming NRL into the 2030s. But wouldn’t you know it, the search ended up settling on V’landys, who will combine the role with his existing duties as Australian Rugby League Commission chairman. There is talk he may be paid up to $3 million a year – roughly double what Abdo was banking.



V’landys has told friends he feels a genuine emotional pull about leaving Racing NSW. Fair enough. While things have become tricky of late – V’landys and the organisation found themselves in far too many legal and political scraps – his impact on the industry is undeniable. “He will go down as one of the best, if not the best, sporting administrators in Australian history,” says champion trainer Chris Waller. “When he came in he promised to double the prize money and introduce this and that, and everyone thought ‘what a load of nonsense’. And I was very sceptical. But everything he said, he did. Sure, he may have made a few mistakes over the time, but overall his impact has been quite amazing.” Peter V’landys during a trip to Royal Ascot in 2022. Getty The best indicator of V’landys’ success in pulling NSW racing out of its doldrums is the ferocious way in which Victorian racing authorities responded to new events in Sydney like The Everest, now the world’s richest turf race and attracting a new generation of racegoers. The stuffy Melbourne establishment still hates it – something V’landys has taken great delight in.



His willingness to go to court to secure a 1.5 per cent tax on online wagering operators that take bets on races in NSW has delivered annual fees of at least $150 million. The windfall allowed V’landys to act as a generous benefactor, throwing cash around like confetti and winning friends and allies in the process. Racing NSW says V’landys’ initiatives as chief executive since 2004 have delivered $3.5 billion in new funding, with total new recurring annual revenues nudging the $375 million mark. Saturday metropolitan prize money is up from $45,000 in 2004 to $160,000 now, and country TAB prizes up from $5000 to $27,000. V’landys’ right-hand man, chief operating officer Graeme Hinton, is in the box seat to take over. V’landys also secured a big federal government rescue package during the equine influenza outbreak of 2007. Related Article Exclusive

NRL grand final Fallout with star leaves NRL with no pre-game entertainment for grand final But it has not all been sunshine and rainbows. V’landys arguably stayed too long. He was sometimes too eager for a fight. There has been much speculation about what a review into the laws governing racing in NSW, led by former health minister Brad Hazzard, might say. The report is sitting on the government’s desk. What’s in it depends on who you ask. Some believe Hazzard has stuck to his brief and merely scrutinised the Thoroughbred Racing Act. Others reckon it could make some pointy observations about corporate culture at Racing NSW. V’landys is known to be a bit of a tyrant in the office and a notorious cheapskate. Staff at the racing regulator required permission to print a colour photocopy, and catching cabs was banned if a meeting venue was within the CBD.



That approach has made its way to the NRL’s Sydney headquarters, with biscuits in the kitchen cut back and indoor pot plants banished and replaced with footballs. “You don’t have to water the footballs,” he explained. Staff who had great affection for Abdo are much more cautious about how V’landys does business. As chair of the game, his big thinking was chaotic but at least good fun. As a nuts and bolts manager, some say he is just chaotic. V’landys’ critics believe the embarrassing collapse of talks with singer Tones and I over a performance for the league’s October 4 grand final could be a sign of things to come. The debacle means there will be no major act at the game. The singer’s management says an offer was only presented on September 5 – one month before the big day. Once V’landys gets his racing farewell out of the road on Thursday morning, he and the ARLC commission will need to start answering questions about how this NRL leadership experiment is going to work. Former NRL chief executive Andrew Abdo and ARL Commission chairman Peter V’landys. Nick Moir V’landys once thought the idea was a shocker. Amid speculation in 2020 that V’landys might have a stab at combining the chief executive and chairman roles, he said: “There needs to be a segregation between the board and management. I’ve always believed in proper corporate governance, so it would be hypocritical to do anything other than that.”



Putting so much power in the hands of one man provides real potential for things to go wrong. What are the safeguards? Appointing a couple of commissioners to mediate in disputes with internal or external stakeholders isn’t enough – particularly when most of the members of the commission are diehard V’landys loyalists. He is likely to be appointed on a contract of three years, which would take him close to 70 years of age. V’landys may have faults, but a lack of energy and focus on work isn’t one of them. Once he’s landed in the big chair at Driver Avenue, he might be able to stay as long as he likes. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.
